QP2309 Q2 - Recognized Organizations, the other side of how an Administration reaches a ship it does not board

blocks.h: 1. What the goal says, and what equality means on a ship

blocks.p: The United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development sets seventeen goals, and the one this stem quotes is to achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls. Applied to a ship, that does not mean pretending the ship is a neutral place. It means that a seafarer's access to the job, to training, to promotion and to a safe working and living environment does not depend on her sex - and, because a ship is also a home, that the accommodation, the sanitary arrangements, the medical provision and the standards of behaviour on board are designed for a mixed crew rather than merely tolerated by a minority within it.

Two distinctions carry the rest of the answer. First, equality of opportunity is not equality of outcome: the obligation is to remove barriers, not to guarantee proportions. Second, and this is what the examiner is really testing, gender balance is an aspiration but non-discrimination is already law. Under the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 each Member must satisfy itself that its law respects the fundamental right to the elimination of discrimination in respect of employment and occupation, and every seafarer has the right to a safe and secure workplace and to decent working and living conditions. Those obligations reach the ship whether or not any programme exists.

ul: It is a matter of right, not of favour. Excluding half the population from a profession is discrimination in respect of employment and occupation, which the Convention's fundamental rights article requires each Member to eliminate. That reason is first and it is sufficient on its own.

The industry needs the people. Shipping recruits officers from a shrinking pool and competes with shore employment offering a normal domestic life. A profession that draws from half its potential workforce is choosing to worsen its own shortage.

Selecting from a wider pool raises quality. If the best candidate for a fourth engineer's berth is excluded before she applies, the berth goes to someone less good. That follows from restricting the field and holds regardless of any argument about aptitude.

Mixed teams manage risk differently. A crew sharing one background tends to share its blind spots, and the human-element failures behind most casualties - unchallenged authority, poor communication, reluctance to speak up - are exactly those a more varied team is less prone to. Put this as diversity of perspective, never as a claim about the qualities of either sex.
Retention. Recruiting women and losing them within a contract or two costs more than not recruiting them. Retention is decided by conditions on board, which is what limb (c) is about.

It is a commercial expectation. Charterers, financiers, insurers and terminals increasingly ask about the social element of an operator's practice, so a policy that cannot be evidenced is a commercial exposure as well as an ethical one.

It raises the profession's own standards. Accommodation, sanitary arrangements, protective equipment sizing, medical provision and shipboard behaviour improve for everyone once they are designed for a mixed crew instead of assumed for a single one.

blocks.p: One caution is worth a mark in itself: the case does not need exaggerating. Quoted figures for the proportion of women in the seafaring workforce vary considerably between sources. This answer quotes none, because an unsourced statistic in a script is a liability and the argument above stands without one.

blocks.h: 3. (b) What the International Maritime Organization does

blocks.p: The Organization's work here is programme work rather than regulation. There is no convention on gender and no ship is certified for it. What the Organization does, through its technical cooperation function, is build the supply of qualified women and make the profession visible to them:

ul: a long-standing women in maritime programme under the Integrated Technical Cooperation Programme, directed at access to maritime training and to posts in maritime administrations;
support for regional women in maritime associations, giving a professional network across administrations and industry in each region;
fellowships and reserved places for women at the Organization's own academic institutions, including the World Maritime University and the International Maritime Law Institute;
a World Maritime Day theme devoted to women in the maritime community, used to put the subject before Member States and industry for a full year;

gender-parity mechanisms written into ordinary technical programmes - the most durable form, because it does not depend on a separate initiative surviving. The freshest worked example at this sitting comes from an instrument with nothing to do with gender: the capacity-building programme described in the appendix to the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, adopted on 7 July 2023, provides for two trainees, one female and one male, to go on to a World Maritime University scholarship;
the same Strategy's insistence that the human element and the impact on seafarers be addressed in the energy transition - which is where the next generation of shipboard jobs is being created.

blocks.p: What is deliberately not said: no resolution number is given for any of this. The Organization has adopted instruments touching the subject, but no licensed text of one is held for this answer, and inventing a number to look authoritative is exactly the error that costs marks in the oral.

blocks.h: 4. (b) What the Government of India does

blocks.p: India's maritime administration is the Directorate General of Shipping, acting under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, which is the statute in force at this sitting. Its instruments are the ordinary administrative ones - training and examination rules, certification requirements, approval of maritime training institutes, and notices to industry - and the measures relevant here work at that level:

ul: Admission to training on the same terms. Women are admitted to approved Indian maritime training institutes and to the pre-sea and post-sea courses leading to certificates of competency, in the engineering stream as well as the nautical one.

Certification and service in all departments and ranks. Eligibility for a certificate of competency and for shipboard service is not restricted by sex, so there is no legal barrier to a woman holding the Chief Engineer's certificate this very examination leads to.

Conditions attached to institute approval. The approval regime is the practical lever: separate accommodation and sanitary facilities, safeguarding requirements and complaint mechanisms are conditions of running a course, not aspirations.

Training-berth availability. The recurring obstacle for an Indian cadet is not admission but obtaining a training berth, and administrative and industry pressure on owners to provide them is where policy meets reality.

Implementation of the Maritime Labour Convention through national law. India's ratification carries the Article III and Article IV obligations into the domestic regime, which is what gives a woman seafarer on an Indian ship an enforceable position rather than a policy statement.
Promotion and visibility - recognition of women officers, participation in the regional women in maritime association, and encouragement of owners to recruit and retain women.

blocks.p: Again, no circular, rule, notice or scheme number is asserted. The administration issues numbered instruments; a candidate who has one in front of him should cite it, and one who does not should describe the measure and say what it does. That scores. Inventing a number does not.

blocks.h: 5. What already binds the ship, before any initiative

blocks.p: Limb (c) becomes a management answer rather than a set of good intentions the moment it is anchored on obligations that already exist. Before any programme reaches the gangway the Chief Engineer is working to Article IV - a safe and secure workplace and decent living conditions; Standard A3.1 - the individual sleeping room on ships other than passenger ships, and separate sanitary facilities; Regulation 5.1.5 and Standard A5.1.5 - an on-board complaint procedure, an impartial adviser, a right of direct complaint to the master and to the competent authority, and an express prohibition on victimizing a complainant; and Guideline B4.3.1, which places harassment within occupational safety and health.

blocks.h: 6. (c) As Chief Engineer - the physical ship

ul: Accommodation and sanitary arrangements. Confirm before she joins that the individual cabin the Convention requires is actually allocated and lockable and that private, secure sanitary facilities exist. If the arrangement depends on sharing, that is my problem to solve before arrival, not hers to raise afterwards.

Protective equipment that fits. Boiler suits, gloves, safety shoes, harnesses, breathing apparatus face masks and immersion suits stocked in the full range of sizes. Ill-fitting equipment is a direct safety failure, and it is the most visible and most easily corrected signal that a ship was not expecting her.

Workshop and machinery-space practicalities. Lifting aids and correct tooling used as routine rather than as a concession, so that no job in the engine room is done by main force alone. That is good practice for every engineer and it removes the argument before it is made.
Medical provision. Ensure the medical locker and the ship's medical arrangements match the crew actually carried, and that confidentiality in medical matters is real.
Safety equipment sizing proved in drills, not assumed from the inventory.

blocks.h: 7. (c) As Chief Engineer - the allocation of work

ul: Allocate work by rank and competence and by nothing else. The most damaging thing a Chief Engineer can do is protect a woman engineer from the dirty or heavy jobs. It looks like consideration; it is exclusion, it destroys her credibility with the ratings, and it leaves her under-prepared for her next certificate.
Give the same watch and project responsibility - the same overhauls, the same faults to diagnose, the same ownership of a survey item - and hold it to the same standard.
Appraise honestly. Feedback withheld for fear of appearing harsh is the quiet way careers end. She is entitled to the same correction as anyone else and to the same record of her competence.

Mentor, and be seen to. A junior who is the only woman on board has no peer to ask. Planned time on machinery and on certificate preparation costs little and is what converts recruitment into retention.
Include her in the department's decisions - planned maintenance, the repair list, the pre-arrival plan - so that authority follows the rank rather than the individual.
Watch the workload in the hours-of-rest records. A junior given every awkward job, or excluded from every desirable one, shows up there before she says anything.

blocks.h: 8. (c) As Chief Engineer - behaviour, complaints and accountability

ul: Set the standard explicitly and early. At the departmental meeting on joining, state what is expected and what will not be tolerated - as an instruction from the head of department, not as a policy reading. The standard on a ship is whatever the senior officers visibly accept.
Deal with the first incident, however small. A remark left uncorrected is a permission. Correcting it once, immediately and privately, prevents almost everything that would otherwise follow.

Make the complaint route real. Ensure every member of the department holds the on-board complaint procedure, knows who the impartial adviser is, and knows that the right to go to the master or to the competent authority is not affected by raising it with me first.

Protect the complainant. Victimization is prohibited under the Convention. If a complaint is raised, nothing may change in her work allocation, her appraisal or her treatment because of it - and I must be seen to ensure it.
Treat harassment as an occupational safety and health matter, which is what the Convention's own guideline makes it: risk-assess it, take it to the safety committee, record it like any other hazard.

Use the safety management system. Report and record under the SMS so the Company and the designated person see the pattern, and so the response does not depend on which Chief Engineer happens to be aboard.
Brief the reliefs. A standard that survives one contract and lapses at the next is not a standard. Hand over the department's expectations as deliberately as the machinery condition.
Be careful with visibility. Singling someone out as an example isolates as effectively as ignoring her. The objective is that within a few weeks she is simply the fourth engineer.

blocks.p: The honest summary, and a good closing line: the initiatives in limb (b) can only bring a woman to the gangway. Whether she stays in the profession is decided almost entirely by what happens in the six months after she walks up it - and in the engine room, that is decided by the Chief Engineer.

The examiner has printed three limbs and an instruction to introduce the subject briefly, so four blocks of marks are already allocated and the order is fixed. Candidates lose marks here in two predictable ways: they write an essay on why diversity is good and never reach limb (c), or they treat limb (c) as a list of pieties. The structure above prevents both. Section 1 is the brief introduction the stem asks for and no more. Section 2 answers (a) as seven separately countable propositions rather than one argument. Sections 3 and 4 split (b) by actor, because the stem names two of them and an answer that blurs the Organization's programme work into the Indian administration's statutory work has answered half a question twice.

Section 5 is the section that separates a management answer from a well-meaning one. Anchoring limb (c) on obligations that already bind the ship converts everything after it from opinion into duty, and it is where the Convention's article and standard numbers earn their marks. Sections 6 to 8 then answer (c) in the order the Chief Engineer actually meets the problem - the ship before she arrives, the work once she is aboard, and the behaviour that decides whether she stays.

ul: Quoting a percentage for women in the seafaring workforce. The figures vary widely between sources and an examiner who knows a different one will mark it wrong. The argument does not need it.
Inventing a resolution number, circular number or scheme name to look authoritative. Describing what a measure does scores; a wrong number does not, and it invites an oral question you cannot answer.

Arguing that women bring particular qualities - better communication, more caution. It is unnecessary, it is a claim about sex rather than about diversity of perspective, and it is easy to attack. Argue from the wider pool and from varied perspective instead.
Writing limb (c) as policy statements. The examiner asked what you would do, so every proposition should be an action a Chief Engineer can actually take on a ship.
Protecting her from heavy or dirty work and presenting it as consideration. This is the single most common well-intentioned error in the answer and it deserves to be named as an error.
Running out of time. Limb (c) carries the applied marks and is the part most candidates leave until there are ten minutes left.
The stem is not a grammatical sentence. It quotes the goal's title without quotation marks. Do not spend time on it and do not correct it; open by naming the goal and move on.
Equality of opportunity versus equality of outcome. An answer that promises proportions has claimed something no obligation requires. Say that the duty is to remove barriers.
Aspiration versus law. Gender balance is an aspiration; non-discrimination is a binding obligation. Candidates who miss this write the whole answer in the language of policy and never cite anything.

Two actors in limb (b). The Organization and the Government of India do different things by different means - programme work under technical cooperation, and administration under a national statute. Answer them separately.
The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 governs this sitting. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026, thirty months after this paper. Do not import it.
The 2022 amendments to the Convention are not in force at this sitting - they enter force 23 December 2024. Work from the Convention as amended through the 2018 set.
Which article of the Maritime Labour Convention makes non-discrimination a fundamental right, and what does it require of a Member?
What does Standard A3.1 require about sleeping rooms, and does it differ on a passenger ship?
A rating makes a remark to the fourth engineer in the workshop. What do you do, and when?
She raises a complaint against the second engineer. Walk me through the on-board complaint procedure and tell me what protection she has.
Who is the impartial adviser, and can she complain to anyone outside the ship?
Your predecessor kept her off the purifier overhauls to be kind. What is wrong with that, and what will you do about it?
What would you check before she joins, and who is responsible if the cabin is not right?

blocks.p: The route is GOAL - WHY - IMO - INDIA - LAW - SHIP - WORK - PEOPLE. The first is the introduction, the second is limb (a), the third and fourth are limb (b), and the last four are limb (c) with the binding obligations placed first so that everything after them is a duty rather than an intention. If time runs short, the four limb-(c) sections compress to their opening bold phrases and still score, because each is a separate proposition.

ul: MLC 2006 Article III(d) - elimination of discrimination in respect of employment and occupation; the fundamental right the whole answer rests on.
MLC 2006 Article IV - safe and secure workplace; decent working and living conditions.
MLC 2006 Standard A3.1 - accommodation and sanitary facilities; the individual sleeping room on ships other than passenger ships.
MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.5 / Standard A5.1.5 - on-board complaint procedure, impartial adviser, direct complaint, prohibition on victimization.
MLC 2006 Guideline B4.3.1 - occupational safety and health; the route by which harassment is handled as a hazard.
UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (2015) - the framework the stem invokes.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - the Indian statute in force at this sitting; the source of training, certification and institute-approval powers.
2023 IMO GHG Strategy, adopted 7 July 2023 - appendix capacity-building programme, used only as a worked example of gender parity built into an ordinary technical programme.
No workforce statistic is given. Published figures differ materially between sources and MIW holds no licensed copy of any of them.
No Assembly resolution is cited for the Organization's gender work. Instruments touching the subject exist; MIW holds no licensed text and will not assert a number it has not read.
No Indian instrument number is cited. The Directorate General of Shipping issues numbered orders and circulars; none is held for this subject, so each measure is described by its effect.

The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy is cited by identity and adoption date only. The corpus holds the resolution but records its title-page identity confirmation as blocking for citation, so no text is quoted from it.
The seven propositions in limb (a) are an argued case, not a finding of fact, and are offered as such.

questions.understand_first: A ship is not only a place of work; it is also where the crew live for months at a time, with no way of going home at the end of a shift. That single fact is what makes this subject different from the same subject ashore. If a workplace is unwelcoming you can leave it at five o'clock. If a ship is, you cannot. So the question splits naturally into two halves that people often blur together. One half is about getting in - whether a woman can train, qualify, find a berth and be promoted on the same terms as anyone else. Organisations and governments work on this half, and they do it by opening training, funding places, building professional networks and leaning on owners to provide berths. The other half is about staying, and almost none of it is decided ashore. It is decided by whether the cabin locks, whether the overalls fit, whether she gets the interesting jobs or the safe ones, and whether the first crude remark is corrected or allowed to stand. The head of department decides all four. There is also a distinction worth holding on to, because the examiner is testing it: wanting more women at sea is an ambition, but not discriminating against them is already an obligation. The first has no legal force and the second does, and an answer that only ever speaks in the language of ambition never reaches the part that binds the ship.
questions.memory_cue: GOAL - WHY - IMO - INDIA - LAW - SHIP - WORK - PEOPLE (1 to 8). The middle two are limb (b)'s two actors and the last three are limb (c); step 5 is the hinge that turns intentions into duties.

retrieval_cards.answer: Balance is an aspiration with no legal force. Non-discrimination is a binding obligation: under MLC 2006 Article III(d) each Member must satisfy itself that its law respects the fundamental right to elimination of discrimination in employment and occupation. An answer written only in the language of aspiration never cites anything.

retrieval_cards.answer: Article IV - safe and secure workplace and decent living conditions. retrieval_cards.answer: Keeping her off the dirty or heavy jobs. It looks like consideration but it is exclusion: it destroys her credibility with the ratings and leaves her under-prepared for her next certificate. Allocate work by rank and competence and by nothing else.

retrieval_cards.answer: The Organization does programme work under technical cooperation - training access, regional associations, fellowships, a World Maritime Day theme, parity built into ordinary programmes. There is no convention on gender. retrieval_cards.prompt: What two things should you refuse to write in this answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: A percentage for women in the seafaring workforce, because published figures differ widely and an examiner with another one marks it wrong; and any resolution, circular or scheme number you have not actually read. Describe what the measure does instead - that scores, and a wrong number invites an oral question you cannot answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A rating makes a crude remark to the fourth engineer in the workshop. What do you do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Correct it once, immediately and privately - a remark left uncorrected is a permission, and dealing with the first incident prevents almost everything that follows. Then record it under the safety management system so the Company and the designated person see the pattern, and so the response does not depend on which Chief Engineer is aboard.

The applied limb is the discriminator: any candidate can argue that diversity is good, and few can say what they would check before she joins.

blocks.p: A Recognized Organization is an organization to which a flag Administration has delegated authority to carry out statutory survey and certification work on its behalf - most commonly, but not necessarily, a classification society.

Two points carry the marks in the definition. First, the delegation is of function, not of responsibility: the Administration remains responsible for the statutory certification of its ships and cannot answer a casualty by pointing at its RO. Second, classification society and Recognized Organization are not synonyms. A society classes ships under its own rules as a commercial matter; it becomes an RO only where an Administration has delegated statutory work to it, only to the extent of that delegation, and only for that flag. The same society may be an RO for one flag and not for another, and may hold different scopes from different flags. One surveyor attending one ship may therefore be acting in two distinct capacities during the same visit - as class, and as the flag State.

blocks.h: 2. Recognition and authorization are two separate acts

blocks.p: The Code turns on a distinction candidates routinely blur, and stating it early makes the rest of the answer coherent. Recognition is the flag State's assessment of an organization against the Code's mandatory requirements. Authorization is the separate and later act of delegating specified statutory functions to an organization that is already recognized. It follows that an organization may be recognized and still not authorized for a particular ship type or a particular convention, and that capability is assessed function by function rather than once and for all. The enabling provision expressly forbids a flag State to authorize functions beyond an RO's capabilities.

blocks.h: 3. The RO Code, and how a code becomes binding

blocks.p: The Code for Recognized Organizations was adopted by resolution MSC.349(92) of 21 June 2013 and by resolution MEPC.237(65). Its purpose is to provide a harmonised, transparent and independent international standard against which organizations are assessed for recognition and authorization, together with guidelines for flag State oversight - so that a delegation is measured against one international benchmark instead of each flag's own judgement. Before it, the criteria were spread across Assembly resolutions and applied unevenly.

It was made mandatory from 1 January 2015 by resolutions MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92) and MEPC.238(65), which amended SOLAS, MARPOL Annexes I and II and the 1988 Load Line Protocol; the SOLAS hook is regulation XI-1/1. Recognise the technique, because it is worth a mark in the oral: a code is drafted as a standard and then made binding by amending the conventions that refer to it - exactly as the ISM Code and the III Code were.

blocks.h: 4. Salient feature - three parts, and which of them bind

ul: Part 1 - general provisions: purpose, definitions, application, the power to delegate, and the duty to notify the Organization.
Part 2 - mandatory requirements, on the organization and on the flag State alike.
Part 3 - guidelines for flag State oversight of ROs.
Parts 1 and 2 are mandatory; Part 3 is recommendatory. This is the single most examinable fact about the Code's structure and it is often got wrong.

blocks.p: The consequence is visible in the drafting: Part 2 says 'shall' and Part 3 says 'should'. The adopting resolution recommends Governments to use Part 3 as a basis for their standards unless their national requirements provide at least an equivalent degree of safety - which is why flag States' oversight programmes differ in form while converging in substance. The Code's scope paragraph establishes four things, and they map onto this question exactly: what an organization must satisfy to be recognized; what an RO must satisfy when performing the work; what flag States must do when authorizing; and guidance on oversight.

blocks.h: 5. Salient feature - what the organization itself must satisfy

blocks.p: Part 2 opens with the controlling proposition that delegation is subject to confirmation of the organization's capability to deliver high standards of service and to comply with the Code and applicable national legislation. The demonstration is the organization's; the confirmation is the flag State's. The assessment then runs through:

ul: General requirements - legal personality, technical, managerial and research capability, a qualified surveyor and auditor cadre, a code of ethics, and independence.

Management and organization - a documented quality, safety and pollution-prevention policy, a quality manual, control of documents and records, organizational structure, communication internally, with the flag State and between ROs, and management review.
Resources - personnel, infrastructure and work environment adequate to the tasks assigned.
Processes - design and development control, control of service provision, subcontracting and service suppliers, control of measuring devices, and a complaints and appeals process.
Performance measurement - internal audit, vertical contract audit, and control of non-conformities including statutory deficiencies.

Certification of the quality management system - a system no less effective than the ISO 9000 series, periodically assessed and certified by a qualified body accredited by a body signatory to the International Accreditation Forum arrangement and independent of the ROs and their associations.

blocks.p: Two of these deserve naming. Independence is the head the Code is really defending, because the structural weakness of the whole arrangement is that the body surveying the ship is paid by the owner of it; the revenue-dependence rule and the prohibition on certifying what you designed, supplied or maintain are the direct answer. And the vertical contract audit is what distinguishes a real assessment from a paper one, because it follows a single ship's certification right through the organization instead of sampling processes in isolation. Qualification is not left general either: an appendix sets out the training and qualification of plan-approval, survey and audit staff, and another specifies the functions ROs perform by elementary module.

blocks.h: 6. Salient feature - what the flag State must do when it authorizes

blocks.p: This is the only part of the Code that is a procedure rather than a standard, and it is where marks are most often left behind.

ul: Rest the delegation on its conventional basis - SOLAS regulation I/6, Load Lines article 13, MARPOL Annex I regulation 6, MARPOL Annex II regulation 8 and TONNAGE article 6 - and only for ships entitled to fly its flag.

Specify the authority conferred. The word to underline is specify: a general authorization to 'act on our behalf' does not satisfy the Code. Scope is written down function by function and convention by convention, and it must cover the unglamorous end too - corrective actions and the withdrawal or cancellation of certificates. A flag State that has not said who may withdraw a certificate has not finished authorizing.

Make a formal written agreement. An appendix sets out its minimum elements: application and purpose; general conditions; execution of the functions, including general and special authorization and cooperation with port States to rectify reported deficiencies; the legal basis of those functions, with interpretations, deviations and equivalent solutions; reporting to the flag State; exchange of information and rule development; and other conditions.

Notify the Organization. The flag State communicates to and deposits with the Secretary-General a list of its ROs together with the specific responsibilities and conditions of the delegated authority. This is what lets a port State know, before it inspects, exactly what the certificate in front of it represents.

blocks.h: 7. How Administrations monitor - the oversight programme

blocks.p: Monitoring is easiest to reproduce as before, during and after the delegation.

Before - assess the organization against Part 2, confirm capability function by function, and reduce the delegation to a written agreement defining scope and limits, applicable national law and interpretations, the instructions to be followed where a ship is found unfit to proceed to sea, and the records to be kept.
During - Part 3 supplies four mechanisms, and they should be given as such:

ul: Supervision of the delegated duties, whose common thread is access: to the RO's quality management system documentation, to its internal instructions, circulars and guidelines, to its documentation relevant to the flag State's fleet, to cooperation with the flag State's own inspection work, and to information and statistics such as damage and casualties relevant to that fleet. Oversight is impossible if the flag State sees only the certificates the RO chose to issue.

A system to ensure the adequacy of the statutory work - procedures for communication and for reporting by the RO and the processing of those reports; additional ship inspections by the flag State; technical consultation between ROs where certificate validity may be affected; acceptance of the RO's independent QMS certification; and verification of the statutory work itself.

Auditing. The flag State should satisfy itself that the RO has an effective quality management system and may rely upon audits carried out by an accredited certification body. That permission is what makes oversight affordable, and it is precisely why the certifying body must be accredited and independent. The auditor advances three principles - ethical conduct, fair presentation (including reporting significant obstacles and unresolved diverging opinions) and due professional care.

Managing the programme - objectives and extent scaled to the size, complexity and location of the authorizations; responsibilities, resources, procedures and records; and periodic monitoring and review of the programme itself. The flag State's own additional ship inspections sit inside this programme, not beside it: inspecting a sample of the RO's ships is one monitoring activity, not a substitute for oversight.

blocks.h: 8. Performance indicators, and the duty that cannot be delegated

blocks.p: The stem asks how Administrations monitor, and monitoring without measurement is inspection. The Code offers indicators for evaluating an RO's performance: port State performance of the RO; the results of its internal audits; the results of third-party quality management system audits; the results of previous performance monitoring; and the condition and compliance of the ships it surveys and certifies.

Where a shortfall is found, the response runs along the authorization that was granted. Because the scope was specified, it can be narrowed - by ship type, by convention, by function - as readily as suspended or withdrawn, and corrective action can be required under the written agreement. Because the RO's reporting duties are conditions of the authorization rather than courtesies, a failure to report a detainable deficiency or a withdrawal of class is itself a compliance failure and not merely poor service.

The chain then closes above the Administration, and this is the point that finishes the answer. The flag State's own performance is not unexamined: under the IMO Member State Audit Scheme it is audited against the III Code, whose Part 2 requires an oversight programme for delegated authority, and against the obligations set out in the Assembly's non-exhaustive list - at this sitting resolution A.1157(32). So the RO answers to the Administration and the Administration answers to the Organization.

End on the proposition the whole scheme rests on: the flag State may delegate the work; it cannot delegate the responsibility. The certificates carry its name, the obligation to the other Contracting Governments remains its own, and Part 3 exists because an assessment made on the day of appointment says nothing about the state of the organization five years later.

The stem is three questions in one sentence and the examiner has weighted it at sixteen marks with no internal split. That is a trap in itself: candidates spend the time on the definition, which is worth least, and arrive at monitoring with two lines left. The structure above allots one section to the definition, one to the distinction that makes the rest coherent, three to the Code and three to monitoring - roughly the proportions the three questions deserve.

Note what section 2 is doing. Recognition and authorization are separate acts, and once that is on the page every later point has somewhere to attach: capability is assessed function by function because authorization is function-specific; the scope must be specified because authorization is not general; the delegation can be narrowed rather than withdrawn because it was specified in the first place. A candidate who omits the distinction has to argue each of those separately and usually does not.

The before/during/after framing in section 7 is deliberately not the Code's own section order. It is the order an Administration actually works in, it is far easier to reproduce under time pressure, and it makes the Part 3 mechanisms fall out as a list rather than having to be recalled by number.

ul: Treating 'classification society' and 'Recognized Organization' as the same thing. They are different capacities, and the same society is an RO only for the flags that have delegated to it and only within that delegation.
Saying the Administration delegates its responsibility. It delegates the function. The responsibility stays, and this is the single proposition the examiner most wants to see.
Getting the mandatory boundary wrong. Parts 1 and 2 are mandatory, Part 3 is recommendatory. An answer that makes the oversight guidelines binding has misdescribed the instrument.

Listing the Part 2 headings without saying what the Code is defending. The heads exist to protect independence, and an answer that never identifies that has described the requirements without understanding them.

Answering 'how do Administrations monitor' with 'they audit them'. The question is worth several marks and wants mechanisms - access, reporting, additional inspections, reliance on accredited audits, and a managed programme with indicators.
Spending the marks on the definition. It is the shortest of the three questions and it is worth the least.
Importing 33rd Assembly resolution numbers. See the traps below.

The Assembly obligations list at this sitting is A.1157(32), not A.1187(33). A.1187(33) was adopted 6 December 2023, three months after this paper, and it revoked A.1157(32). Circulating material written for a 2024 or later sitting cites the later number and it is wrong here.
Recognized and authorized are not the same. Expect to be asked whether an RO recognized by a flag may survey any ship of that flag. It may not - only within its specified authorization.

Part 3 is guidance. Expect 'is the flag State obliged to follow Part 3?' The answer is that the resolution recommends it as a basis unless national requirements give at least an equivalent degree of safety.
The quality system certifier must be independent of the ROs and their associations. The obvious wrong answer is that the RO's own association can certify it.
'Specify' is the operative word in authorization. A general authorization does not satisfy the Code, and the scope must extend to withdrawal and cancellation of certificates.
The RO Code is mandatory from 1 January 2015 - not from its adoption in 2013. Adoption and entry into force are different events and this question invites the confusion.
Which resolutions adopted the RO Code, and when did it become mandatory? By what route?
Your ship is classed with a society. Is that society your flag State's RO? How would you find out?
What is a vertical contract audit and why does it tell the flag State more than a process audit?
Who certifies the RO's quality management system, and why can the RO's own association not do it?
Give me three things the written agreement between flag State and RO must cover.
The RO finds a detainable deficiency and does not report it. Is that poor service or a compliance failure?
How does IMO check that the flag State is doing any of this?
Can a flag State narrow an authorization instead of withdrawing it? On what basis?

blocks.p: The route is WHO - TWO ACTS - THE CODE - THREE PARTS - THE ORGANIZATION - THE FLAG STATE - OVERSIGHT - INDICATORS. Within monitoring, hold BEFORE / DURING / AFTER, and within 'during' hold ACCESS - ADEQUACY - AUDIT - PROGRAMME. The closing line is a single sentence worth memorising verbatim: the flag State may delegate the work, it cannot delegate the responsibility.

THE RO CODE ITSELF IS TEMPORALLY STABLE AND NEEDS NO REVERSAL. Adopted by MSC.349(92) and MEPC.237(65) in 2013, mandatory from 1 January 2015, and unchanged in structure between this sitting and both donors. Every Part 2 and Part 3 statement carried from QP2408 Q1 is therefore as true in September 2023 as in August 2024.

questions.understand_first: A flag State promises the rest of the world that its ships meet the conventions, and then has to make good on that promise on ships that are scattered across the planet and hardly ever come home. Almost no administration has surveyors everywhere its ships trade, so it hires organisations that do - normally the classification societies, which already have a global surveying network built for their own commercial work. That is the whole idea, and everything else follows from one uncomfortable feature of it: the organisation doing the checking is paid by the owner being checked. So the rules that govern the arrangement are mostly about keeping that from mattering - the organisation must be genuinely independent, must not certify something it designed or maintains, must run a quality system that somebody unconnected with it certifies, and must open its internal instructions and its files to the flag State rather than handing over only the certificates it chose to issue. There is also a distinction that unlocks the subject. Being judged fit is one thing; being handed a particular job is another, and they happen at different times. An organisation can be assessed as competent overall and still not be permitted to touch a chemical tanker or issue a particular certificate, because the permission is written down job by job. And the thing that never moves, whatever is delegated: the flag State is still the one who answers for the certificate. The work can be handed out. The responsibility cannot.
questions.memory_cue: WHO - TWO ACTS - THE CODE - THREE PARTS - ORGANIZATION - FLAG STATE - OVERSIGHT - INDICATORS (1 to 8). Inside step 7 hold BEFORE / DURING / AFTER, and inside 'during' hold ACCESS - ADEQUACY - AUDIT - PROGRAMME.

points: An organization to which a flag Administration has delegated statutory survey and certification work
Usually but not necessarily a classification society
The delegation is of function, not of responsibility
Class and RO are different capacities - same society, different hats, flag by flag

points: Recognition is assessment against the mandatory requirements
Authorization is the later delegation of specified functions

A harmonised, transparent and independent international standard replacing scattered Assembly criteria
Mandatory from 1 January 2015 by MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92) and MEPC.238(65)
Amending SOLAS, MARPOL Annexes I and II and the 1988 Load Line Protocol; SOLAS XI-1/1 is the hook

Parts 1 and 2 mandatory, Part 3 recommendatory - the most examinable structural fact
Part 2 says shall, Part 3 says should
The resolution recommends Part 3 unless national requirements give at least equivalent safety

points: Demonstration is the organization's, confirmation is the flag State's
General requirements including legal personality, competence, ethics and independence

Independence is the head the Code is really defending

During, mechanism one - ACCESS to the QMS, internal instructions, fleet documentation, casualty statistics
Mechanism two - a system to ensure adequacy: reporting, additional flag State inspections, inter-RO consultation
Mechanism three - auditing, with permission to rely on accredited independent audits; ethical conduct, fair presentation, due professional care
Mechanism four - a managed programme with objectives, resources, records and periodic review

points: Port State performance; internal audit results; third-party QMS audit results; previous monitoring; condition of the ships certified
A specified authorization can be narrowed as readily as withdrawn

quick_revision.recall_15s: An RO does the flag State's statutory work for it. Delegation of function, not responsibility. Recognition (assessed against the Code) is not authorization (specified functions delegated). The Code is MSC.349(92)/MEPC.237(65), mandatory 1 January 2015, in three parts - 1 and 2 mandatory, 3 recommendatory. Monitoring is before / during / after: assess and agree, then access, adequacy, audit, programme, then indicators and the power to narrow or withdraw.
quick_revision.critical_numbers: MSC.349(92) of 21 June 2013 and MEPC.237(65) - adoption. 1 January 2015 - mandatory, by MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92) and MEPC.238(65). SOLAS XI-1/1 - the hook. Three parts, of which two are mandatory. Five RO performance indicators. A.1070(28) - III Code, mandatory 1 January 2016. A.1157(32) - the obligations list at this sitting.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 - the provision that makes the RO Code mandatory. If you remember one citation, remember that adoption in 2013 and mandatory application from 1 January 2015 are two different events joined by that regulation.
quick_revision.major_trap: Citing A.1187(33) for the obligations list. It was adopted 6 December 2023, three months after this sitting, and it revoked A.1157(32). Almost every piece of circulating material is written for a later sitting and carries the wrong number for this paper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Recognized Organization question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 what an RO is; 2 recognition versus authorization; 3 the Code and how it binds; 4 three parts and which are mandatory; 5 what the organization must satisfy; 6 what the flag State must do when authorizing; 7 how it monitors - before, during, after; 8 performance indicators and the undelegable duty.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a Recognized Organization, and give the two points that carry the marks.
retrieval_cards.answer: An organization to which a flag Administration has delegated authority to carry out statutory survey and certification on its behalf, usually a classification society. First, the delegation is of function, not responsibility - the Administration remains answerable. Second, class and RO are different capacities: a society is an RO only for flags that delegated to it and only within that delegation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Recognition or authorization - what is the difference?
retrieval_cards.answer: Recognition is the flag State's assessment of an organization against the Code's mandatory requirements. Authorization is the separate later act of delegating specified statutory functions to an already recognized organization. An organization can be recognized and still not authorized for a particular ship type or convention, and a flag State must not authorize beyond capability.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How did the RO Code become mandatory, and when?
retrieval_cards.answer: Adopted by MSC.349(92) of 21 June 2013 and MEPC.237(65), then made mandatory from 1 January 2015 by MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92) and MEPC.238(65), which amended SOLAS, MARPOL Annexes I and II and the 1988 Load Line Protocol. The SOLAS hook is regulation XI-1/1. Adoption and mandatory application are different events.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the three parts of the RO Code and which bind?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part 1 general provisions; Part 2 mandatory requirements on the organization and on the flag State; Part 3 guidelines for flag State oversight. Parts 1 and 2 are mandatory, Part 3 is recommendatory - Part 2 says shall and Part 3 says should. The resolution recommends Part 3 as a basis unless national requirements give at least equivalent safety.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does an Administration monitor its ROs?
retrieval_cards.answer: Before: assess against Part 2 and reduce the delegation to a written agreement fixing scope and limits. During: access to the RO's quality system, internal instructions and fleet files; a system ensuring adequacy, with RO reporting and additional flag inspections; auditing, with reliance permitted on accredited independent audits; and a managed programme. After: evaluate against performance indicators and narrow, suspend or withdraw.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Assembly resolution is the obligations list at a September 2023 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: A.1157(32). Not A.1187(33) - that was adopted 6 December 2023, three months after the sitting, and it revoked A.1157(32). Study material written for 2024 or later sittings carries the later number and is wrong for this paper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must the body certifying an RO's quality system be independent of the ROs and their associations?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the structural weakness of the whole arrangement is that the organization surveying the ship is paid by the owner of it. Independence is the head the Code is really defending, and self-certification by the industry's own association would defeat it. The certifier must be accredited by a body signatory to the international accreditation arrangement and recognized by the flag State.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three questions printed as one sentence, moving from identity to instrument to supervision. The examiner is testing whether the candidate understands that statutory certification is the flag State's duty performed by somebody else, and whether he knows the instrument that governs the arrangement and the machinery by which the arrangement is policed. The third question is the discriminator: most candidates can define an RO and name the Code, and few can describe oversight as a programme with mechanisms and indicators.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Sixteen marks on the stem with no printed split. The three questions are not equal in weight: the definition is a short answer, the salient features are the bulk of the instrument knowledge, and monitoring carries the applied marks. The answer allots sections 1 and 2 to the definition and the distinction that makes it usable, sections 3 to 6 to the Code, and sections 7 and 8 to monitoring - deliberately giving monitoring more space than its one clause of stem suggests, because it is where the marks are actually earned.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the delegation is of function and not of responsibility. That the Code is named with its adopting resolutions and its mandatory date. That the three-part structure is given with the mandatory boundary correct. That monitoring is answered with real mechanisms rather than the word 'audit'. And that the answer closes on the flag State's own accountability, which is what turns a description into an understanding of the scheme.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: Build on the RO Code itself - Part 1 sections 4 and 5, Part 2 sections 2 to 8 with appendices 1 to 3, and Part 3 sections 4 to 7 - as established in the MIW verification record for QP2408 Q1, which worked through the text section by section. Take the adoption and mandating chain from the QP2401 record. Corroborate against the corpus copy at 03-imo-instruments/RO-Code but do not rest any section number on it alone, its edition being unverified (RQ-25). Add the III Code and the Member State Audit Scheme for the closing accountability chain. Deliberately NOT planned: any quotation from A.1157(32), which is not held.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - The RO Code is stable and needs no reversal at all. The single moving part is the Assembly obligations list, where the donor's A.1187(33) is three months future at this sitting and must be reversed to A.1157(32). That is a small edit with a large consequence, because it is exactly the kind of number a reviewer would 'correct' back to the later resolution.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MEDIUM. Three levels must not be blurred: the Code is an IMO instrument binding through the conventions; the delegation is an act of national law by a flag Administration; and the classification work the same society does is contractual and not statutory at all. An answer that treats an IACS resolution or a class rule as part of the statutory chain has the levels wrong. Where India is concerned the Administration is the Directorate General of Shipping acting under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: 'Salient features' is undefined and could mean the Code's structure, its requirements, or its legal effect; the answer covers all three rather than choosing, because each is separately markable. 'Monitor' is likewise undefined and is taken to include the before-and-after acts of assessment and sanction as well as the during-delegation supervision, since an answer confined to the middle would omit the written agreement and the power to withdraw.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections. Prose for the definition and the distinction, because they are arguments rather than lists. Bulleted lists for the Code's parts, the organization's requirements, the flag State's procedural duties and the oversight mechanisms, so that each is separately countable. A before/during/after frame inside the monitoring section. A single-sentence closing proposition on the undelegable responsibility.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That resolution A.1157(32) is the non-exhaustive list of obligations under instruments relevant to the III Code operative at a September 2023 sitting, A.1187(33) having been adopted 6 December 2023 and having revoked it.
reverify_before_publication.why: This is the one reversal in the question and it is the claim most at risk of being silently undone. Every other paper in the corpus sits after 6 December 2023 and correctly cites A.1187(33), so a reviewer moving between papers will see this number as an error. It is not. The identity and the revocation date come from MIW's own read-at-source records; MIW holds no copy of A.1157(32) itself.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The RO Code section-level content - Part 2 sections 2 to 8, appendices 1 to 3, Part 3 sections 4 to 7 - reproduced here.
reverify_before_publication.why: Carried from the MIW verification record for QP2408 Q1, where it was established against the text. The corpus copy of the Code corroborates but its edition and completeness are unverified (RQ-25), so this is authoritative internal reuse rather than a fresh primary read.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the RO Code was adopted by MSC.349(92) on 21 June 2013 and by MEPC.237(65), and became mandatory on 1 January 2015 by MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92) and MEPC.238(65).
reverify_before_publication.why: Established in the QP2401 record and stable. Recorded because adoption and mandatory application are commonly conflated and the distinction is examinable.

reuse_evidence: TIER D - NEAR PRINTED RECURRENCE, adjudicated by reading both printed stems in full. QP2402-Q5 (February 2024) prints: 'What are the ongoing developments at IMO with respect to the technical and operational measures to be invoked on board ships for combating greenhouse gas emissions from ships? (16)'. This paper prints the identical sentence with two words inserted - 'and market-based' - and the same (16).

QUESTION DELTA: a third class of measure becomes examinable. It is not a cosmetic addition. The technical and operational measures are IN FORCE and can be described as law; the market-based measures at this sitting are NOT ADOPTED and can only be described as a work programme with a deadline. The answer must handle two different kinds of statement, and saying which is which is where the marks are.

DEPTH DONOR FOR THE ADDED LIMB, READ AND USED FOR STRUCTURE ONLY: QP2408-Q4 (August 2024) is a full market-based-measures question. Its analytical categories - levy, emissions trading, feebate - are verified and transfer. Its FACTUAL ANCHORS DO NOT: it is built on MEPC 81, which concluded 22 March 2024, six months after this sitting, and it correctly states for its own sitting that the EU scheme had applied to shipping from 1 January 2024. Both are reversed here. See temporal_review.

READ AND CLASSIFIED NEAR FAMILY: QP2407-Q4 (July 2024), QP2409-Q3 (September 2024) and QP2411-Q7 (November 2024) are revised-GHG-Strategy questions. They are used only for the Strategy's own architecture - vision, levels of ambition, indicative checkpoints, guiding principles - which is fixed by the resolution and does not move with the sitting.
DIRECTION: every donor is later - QP2402 by five months, QP2408 by eleven. Nothing sitting-relative is inherited.
questions.question_delta: Two words: this paper inserts 'and market-based' into the donor's list of measure classes. Everything else in the printed stem is identical, including the repeated 'and' which this paper also prints. The consequence is substantial - roughly a third of the answer is new material that the donor does not contain, and it is the third that cannot be stated as law. The other consequence is temporal and runs the other way: at this sitting the ongoing market-based work is only two months old, whereas the donor's sitting could describe it as a year-old programme.
questions.verification_status: The Annex VI chapter 4 content - EEDI, EEXI, the three-Part SEEMP, the fuel oil consumption data collection system and the CII rating with its D-for-three-years and E-for-one-year corrective action trigger - is carried from the MIW verification record for QP2402 Q5, where each was established against the regulation. The Strategy's own architecture - vision, four levels of ambition, two indicative checkpoints, the guiding principles, and the basket comprising a technical and an economic element to be finalized and agreed by 2025 on a well-to-wake basis - is carried from the QP2402, QP2409 and QP2408 records, which read MEPC.377(80) at source. The three types of economic instrument are carried from the QP2408 record. Every one of those sources is either the resolution text, which does not move, or a regulation unchanged since 1 January 2023, so the substance required no reconstruction. What was rebuilt from scratch is the position statement: where the work stood in September 2023 rather than in February or August 2024. The precise state of the intersessional working-group programme in the weeks immediately around this sitting is not asserted. No claim is made about the first CII ratings. 2023 is the first full data year and the answer says only that no rating had yet been issued, which follows from the regulation's own reporting cycle.

blocks.h: 1. The 2023 Strategy - the frame every measure now serves

blocks.p: The governing instrument is the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, resolution MEPC.377(80), adopted at MEPC 80 on 7 July 2023 - two months before this examination - and it revoked the 2018 Initial Strategy from that date. Note what it is: a policy instrument, not law. It binds nobody directly. It works by committing the Committee to develop measures which then become law as amendments to MARPOL Annex VI.
Vision: to phase out GHG emissions from international shipping as soon as possible, while promoting a just and equitable transition.

Levels of ambition: carbon intensity of new ships to decline through strengthened design requirements; carbon intensity of international shipping to decline, reducing CO2 per transport work by at least 40% by 2030 against 2008; uptake of zero or near-zero GHG technologies, fuels and energy sources to reach at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used by international shipping by 2030; and GHG emissions to reach net zero by or around, i.e. close to, 2050.

Indicative checkpoints - absolute, where the ambitions are intensity-based: total annual GHG emissions to fall against 2008 by at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030, and by at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040. Two features change everything downstream: the targets are GHG and not CO2 alone, so methane and nitrous oxide count, and they are measured well-to-wake, so a fuel that is clean at the funnel but dirty to produce earns no credit.

blocks.h: 2. The three classes of measure, and what separates them

blocks.p: The examiner has named three classes and they are not three flavours of the same thing. Say what divides them before describing any of them:

ul: a technical measure acts on the ship as built - it forces efficiency into the hull, propeller and machinery and is verified once, by calculation, against a design index;
an operational measure acts on how the ship is run - speed, routeing, trim, hull and propeller condition, cargo and ballast planning - and is verified continuously, from reported data;
a market-based measure acts on price. It mandates no design and no operating practice; it attaches a cost to emitting and lets the owner choose how to respond.

blocks.p: The second division is the one that decides how this answer is written. The technical and operational measures are in force and can be stated as law. The market-based measures are not adopted and can only be stated as a work programme. A question about ongoing developments is asking the candidate to know which is which.

blocks.h: 3. The technical measures in force - EEDI and EEXI

blocks.p: The Energy Efficiency Design Index, under Annex VI chapter 4, requires a new ship's attained EEDI to be no greater than the required EEDI for her type and size, the required value tightening in successive phases. It is a design measure, applied at the drawing board.

The Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index, regulations 23 and 25, in force 1 January 2023, extends the same design-type calculation to existing ships, which was the gap in the original scheme. Compliance is assessed once, at the first annual, intermediate or renewal survey on or after 1 January 2023, and is commonly achieved by engine or shaft power limitation or by fitting energy saving devices. Both indices are one-off design compliance: neither limits how the ship is subsequently operated, which is exactly why an operational measure was needed alongside them.

blocks.h: 4. The operational measures in force - SEEMP Part III and the CII

blocks.p: The Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan, regulation 26, now has three Parts. Part I is the ship-specific energy efficiency plan; Part II is the fuel oil consumption data collection plan; and Part III, required on board on or before 1 January 2023, describes how the ship will achieve her required CII, with implementation, monitoring and self-evaluation. The operative guidance is the 2022 SEEMP Guidelines, resolution MEPC.346(78).

The operational carbon intensity indicator, regulation 28, applies to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above and is the genuinely new operational measure. The ship calculates her attained annual operational CII, compares it against the required CII - a reference line reduced by an annual reduction factor - and receives a rating from A to E. A ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E for a single year, must develop a plan of corrective actions in SEEMP Part III. 2023 is the first full data year, so at this sitting no ship has yet been rated: the scheme is running but has produced nothing.

blocks.h: 5. The data foundation the whole scheme rests on

blocks.p: Regulation 27 has required ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above to collect and report fuel oil consumption data since calendar year 2019. The Administration verifies the data, issues a Statement of Compliance and transmits the data to the IMO Ship Fuel Oil Consumption Database. It is not itself a reduction measure, and candidates often omit it for that reason - which is a mistake. Every carbon-intensity calculation and every future policy decision depends on it, the Strategy relies on it for annual emission estimates, and no market-based measure could be administered without it.

blocks.h: 6. The market-based measures - what is under development

blocks.p: This is where the word ongoing does its work, and it is the part of the answer most candidates never reach. The Strategy requires a basket of candidate mid-term measures comprising both of the following, together and not as alternatives:

ul: a technical element - a goal-based marine fuel standard regulating the phased reduction of the GHG intensity of marine fuel; and
an economic element - a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism.

blocks.p: The logic of pairing them is worth a mark: the standard compels the transition while the price funds it and closes the cost gap between fossil and zero-carbon fuel. Neither alone would do both.
The economic element is not yet chosen, and three structurally different forms are under discussion:

ul: a levy or contribution per tonne of GHG emitted - it fixes the price and leaves the emissions uncertain, is simple to administer, and generates large predictable revenue whose distribution then becomes the whole negotiation;
an emissions trading system, cap and trade - it fixes the emissions and leaves the price uncertain, and is administratively heavier;
a feebate - a fee on high-intensity fuel funding a rebate on low-intensity fuel, which transfers less money overall but requires a benchmark that must ratchet or the incentive decays.

blocks.p: Real proposals before the Committee are hybrids of these - a levy returning part of its revenue as a reward for low-intensity fuel is a feebate in a levy's clothing - so treat the three as analytical categories rather than watertight boxes.

The Strategy fixes the process as firmly as the substance: the basket is to be finalized and agreed by the Committee by 2025, with entry into force to be defined thereafter; it must be developed on a well-to-wake basis under the life cycle guidelines; and it must be accompanied by a comprehensive assessment of impacts on States, with particular attention to least developed countries and small island developing States. The guiding principles constrain the design and are why this has taken so long - non-discrimination and no more favourable treatment from MARPOL, set against common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities in the light of different national circumstances from the climate regime. Reconciling those two is the negotiation.

blocks.h: 7. The rest of the ongoing work programme

ul: A review of the short-term measures - the technical and operational measures now in force - is required, to be completed by 1 January 2026.

Life cycle assessment. The Guidelines on life cycle GHG intensity of marine fuels, resolution MEPC.376(80), were adopted alongside the Strategy on 7 July 2023 and underpin the well-to-wake basis of everything in the basket.

Safety. The Maritime Safety Committee is developing a safety regulatory framework for new technologies and alternative fuels - the safety counterpart to the environmental measures, and the reason an ammonia or hydrogen answer must never be given on environmental grounds alone.

Other candidate mid-term work named in the Strategy: measures addressing methane and nitrous oxide, incentives for first movers, onshore power supply and port-side developments, national action plans, and research and development.
Long-term measures are deliberately left undefined - measures finalized and agreed beyond 2030, to be developed as part of the 2028 review, once the basket is in force and its effect can be measured.

blocks.h: 8. Where the work stands at this sitting

blocks.p: Stating the boundary is part of a correct answer to a question about ongoing work, and it is what separates a candidate who has read the Strategy from one who has read about it.

ul: The Strategy is two months old. It was adopted on 7 July 2023 and it replaced the 2018 Initial Strategy on that date. An answer written on the Initial Strategy is out of date by two months.

No mid-term measure has been adopted. There is no IMO carbon price, no levy, no emissions trading system and no marine fuel GHG-intensity standard in force anywhere. The basket exists as a requirement with a deadline, not as an instrument.
The impact assessment is not complete, and the Strategy makes agreement conditional on it.
No CII rating has been issued to any ship; 2023 is the first data year.

The only carbon pricing that reaches shipping at all is regional, not IMO. The European Union has legislated to extend its emissions trading system to maritime transport from 1 January 2024 - which is after this sitting. Identify it as regional, note that it is one of the pressures making a global measure urgent, and do not present it as an IMO measure or as something already applying to the ship.

blocks.p: The closing proposition: at this sitting the technical and operational measures are on board and enforceable, and the market-based measures are a mandate with a date on it. That is precisely what 'ongoing developments' means here, and saying it plainly is worth more than any additional detail.

The examiner has named three classes of measure and asked what is ongoing. Two things follow. First, the answer must be organised so that all three classes are visibly covered - an answer that describes EEXI and CII beautifully and never reaches market-based measures has left roughly a third of the marks on the table. Second, and less obvious, the word 'ongoing' makes the status of each measure part of the answer rather than background to it.

That is why sections 2 and 8 exist. Section 2 gives the candidate a one-line test for each class - ship as built, how she is run, price - and then draws the line that matters: in force versus under development. Section 8 then closes the answer by stating exactly what has and has not happened. Between them they convert a recitation into a position statement, and they are cheap to write.

Section 5 is included deliberately even though the data collection system is not a reduction measure. It is the foundation every other measure stands on, no market-based measure could be administered without it, and candidates who omit it usually do so because they have learned the measures as a list rather than as a system.

ul: Never reaching market-based measures. The examiner named them; a third of the answer is missing without them.
Describing the European scheme as the answer. It is regional, and at this sitting it does not yet apply to shipping at all.
Writing the answer on the 2018 Initial Strategy. It was revoked on 7 July 2023, two months before this paper.

Confusing the two elements of the basket with the types of economic instrument. The basket is technical plus economic; the economic element may take the form of a levy, an emissions trading system or a feebate.
Treating the Strategy as law. It is a policy instrument; it becomes law only through amendments to MARPOL Annex VI.
Saying ships are being rated A to E. The scheme is running but 2023 is the first data year and no rating has been issued.
Giving a carbon price or levy rate. None had been agreed and an invented figure is indefensible.
Treating EEXI as an operating restriction. It is one-off design compliance, even where it is met by power limitation.

MEPC 81 has not happened at this sitting. It concluded 22 March 2024, six months later. Almost all circulating material on market-based measures is written around it, and importing it is the single most likely contamination on this question.

The European emissions trading system does not yet apply to shipping. It applies from 1 January 2024. Material written for any 2024 sitting states, correctly for itself, that it already applies - which is wrong here.
Adopted is not in force, and a Strategy is neither. The Strategy was adopted 7 July 2023 and is operative as strategy; nothing in the basket is adopted at all.
GHG, not CO2. The targets cover methane and nitrous oxide, which is what makes LNG a more complicated answer than it looks.
Well-to-wake, not tank-to-wake. A fuel clean at the funnel and dirty to produce earns no credit, and this is the whole reason the life cycle guidelines were adopted alongside the Strategy.

The 40% and the 20/30% figures are different kinds of number. The first is carbon intensity per transport work; the second is total annual emissions. Both are against 2008 and candidates routinely merge them.
'Striving for' is not a target. It is the compromise wording that allowed adoption, and describing the higher figure as the commitment overstates the instrument.
Which resolution is the current GHG Strategy, when was it adopted, and what did it replace?
Give me the four levels of ambition and the two indicative checkpoints, and tell me which are intensity and which are absolute.
What is the difference between EEDI and EEXI, and is either an operating restriction?
How is your CII rating calculated, and what happens if you are rated D three years running?
What is in the basket of mid-term measures, and by when must it be agreed?
Levy, emissions trading or feebate - what does each fix and what does each leave uncertain?
Why does the Strategy insist on a well-to-wake basis?
Is the European emissions trading system an IMO measure? Does it apply to your ship today?

blocks.p: The route is STRATEGY - THREE CLASSES - TECHNICAL - OPERATIONAL - DATA - MARKET - PROGRAMME - WHERE WE STAND. Within the market section hold BASKET (technical + economic) - TYPES (levy / ETS / feebate) - PROCESS (2025, well-to-wake, impact assessment). The one-line test for the three classes is BUILT / RUN / PRICED, and it is worth writing into the answer because it earns a mark and it stops the candidate blurring the classes later.

ul: MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023 - the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy; revoked the 2018 Initial Strategy from that date; section 4.5 fixes the basket.
MEPC.376(80), adopted 7 July 2023 - Guidelines on life cycle GHG intensity of marine fuels; the well-to-wake basis.
MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 regulations 22 and 24 - attained and required EEDI.
Regulations 23 and 25 - attained and required EEXI, in force 1 January 2023.
Regulation 26 - SEEMP Parts I, II and III; Part III on board on or before 1 January 2023.
Regulation 27 - fuel oil consumption data collection, from calendar year 2019; Statement of Compliance; IMO database.
Regulation 28 - operational CII and the A to E rating; corrective action after D for three years or E for one.
MEPC.346(78) - the 2022 SEEMP Guidelines, operative at this sitting.

The two MEPC 80 resolutions are cited by identity and adoption date only. The corpus holds them but records their title-page identity confirmation as blocking for citation, so nothing is quoted from either. The substance comes from MIW verification records that read the Strategy at source.
No price, levy rate or revenue figure appears anywhere. None had been agreed at this sitting.

The state of the intersessional working group in the weeks around this sitting is not asserted. The paper prints a month and no day, so the answer is anchored on what the Strategy fixed at MEPC 80 rather than on any meeting after it.
The statement that no CII rating had been issued follows from the regulation's own reporting cycle and the fact that 2023 is the first data year; it is not taken from a published list of ratings.
The three types of economic instrument are analytical categories established in MIW's own verified material, not a list taken from the Strategy, which does not choose between them.

notes: THIS IS THE QUESTION THE SEPTEMBER SITTING DATE WAS ESTABLISHED FOR. MEPC 80 adopted the 2023 GHG Strategy on 7 JULY 2023. September is unambiguously after it, so the Strategy is operative and the 2018 Initial Strategy is revoked. Had this been the January, February, March, April or June 2023 paper the answer would have had to be written on the Initial Strategy instead. No day-granularity reasoning is needed and known trap 17 does not arise on this boundary.

REVERSAL 1 - MEPC 81 IS REMOVED ENTIRELY. The market-based-measures donor QP2408-Q4 (August 2024) is built on MEPC 81, which concluded 22 MARCH 2024, six months after this sitting. Its analytical categories (levy, emissions trading, feebate) transfer because they are structural; every factual anchor tied to that session does not, and none appears here. Resolutions MEPC.384(81) and MEPC.385(81) are likewise absent.

REVERSAL 2 - THE REGIONAL MEASURE IS RE-DATED. QP2408-Q4 states, correctly for August 2024, that the European emissions trading system 'had applied to shipping from 1 January 2024'. At September 2023 it HAS NOT YET APPLIED. The answer states that the European Union has legislated to extend the scheme to maritime transport from 1 January 2024, which is AFTER this sitting, and identifies it as regional rather than IMO. It is named once and is not presented as a live obligation on the ship.

TRAP 17 CONTROLLED ON TWO IN-MONTH BOUNDARIES. Two relevant events fall inside September 2023 - the European fuel-intensity regulation adopted 13 September 2023, and the opening for signature of the high-seas biodiversity agreement on 20 September. The paper prints no day. NEITHER IS USED. The question asks about developments AT IMO, so the answer is anchored on material unaffected by either boundary, which is what trap 17 requires.

THE ANNEX VI MEASURES NEEDED NO REVERSAL. EEDI, EEXI, the three-Part SEEMP, the data collection system and the CII are unchanged between this sitting and both donors; EEXI and SEEMP Part III came into force 1 January 2023, eight months before the sitting.

CII RATINGS RE-DERIVED. The donor QP2402-Q5 states for February 2024 that the first ratings had not yet been issued. That is even more clearly true here: 2023 is the first full data year and it has not ended. The statement is re-derived rather than carried.
NOTHING FROM MEPC 82, MEPC 83, THE 2025 EXTRAORDINARY SESSION OR THE NET-ZERO FRAMEWORK APPEARS. All are future by between one and two years.
NO 33RD ASSEMBLY MATERIAL IS USED - the A.118x(33) set was adopted 6 December 2023, three months after this sitting.

questions.understand_first: There are only three ways to make a ship emit less, and the examiner has named all three - which is a gift, because it gives the answer its own structure. You can build her better, so that the hull, propeller and machinery need less fuel for the same work. You can run her better, which is mostly about speed, routeing, trim and keeping the hull and propeller clean. Or you can make emitting expensive and let the owner work out his own answer. The first two are prescriptive: someone writes down what the ship must achieve and a surveyor checks it. The third is not - it mandates nothing at all, it just changes the arithmetic, and that is precisely why it is both the most powerful and the hardest to agree. The other thing to hold on to is a difference in status, because the question asks what is ongoing. The build-better and run-better measures already exist as enforceable requirements that a ship is surveyed against today. The make-it-expensive measures do not exist at all yet; what exists is a decision that they will be created, a description of what shape they must take, and a deadline. Those are two completely different kinds of statement, and an answer that reports them in the same voice - as though a carbon price were already sitting alongside the design index - has got the question wrong even where every individual fact in it is right.
