decomposition_gate.question_intent: A status question disguised as a knowledge question. The examiner names three classes of measure and asks what is ongoing, so he is testing three things at once: whether the candidate can distinguish the classes, whether he knows the content of each, and - the discriminator - whether he knows which of them are enforceable requirements today and which are a work programme. A candidate who reports all three in the same voice has failed the third test even if every fact is right.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Sixteen marks on the stem, no printed split. Three named classes suggests roughly equal thirds, but that would misallocate: the technical and operational measures are settled and can be stated compactly, while the market-based limb is the newest, the least well known and the one the donor question did not contain. The answer gives sections 3 to 5 to the measures in force, section 6 the single largest share to the market-based limb, and sections 2 and 8 to the status framing that the word 'ongoing' requires.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: The current Strategy named with its resolution and adoption date. The Annex VI measures named with what each actually does, not merely listed as acronyms. The basket given as a technical element plus an economic element rather than as a vague reference to carbon pricing. An explicit statement of what has not yet happened. And the regional European scheme correctly placed as regional and, at this sitting, not yet applying.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: Anchor the in-force measures on MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 regulations 22 to 28, as established in the MIW verification record for QP2402 Q5. Anchor the Strategy's architecture and the basket on MEPC.377(80), as read at source in the QP2402, QP2409 and QP2408 records. Take the three economic instrument types from the QP2408 record, where they are established as analytical categories. Cite MEPC.376(80) for the well-to-wake basis and MEPC.346(78) for the SEEMP guidance. Deliberately NOT planned: any quotation from MEPC.376(80) or MEPC.377(80), whose corpus copies are recorded as blocking for citation; any price or rate; anything from MEPC 81 onwards.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH - the highest on this paper. The subject was moving fast at this sitting and almost all published material on it is written for a later one. Three distinct forward traps exist: MEPC 81 and everything after it; the European emissions trading system's application date; and the temptation to write on the revoked 2018 Initial Strategy, which is a backward trap of only two months. The Strategy itself is two months old, which means the answer must be current to within weeks in one direction and clean of a six-month forward window in the other.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MEDIUM. The question says 'at IMO', so regional measures are context and not content. The European scheme must be named once, identified as regional, and dated correctly - at this sitting it is legislated but not yet applying to shipping. The second jurisdictional point is internal to IMO: the Strategy is a policy instrument of the Committee and binds nobody; only amendments to MARPOL Annex VI bind ships. Presenting the Strategy as law is a jurisdiction error, not merely a loose phrase.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: The stem prints 'and' twice - 'the technical and operational and market-based measures' - which is preserved and not remarked on. 'Ongoing developments' could mean only work in progress, which would exclude the measures already in force; that reading is rejected, because the examiner names the technical and operational classes expressly and they are in force. blocks.h: 1. What the Organization is, and the organs through which it works

blocks.p: The International Maritime Organization is the specialised agency of the United Nations responsible for the safety and security of shipping and for the prevention of pollution from ships. It works through a two-tier governing structure - an Assembly and a Council - together with five main committees supported by seven sub-committees, all served by a permanent Secretariat headed by the Secretary-General.

The division of labour is worth stating at the outset because it organises everything that follows: the governing organs decide policy, budget and membership; the technical output that actually reaches a ship comes almost entirely from the committees.

ul: The highest governing body. All Member States sit in it.
Meets in regular session once every two years.
Approves the work programme, votes the budget and determines the financial arrangements.
Elects the Council.
Receives the reports of the Council and of the committees.

Adopts Assembly resolutions - recommendations, guidelines and codes. Worked example at this sitting: resolution A.1155(32), the Procedures for Port State Control, adopted at the 32nd Assembly in December 2021.

40 Members, elected by the Assembly for a two-year term, in three categories: (a) ten States with the largest interest in providing international shipping services; (b) ten States with the largest interest in international seaborne trade; and (c) twenty States elected to secure geographical representation, having special interests in maritime transport or navigation.

Between Assembly sessions it performs all the functions of the Assembly, with one reservation: the function of making recommendations to Governments on maritime safety and pollution prevention is reserved to the Assembly itself. That single exception is the most examinable fact about the Council.
Supervises the work of the Organization and co-ordinates the activities of its organs.
Considers the draft work programme and budget and submits them to the Assembly with its comments.
Appoints the Secretary-General, subject to the approval of the Assembly.

blocks.p: One live boundary should be flagged rather than glossed. Resolution A.1152(32), adopted December 2021, would enlarge the Council from 40 to 52 Members. It amends the Convention on the Organization and requires acceptance by two thirds of Members; it was not in force at this sitting, so the figure to write is 40.

blocks.h: 4. The five main committees and what each owns

rows: Maritime Safety Committee (MSC)
The highest technical body. Navigational safety, construction and equipment, manning from a safety standpoint, casualty investigation, salvage and rescue
Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC)
Prevention and control of pollution from ships - MARPOL and its amendments, ballast water, anti-fouling, and greenhouse gas measures
Legal Committee
Any legal matter within the scope of the Organization - the liability and compensation conventions in particular
Technical Cooperation Committee
The Organization's technical assistance work, particularly for developing States
Facilitation Committee
Elimination of unnecessary formalities and red tape in international shipping - the FAL Convention

blocks.p: All five are open to all Member States. MSC and MEPC are the two that adopt amendments to the mandatory instruments, which is why they are the committees a marine engineer meets.

blocks.h: 5. The seven sub-committees and the support they provide

blocks.p: The sub-committees are HTW (Human Element, Training and Watchkeeping), III (Implementation of IMO Instruments), NCSR (Navigation, Communications and Search and Rescue), PPR (Pollution Prevention and Response), SDC (Ship Design and Construction), SSE (Ship Systems and Equipment) and CCC (Carriage of Cargoes and Containers).

Their role is preparatory and technical. A committee sits for about a week and cannot itself draft detailed regulation, so it remits the work to the sub-committee holding the relevant expertise. The sub-committee develops the draft text, guideline or unified interpretation, resolves the technical argument, and reports back to its parent committee - MSC, MEPC, or both where a subject straddles them.

The sentence that earns the mark here: a sub-committee adopts nothing. It prepares, the parent committee approves, and the committee or the Assembly adopts. That division is what keeps technical depth and treaty-making authority in different hands.

A convention is a formal, legally binding treaty between States. It is negotiated and adopted at a diplomatic conference or by the Assembly; it is then opened for signature, ratification, acceptance, approval or accession; and it enters into force only when the conditions written into the convention itself are satisfied - typically a stated number of Contracting States representing a stated share of world gross tonnage. It binds only those States that have become party to it, and it reaches a ship through the law of her flag State.
Worked example: the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974.

Three distinctions belong in the definition because the examiner is testing them: adoption is not signature, signature is not ratification, and ratification is not entry into force. They are four separate events and a convention adopted years ago may still not be in force.

blocks.h: 7. Protocol, Code and Resolution distinguished, with examples

rows: Protocol

A separate treaty instrument that amends, supplements or modifies a parent convention, used where the change is too large for the ordinary amendment procedure. It is itself subject to ratification, and a State may need to be party to both
The 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and to the Load Lines Convention, which introduced the harmonized system of survey and certification; the 1978 and 1997 Protocols to MARPOL
Code
A detailed technical instrument. Of itself it is advisory; it becomes mandatory only when a convention makes it so. Mandatory status is a property of the route, never of the word on the cover

The ISM Code, adopted by resolution A.741(18) and made mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX. Contrast the Code for Recognized Organizations, made mandatory through SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 from 1 January 2015
Resolution

A formal decision of an organ of the Organization - the Assembly, MSC or MEPC. It may be advisory, or it may be the vehicle by which a mandatory amendment is adopted. The word tells you the form, not the force
A.1155(32), the Procedures for Port State Control - advisory. Contrast MEPC.328(76), the resolution adopting the revised MARPOL Annex VI, which is mandatory once it enters into force

blocks.h: 8. The pattern that ties the four together

blocks.p: Finish on the point the four examples exist to make, because it is what turns a list into an explanation: binding force is a property of the route an instrument has taken, not of the name it carries.

ul: A convention binds because States have ratified it and the entry-into-force conditions are met.
A protocol binds on the same footing, because it is itself a treaty requiring ratification.
A code binds only where a convention has reached out and made it mandatory - so the same document can be recommendatory for one purpose and mandatory for another.
A resolution may be a recommendation with no binding force at all, or it may be the instrument through which a mandatory convention amendment is adopted and brought into force under tacit acceptance.

blocks.p: That last mechanism is worth naming. Under tacit acceptance an amendment adopted by MSC or MEPC enters into force on a stated date unless a specified proportion of Contracting Governments objects. It is what allows the technical instruments to be kept current without re-ratification, and it is the practical reason the committees, rather than the Assembly, are where a marine engineer's regulation comes from.

This is a two-limb question of equal weight, and the commonest failure is to spend twelve marks' worth of time on limb (a), which is largely recall, and reach limb (b) with nothing left. Limb (b) is the harder limb and it is worth exactly the same. Budget the time before starting.

Within limb (a) the printed stem asks four things - the structure, the Assembly, the Council, the main committees, and then the sub-committees' supporting role. Sections 1 to 5 answer them in that order, which means the marks can be found by the examiner without hunting. Section 1 exists to give the shape in one paragraph so that the reader knows where each later section fits; it also lets the answer state the division between governing organs and technical output, which is the single most useful sentence in the limb.

Limb (b) is answered as a table rather than as prose, deliberately. The question asks for differences and examples, so a table with an instrument, its nature and an example puts every mark on the page in a form the examiner can tick. Section 8 then adds what a table cannot: the pattern connecting the four. That section is where a good answer separates itself, because it converts four definitions into one principle.

ul: Running out of time in limb (b). It carries half the marks and is usually written in five minutes.
Saying the Council has 52 Members. The enlargement was adopted but not in force at this sitting; the answer is 40.
Forgetting the one function the Council may not perform - making recommendations to Governments on safety and pollution prevention. It is the most likely single-mark question in the oral.
Saying sub-committees adopt regulations. They adopt nothing; they prepare and report.
Saying that a Code is recommendatory, full stop, or that a Code is mandatory, full stop. Both are wrong. It depends entirely on whether a convention has made it mandatory.
Treating 'resolution' as meaning 'not binding'. A resolution is a form of decision; MSC and MEPC adopt mandatory convention amendments by resolution.
Confusing adoption with entry into force. They are separate events, often years apart.
Naming the Secretary-General. It adds nothing, and if the name or the term is wrong it costs.

The Assembly resolution example must pre-date the sitting. The 33rd Assembly met on 6 December 2023, three months after this paper. A.1185(33), A.1186(33), A.1187(33) and A.1188(33) did not exist. Use a 32nd Assembly resolution - A.1155(32) serves, and it is also this paper's Q9 instrument.

40, not 52. A.1152(32) would enlarge the Council but requires acceptance by two thirds of Members and was not in force. Flagging that you know the amendment exists and is not in force scores better than either bare figure.
Five main committees, seven sub-committees. Both numbers are asked for directly and both are easy marks.
The Assembly meets every two years, not annually.
Mandatory status is a property of the route. The examiner is testing whether you understand that the same Code can be recommendatory and mandatory in different contexts.
Tacit acceptance is the mechanism worth naming in limb (b). It explains why the committees matter more than the Assembly to a working engineer.
How many States sit on the Council, in what categories, and for how long?
Is there anything the Council cannot do that the Assembly can?
Name the five main committees. Which two adopt amendments to the mandatory instruments?
Name the sub-committees. Can a sub-committee adopt a guideline?
Is the ISM Code mandatory? Why? What makes it so?
Is a resolution binding?
What is tacit acceptance and why does it exist?
A convention was adopted in 1996. Is it in force? How would you find out?

Limb (b): CONVENTION - PROTOCOL - CODE - RESOLUTION, then the one-line principle route, not name. If time is short, the table in section 7 plus that one line will still score most of limb (b).

questions.understand_first: The Organization is easiest to hold in the head if you separate who decides from who does the technical work. At the top sit the member governments themselves, meeting only occasionally, who approve the money, the programme of work and the membership of the smaller body that runs things between their meetings. That smaller executive body can do almost everything the full membership can, with one pointed exception: it cannot itself make recommendations to governments about safety and pollution, because that is the one power the membership kept for itself. Neither of those bodies, though, writes the rules an engineer actually meets. Those come from the committees - one for safety, one for the marine environment, and three others - and beneath them from specialist groups that grind through the technical drafting and then hand the result upwards. The specialists never adopt anything; they prepare, and someone above them decides. That separation is deliberate, and it keeps expertise and authority in different hands. The second half of the question is really about one idea: whether a document binds you has nothing to do with what it is called. A treaty binds because states have signed up and enough of them have done so. A technical manual binds only if some treaty reaches out and says it does - which means the very same manual can be advisory in one context and compulsory in another. And a formal decision of a committee can be a mere suggestion or the instrument that changes a treaty, depending entirely on what the committee was doing when it took it. Read the route, never the cover.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Assembly (all Members, every two years) - Council (40, three categories) - five main committees - seven sub-committees - Secretariat. The Council does everything the Assembly does except recommend to Governments on safety and pollution. Sub-committees adopt nothing. Limb (b): convention and protocol bind by ratification; a code binds only where a convention says so; a resolution may be advice or a mandatory amendment. Route, not name.
keywords: HTW III NCSR PPR SDC SSE CCC
quick_revision.critical_numbers: Two years between regular Assembly sessions. 40 Council Members - 10 / 10 / 20 in categories (a), (b) and (c) - for a two-year term. Five main committees. Seven sub-committees. A.1152(32) would make the Council 52 but was not in force at this sitting. 1974 SOLAS; 1988 Protocols; 1978 and 1997 MARPOL Protocols.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: The Convention on the International Maritime Organization itself - it is the constitution that fixes the Assembly's functions, the Council's forty Members in three categories, and the one function the Assembly reserves to itself. Every figure in limb (a) comes from it.
quick_revision.major_trap: Using a 33rd Assembly resolution as the worked example. The 33rd Assembly met on 6 December 2023, three months after this sitting, so A.1185(33) through A.1188(33) do not exist here. Use A.1155(32). The companion trap is writing 52 for the Council: the enlargement was adopted but not in force, so the answer is 40.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the IMO structure and instruments question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb (a): 1 what the Organization is and its organs; 2 the Assembly; 3 the Council; 4 the five main committees; 5 the seven sub-committees. Limb (b): 6 what a convention is; 7 protocol, code and resolution with examples; 8 the pattern - binding force follows the route, not the name.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Council composition and term?
retrieval_cards.answer: 40 Members elected by the Assembly for a two-year term in three categories: ten States with the largest interest in providing international shipping services; ten with the largest interest in international seaborne trade; and twenty elected to secure geographical representation. A.1152(32) would enlarge it to 52 but was not in force at this sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What can the Assembly do that the Council cannot?
retrieval_cards.answer: Make recommendations to Governments on maritime safety and pollution prevention. Between Assembly sessions the Council performs all the Assembly's functions with that single exception, which the Assembly reserves to itself. It is the most examinable fact about the Council.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the seven sub-committees and say what they may adopt.
retrieval_cards.answer: HTW, III, NCSR, PPR, SDC, SSE and CCC. They adopt nothing. Their role is preparatory and technical - they develop draft text, guidelines and unified interpretations, resolve the technical argument, and report to MSC, MEPC or both. The parent committee approves; the committee or the Assembly adopts.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a convention, and name the four separate events in its life.
retrieval_cards.answer: A formal legally binding treaty between States, adopted at a diplomatic conference or by the Assembly, opened for signature, ratification, acceptance, approval or accession, and entering into force only on the conditions written into it - typically a number of States and a share of world tonnage. Adoption, signature, ratification and entry into force are four distinct events.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is a Code mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only where a convention makes it so. Of itself a code is a detailed technical instrument and is recommendatory. Mandatory status is a property of the route, not of the word on the cover - the ISM Code through SOLAS chapter IX, the RO Code through SOLAS XI-1/1 from 1 January 2015. The same document can be advisory in one context and compulsory in another.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Assembly resolution may you use as an example at a September 2023 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: One from the 32nd Assembly or earlier - A.1155(32), the Procedures for Port State Control, adopted December 2021, serves well and is also this paper's Q9 instrument. The 33rd Assembly met on 6 December 2023, three months after the sitting, so A.1185(33) through A.1188(33) did not exist.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is tacit acceptance and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: An amendment adopted by MSC or MEPC enters into force on a stated date unless a specified proportion of Contracting Governments objects. It allows the technical instruments to be kept current without re-ratification, and it is the practical reason a marine engineer's regulation comes from the committees rather than from the Assembly.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two equally weighted limbs testing institutional knowledge and then legal literacy. Limb (a) is largely recall and the examiner can mark it by counting: the organs, the numbers, the committees, the sub-committees, and the one sentence about what a sub-committee may not do. Limb (b) is conceptual and is the discriminator - it tests whether the candidate understands that the binding force of a maritime instrument is determined by the route it took rather than by its title, which is the idea that makes the whole regulatory system intelligible.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Eight and eight, printed. That equality is itself the most important allocation fact, because limb (a) invites over-writing and limb (b) is where candidates run out of time. Within limb (a) the stem asks for the structure, three named bodies and the sub-committees' role, so five sections. Within limb (b) it asks for a definition, three comparisons and at least one example of each, so a definition section and a comparison table, with a closing section for the connecting principle.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: In limb (a): the two-tier structure named; the Assembly's biennial cycle and its budget and election functions; the Council's forty Members in three categories and the reserved function; the five committees with their subject boundaries; the seven sub-committees named and the statement that they adopt nothing. In limb (b): a definition that separates adoption from entry into force; a clear statement that a code's mandatory status comes from the convention that adopts it; and at least one concrete example against each of the four instruments.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: Anchor limb (a) on the Convention on the International Maritime Organization for the Assembly's functions, the Council's composition and categories, the reserved function and the appointment of the Secretary-General, as established in the MIW verification record for QP2402 Q1. Take the committee and sub-committee descriptions from the same record. Anchor limb (b) on the instruments used as examples - SOLAS 1974, the 1988 SOLAS and Load Lines Protocols, the 1978 and 1997 MARPOL Protocols, the ISM Code with SOLAS chapter IX, the RO Code with SOLAS XI-1/1, and MEPC.328(76). Use A.1155(32) as the Assembly resolution example, cited by identity only. Deliberately NOT planned: any 33rd Assembly resolution, any office-holder, any Member State count.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - The structure itself is stable and needed no reversal. Two facts move and both are handled: the Assembly resolution used as an example must pre-date the sitting, and the Council figure depends on an adopted amendment that was not yet in force. A third, the identity of the Secretary-General, changed within months of this sitting and is avoided entirely rather than dated.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW to MEDIUM. The risk is not between States but between levels of instrument, which is the subject of limb (b) itself. The specific error to avoid is describing a code or a resolution as binding of its own force, or describing the Organization as legislating - it does not; its instruments reach a ship through the flag State's ratification and national law. Where India is concerned that route runs through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 at this sitting.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: 'Structure' could be read as the organs alone or as including the Secretariat and the sub-committee tier; the answer covers all of them because the stem separately asks about sub-committees. 'Various main committees' does not say how many, and the answer states five expressly rather than leaving the number implied. In limb (b) 'resolution' is ambiguous between an Assembly resolution and a committee resolution, and the answer deliberately gives one of each because the distinction between them carries the limb's central point.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections under two printed limb headings. Prose for the opening shape and for the convention definition; bulleted lists for the Assembly and Council functions; a two-column table for the five committees and a three-column table for the four instruments, so that limb (b)'s comparison and examples are visible at a glance. A closing section stating the connecting principle and naming tacit acceptance.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the IMO Council had 40 Members at this sitting, resolution A.1152(32) of December 2021 having been adopted but not being in force.
reverify_before_publication.why: A.1152(32) amends the Convention on the IMO and enters into force on acceptance by two thirds of Members, which can happen at any time and without any shipboard-visible announcement. The statement is anchored to September 2023 and is correct for it, but the underlying fact is acceptance-driven and must be re-checked rather than assumed if the answer is ever re-dated.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That resolution A.1155(32), Procedures for Port State Control, is used as the worked example of an Assembly resolution because the 33rd Assembly set did not exist at this sitting.
reverify_before_publication.why: This is the reversal in the question and it is the claim most at risk of being silently undone, because every other paper in the corpus correctly uses a 33rd or 34th Assembly resolution here. A reviewer moving between papers will read A.1155(32) as stale. It is not - it is the operative example for September 2023.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The seven sub-committees named, and the number five for the main committees.
reverify_before_publication.why: Correct at this sitting. The sub-committee structure has been reorganised in the past, so the number is a fact about the sitting rather than a permanent feature of the Organization, and it is stated that way in the answer.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That MIW holds no copy of A.1155(32) or A.1152(32) and neither was read at source.

questions.verification_status: This question is authored from first principles and from the settled architecture of the grain regime; MIW holds no donor and the corpus holds no copy of the International Grain Code. What is therefore stated with confidence, and what is stated with a recorded limitation, are deliberately separated. The MECHANISM - settlement and void formation, the slide of the grain surface to a new angle of repose, the transverse and vertical movement of G, the irreversibility of a dry-cargo shift as against a liquid free surface, and the consequent reduction in righting lever, maximum GZ, range and dynamical stability - is naval architecture and is derived rather than cited. The REGULATORY ARCHITECTURE - that bulk grain is governed by the International Grain Code adopted by resolution MSC.23(59) and made mandatory through SOLAS chapter VI, that a Document of Authorization is required, and that grain sits outside the IMSBC regime - is settled and is stated as such. The THREE NUMERICAL CRITERIA and the assumed heeling-arm construction are the part MIW cannot presently verify at source: they are universally published, they are the substance of what the question asks for, and they are given in full, but they are graded as authoritative secondary rather than primary and remain graded as authoritative secondary; SOLAS chapter VI regulations 8 and 9 were read at source in laptop review, which primary-verifies the Code identity, the statutory definition of grain, the mandatory hook and the Document of Authorization. No cargo property figure - stowage factor, bulk density or an actual angle of repose for any particular grain - is asserted anywhere, consistent with MIW's standing position on unverified cargo characteristics.
sources: P2 - International Code for the Safe Carriage of Grain in Bulk (International Grain Code), adopted by resolution MSC.23(59): the three intact stability criteria; the assumed heeling arm construction with the value at 40 degrees taken as 0.8 of the value at zero; the assumed shift angles distinguishing filled from partly filled compartments; and the requirement for a Document of Authorization. MIW holds no copy of the Code itself - see unresolved and reverify_before_publication. The Code's identity and its mandatory application are separately primary-verified from SOLAS chapter VI.

P1 - SOLAS chapter VI, regulations 8 and 9, read at source in this session from the corpus copy of the Convention (2024 consolidated edition): regulation 8 defines the International Grain Code as the Code adopted by resolution MSC.23(59), and defines grain as wheat, maize (corn), oats, rye, barley, rice, pulses, seeds and processed forms thereof whose behaviour is similar to that of grain in its natural state; regulation 9 requires a cargo ship carrying grain to comply with the Code and to hold a Document of Authorization, and directs that the Code's requirements be treated as mandatory.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT AND NAVAL ARCHITECTURE, DERIVED: the mechanism of grain shift - settlement of approximately two per cent by volume creating a void beneath the deckhead, the slide of the surface to a new angle of repose on heeling, and the transverse and vertical movement of the centre of gravity that follows.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT AND NAVAL ARCHITECTURE, DERIVED: the effect on the curve of statical stability - a new equilibrium angle where the heeling arm and righting arm curves cross, reduction of the righting lever at every angle, reduction of maximum GZ and its shift to a larger angle, reduction of the range of stability, and reduction of the area under the curve and hence of dynamical stability.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT: the distinction between an irreversible dry-cargo shift and a reversible liquid free surface, which is the single most important physical point in the answer and is the reason grain is regulated by a heeling arm rather than by a virtual rise of G.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT: the construction sequence given for the diagram, and the observation that all three criteria can be read from one drawing, which is what makes the diagram worth the marks the examiner has attached to it.

INTERNAL REUSE (MIW verification records QP2501/Q9 and QP2507/Q4, read in full): the boundary between a liquefaction failure and a shifting-cargo failure, used here only to state what grain is NOT and to keep the two mechanisms apart.
unresolved: MIW HOLDS NO COPY OF THE INTERNATIONAL GRAIN CODE - there is no Grain Code folder in the corpus, and the Intact Stability Code copy carries no text layer. SOLAS CHAPTER VI IS HELD AND WAS READ AT SOURCE in this session, so the mandatory hook, the Code identity, the statutory definition of grain and the Document of Authorization are primary-verified; the Grain Code's own contents are not. The three numerical criteria, the 0.8 factor in the heeling arm construction and the assumed shift angles are therefore given as authoritative secondary knowledge, not as text read at source, and they are flagged for verification against MSC.23(59) before publication.

The assumed grain surface shift angles distinguishing filled from partly filled compartments, and the assumed void depths, are stated at the level of the distinction they draw rather than as quoted values wherever the distinction alone carries the point. Where figures are given they carry the same limitation as the criteria above.

No stowage factor, bulk density or actual angle of repose is given for any grain. These are cargo properties which vary by commodity and by shipment, and MIW's standing position is that no such figure is asserted from an unverified source.
The approximately two per cent settlement figure is the conventional working value used in grain loading practice and is given as such, not as a Code value.

The Intact Stability Code 2008 is held in the corpus by reference but does NOT contain the grain criteria, which live in the Grain Code. It is named in the answer only to place the boundary and nothing is taken from it.

blocks.h: 1. What is being carried, and why grain is regulated apart

blocks.p: Grain in this context means wheat, maize, oats, rye, barley, rice, pulses, seeds and their processed forms having similar behaviour. It is a free-flowing granular cargo, and its defining property for the naval architect is that a heap of it will not stand steeper than its angle of repose.
Two boundaries are worth stating at the outset because they earn marks and prevent the wrong answer:

ul: Bulk grain has its own instrument. It is governed by the International Code for the Safe Carriage of Grain in Bulk - the International Grain Code, adopted by resolution MSC.23(59) - which is made mandatory through SOLAS chapter VI. Grain is expressly outside the IMSBC Code, so an answer built on cargo groups, transportable moisture limits and individual schedules is answering about a different regime.

A shifting cargo is not a liquefying cargo. In liquefaction the cargo takes on the character of a fluid and can slosh to and fro. Grain does neither: it slides once to a new angle of repose and stays there. That single difference dictates everything below.

blocks.h: 2. Why grain shifts, and why the shift does not come back

ul: It settles. Grain loaded into a hold consolidates in the first days of a passage, conventionally taken as of the order of two per cent by volume. Even a compartment filled and trimmed to the deckhead therefore develops a void beneath the deck head.
The void gives the surface somewhere to go. Until the void exists there is nothing to shift into; once it exists, the exposed surface can move.
Rolling does the work. As the ship heels, grain on the high side slides down across the void to the low side, and the surface settles at its angle of repose relative to the new waterline.

The shift is irreversible - this is the crucial point. When the ship rolls back, the grain does not run back up the slope. Gravity moved it down; nothing moves it up. So the ship does not return to upright: she takes up a permanent angle of heel, and the next roll to the same side can move more grain again. A liquid free surface, by contrast, is symmetrical and reversible, which is why it is handled by a virtual rise of G and grain is not.

The centre of gravity moves twice. The cargo's centre of gravity moves transversely, which is what generates the heeling moment, and it also generates a small vertical component as the heap redistributes. Both reduce stability.

blocks.h: 3. From heeling moment to heeling arm

blocks.p: The Code makes the effect calculable rather than leaving it to judgement. Grain loading information approved for the ship gives, for every compartment and every loading condition, an assumed volumetric heeling moment - assumed, because it is a standard calculated allowance rather than a measurement of what any particular cargo will do. The assumption distinguishes a filled and trimmed compartment, where the cargo is confined and the surface can move only a little, from a partly filled compartment, where a large free surface is exposed and the assumed movement is correspondingly greater. That is why the Code presses so hard on filling and trimming: it is buying a smaller assumed moment.
The moments for all compartments are totalled and converted to a heeling arm:

ul: the heeling arm at zero degrees is the total assumed volumetric heeling moment divided by the product of the stowage factor and the ship's displacement;
the heeling arm at forty degrees is taken as 0.8 times the value at zero;
and between them the heeling arm is assumed to vary as a straight line.

blocks.p: That straight line is a deliberate simplification - the real heeling arm is a curve - and it is conservative in the region that matters. What the candidate must remember is that the grain heeling arm is a straight line falling from its value at zero to 0.8 of that value at forty degrees, and that it is drawn on the same axes as the righting arm.
Draw angle of heel horizontally, from zero to about sixty degrees, and lever in metres vertically. Then, in this order:

ol: Plot the ship's curve of statical stability - the righting lever GZ against angle of heel - for the loaded condition, with GM already corrected for the free surface of liquids in tanks.
Mark the angle of flooding on the horizontal axis if it lies below forty degrees, and mark forty degrees.
Plot the heeling arm: a point on the vertical axis at the zero-degree value, a point at forty degrees at 0.8 of it, and a straight line joining them, extended as necessary.
Mark the first intersection of the two lines. This is the angle of heel due to the shift of grain - the ship's new equilibrium - and it is the angle criterion 1 limits.
Find the angle of maximum difference between the two ordinates. Take whichever is least of that angle, forty degrees, and the angle of flooding.

Shade the area enclosed between the righting arm curve and the heeling arm line, from the equilibrium angle to that least angle. This shaded area is the residual, or net, area and it is what criterion 2 measures.

At the origin, draw the tangent to the GZ curve and carry it to the vertical erected at 57.3 degrees, i.e. one radian. The height at which it cuts that vertical is the initial metacentric height GM, which criterion 3 limits.

blocks.p: Label the shaded area, the equilibrium angle and GM. All three criteria can then be read off one drawing, which is exactly why the examiner has asked for a neat diagram rather than three sentences.

blocks.h: 5. What the shift does to the curve of statical stability

ul: The effective righting lever at every angle is reduced by the heeling arm. The curve the ship actually works to is the residual curve - righting arm minus heeling arm - not the curve in the stability book.
The ship no longer floats upright. Equilibrium moves from zero to the angle at which the two curves cross, and she lies at that angle as a steady condition rather than as a transient.
The maximum righting lever is reduced, and the angle at which it occurs moves outwards.
The range of stability is reduced. The residual curve returns to zero at a smaller angle than the original curve, so the ship has less angular margin before capsize.

Dynamical stability is reduced - the area under the residual curve is smaller, so there is less energy available to absorb a gust or a heavy roll. This is the reduction that actually capsizes ships, and it is why the second criterion is expressed as an area rather than as a lever.

Because the initial heel is permanent, the loss is not recovered. The ship sails at the heeled condition, her deck edge is closer to the water on the low side, and any further shift compounds the first rather than cancelling it.
The initial GM is also reduced by the small vertical rise of the cargo's centre of gravity, which steepens nothing and flattens the whole curve near the origin.

blocks.p: In one sentence for the examiner: grain shift converts a symmetrical righting arm curve into a smaller, one-sided residual curve that starts at a heeled equilibrium, peaks lower, ends sooner and encloses less area.

blocks.h: 6. The three minimum intact stability criteria

blocks.p: The Code requires the intact stability characteristics of any ship carrying bulk grain to be shown to meet, throughout the voyage and after allowing for the heeling moments due to grain shift, at least the following:

ol: Angle of heel. The angle of heel due to the shift of grain shall not be greater than 12 degrees - or, for ships constructed on or after 1 January 1994, the angle at which the deck edge is immersed, whichever is the lesser. The purpose is to keep the deck edge out of the water and the ship workable and manoeuvrable.

Residual dynamical stability. In the statical stability diagram, the net or residual area between the heeling arm curve and the righting arm curve, measured from the angle of equilibrium up to the angle of maximum difference between the ordinates, or 40 degrees, or the angle of flooding, whichever is the least, shall in all conditions of loading be not less than 0.075 metre-radians. This is the reserve of energy the ship keeps after the grain has done its worst.

Initial metacentric height. The initial GM, after correction for the free surface effects of liquids in tanks, shall be not less than 0.30 metres. This underwrites the first two, because a ship with too little initial stiffness will fail them at almost any heeling arm.

blocks.p: Two features of the set are worth a sentence each. They are cumulative - all three must be satisfied, and satisfying two is failing. And they must hold throughout the voyage, not merely on departure, which is why consumption of fuel and water from double bottoms has to be planned: burning off bottom weight raises G and can put a ship that sailed compliant outside the criteria days later.

blocks.h: 7. Reading the three criteria off the one diagram

ul: Criterion 1 is a point on the horizontal axis - where the two curves first cross. It must fall at or inside 12 degrees, or inside deck edge immersion for a ship of the later construction date, whichever comes first.

Criterion 2 is the shaded area - bounded below by the heeling arm line, above by the GZ curve, on the left by the equilibrium angle and on the right by the least of the maximum-difference angle, 40 degrees and the flooding angle. It must be at least 0.075 metre-radians.
Criterion 3 is the slope at the origin - the tangent, read at 57.3 degrees, giving a fluid GM of at least 0.30 metres.

The three are not independent. A larger heeling arm pushes the crossing point right, which simultaneously eats into the left-hand end of the shaded area. So a marginal ship usually fails criteria 1 and 2 together, and the way to recover both is the same - reduce the heeling moment.

blocks.h: 8. Reducing the heeling moment, and the document that proves it

blocks.p: The criteria are met by controlling the cargo, not by hoping. The measures a candidate should be able to name:

ul: Fill and trim. A filled, trimmed compartment carries a far smaller assumed heeling moment than a partly filled one. Trimming the surface level and filling every void that can be filled is the cheapest stability the ship will ever get.
Minimise the number of slack compartments, and where a partly filled compartment is unavoidable, place it low and secure its surface.
Secure the surface of a partly filled compartment - overstowing with bagged grain or other suitable cargo, or strapping or lashing the surface, or the traditional saucer and bundling arrangements.
Use longitudinal divisions where fitted - a centreline bulkhead or shifting boards halve the transverse travel and so the heeling moment.
Plan consumption. Keep the ship's GM within the criteria for the whole passage, allowing for the rise of G as double bottom fuel and water are used.
Watch the weather and the rolling, since it is rolling that mobilises the surface in the first place.

blocks.p: Finally, the paperwork, because it is what a surveyor or a port State control officer will actually ask for. A ship loading bulk grain must hold a Document of Authorization issued by or on behalf of the Administration, certifying that she is capable of complying with the Code, together with the approved grain loading information - the stability data and the assumed volumetric heeling moments - by which the master demonstrates, before loading, that the intended condition will satisfy all three criteria for the whole voyage.

The proposition to close on: the criteria do not prevent the grain from shifting. They accept that it will, and require the ship to be able to survive it - upright enough to work, with enough residual energy to absorb a gust, and stiff enough at the start for both of those to be true.

The stem contains two commands joined by a comma - explain how the shift affects the curve, and with a neat diagram explain the minimum criteria. Both must be answered, and candidates habitually do one. The structure above answers the mechanism in sections 1 to 3 and 5, and the criteria in sections 6 and 7, with section 4 - the diagram - deliberately placed between them so that it serves both.

That placement is the single most useful decision in the answer. Drawn once, the diagram carries the equilibrium angle, the residual area and the initial GM, so every criterion in section 6 can be pointed at rather than described in the abstract. The examiner asked for a neat diagram and it is worth real marks; a diagram that appears after the criteria, as decoration, earns far less than one that the criteria are read from.

Section 2 is where the understanding marks are. Almost anyone can list three numbers; the candidate who explains why a dry cargo shift is irreversible, and therefore why it produces a permanent list rather than a symmetrical loss of GM, has shown that he knows why the regime exists. Section 8 then closes the loop from theory to the ship, which is what a management-level paper is testing.

ul: Treating grain shift as a free surface effect and correcting it as a virtual rise of G. A liquid free surface is symmetrical and reversible; a grain shift is one-way. The Code uses a heeling arm precisely because the free surface model does not fit.
Answering from the IMSBC Code - cargo groups, transportable moisture limit, can test. Grain is outside that Code and has its own.
Confusing shifting with liquefaction. Different mechanism, different cargo, different failure.
Drawing the heeling arm as a cosine curve. The Code's assumed heeling arm is a straight line from its value at zero to 0.8 of that at forty degrees.
Giving the residual area limit without saying between which angles it is measured. The bounds are half the criterion.
Forgetting that GM must be the fluid value, corrected for free surface in tanks.
Stating the criteria as alternatives. All three must be met, in all conditions of loading, throughout the voyage.
Omitting the diagram, or drawing it without labelling the shaded area and the equilibrium angle. The stem asks for it by name.

Twelve degrees is not the whole of criterion 1. For ships constructed on or after 1 January 1994 it is twelve degrees or the angle of deck edge immersion, whichever is the lesser. Quoting twelve alone is a half answer.

The upper bound of the residual area is the LEAST of three angles - the angle of maximum difference between the ordinates, forty degrees, and the angle of flooding. Candidates routinely say forty and stop.
0.075 is in metre-radians, not metre-degrees. The unit is part of the mark.
Throughout the voyage, not on departure. Burning double bottom fuel raises G and can put a compliant ship outside the criteria mid-passage. This is a favourite oral follow-up.
The 0.8 factor applies to the heeling arm at forty degrees, not to the righting arm and not to the area.
Grain settles, so even a filled and trimmed compartment shifts. Saying that a full hold cannot shift is wrong and invites the follow-up about the void.
The Document of Authorization is a specific certificate. It is not the stability booklet, though the approved grain loading information accompanies it.
Why does grain shift at all if the hold was filled to the deckhead?
Why can you not treat a grain shift as a free surface correction?
Give me the three criteria, with units.
Between which angles is the residual area measured, and what if the flooding angle is thirty-five degrees?
You sail compliant and burn double bottom fuel for six days. What has happened to your criteria?
What is a Document of Authorization and who issues it?
How would you reduce the heeling moment in a hold you cannot completely fill?
What is the difference between this and a liquefaction failure?

blocks.p: Mechanism: SETTLE - VOID - SLIDE - STAY. Consequence: LIST, LOWER, SHORTER, SMALLER - a permanent list, a lower maximum GZ, a shorter range, a smaller area. Criteria: 12 - 0.075 - 0.30, which reads as angle, area, stiffness. And the one-line reminder for criterion 2's bounds: maximum difference, forty, flooding - take the least.

ul: International Grain Code, adopted by resolution MSC.23(59) - the assumed heeling moments, the heeling arm construction and the three intact stability criteria.
SOLAS chapter VI - the chapter through which the Grain Code is made mandatory, and the source of the Document of Authorization requirement.
IMSBC Code - named only to place the boundary: grain is outside it.
Intact Stability Code 2008 - named only to place the boundary: the general intact stability criteria live there, the grain criteria do not.

Where this answer's authority comes from, and where it stops. SOLAS chapter VI has been read at source: regulation 8 defines the International Grain Code as the Code adopted by resolution MSC.23(59) and defines what counts as grain, and regulation 9 requires a ship carrying grain to comply with the Code and to hold a Document of Authorization, the Code's requirements being treated as mandatory. The Grain Code itself is not held, so the three numerical criteria, the 0.8 heeling-arm factor and the assumed shift-angle distinction are given as settled, universally published professional knowledge rather than as text read at source. They are what the question asks for and they are given in full; check them against your ship's approved grain loading manual, which states them for her.

The mechanism is derived, not cited. Settlement, void formation, the slide to a new angle of repose, the irreversibility of a dry shift and the consequent reshaping of the GZ curve are naval architecture reasoned from first principles; they are not attributed to any instrument and do not need to be.
The approximately two per cent settlement figure is a conventional working value from grain loading practice, given as such and not as a Code value.
No stowage factor, bulk density or angle of repose is given for any grain. These are cargo properties varying by commodity and shipment, and MIW does not assert them from unverified sources.

The assumed shift angles for filled and partly filled compartments are described by the distinction they draw rather than pinned to quoted values, because the distinction is what carries the marks and the values are not held.

notes: THIS QUESTION CARRIES ALMOST NO TEMPORAL RISK, AND THE REASON IS WORTH STATING: it has no donor, so there is no later prose to contaminate it, and its subject matter is naval architecture plus a code whose stability criteria have been stable for decades.
THE INTERNATIONAL GRAIN CODE, MSC.23(59), IS OPERATIVE AT THIS SITTING and was operative long before it. Nothing in the three criteria moved in the relevant period.

SOLAS CHAPTER VI IS OPERATIVE. The SOLAS Consolidated Edition 2024 takes effect 1 July 2024, ten months after this sitting, and is neither cited nor relied on; nothing in this answer depends on an edition boundary.

THE ONE DATE INSIDE THE ANSWER IS A CONSTRUCTION DATE, NOT A SITTING-RELATIVE ONE. Criterion 1 distinguishes ships constructed on or after 1 January 1994. That is a property of the ship, is thirty years past at this sitting, and does not move with the paper.
THE IMSBC CODE IS NAMED ONLY TO EXCLUDE IT. No IMSBC amendment number is cited, so the corpus's open IMSBC acquisition gap (review-queue item RQ-13) does not arise here.
THE INTACT STABILITY CODE 2008 IS NAMED ONLY TO PLACE A BOUNDARY. Its amendment chain is unassembled in the corpus (RQ-18), and because nothing is taken from it that gap does not bite either.
NO 33RD ASSEMBLY MATERIAL, NO MEPC 80 MATERIAL AND NO MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT MATERIAL APPEARS - none is relevant to this question.

questions.understand_first: Think about what a heap of dry grain will and will not do. Pour it out and it forms a cone; tilt the floor and, past a certain slope, the top layer slides down and settles into a new cone. That slope is the only thing holding it in place, and it is not very steep. Now put that heap in a ship's hold. Two things then matter, and they are easy to miss. The first is that grain consolidates after loading, so even a hold packed right up to the deckhead develops a gap underneath it within a day or two - and a gap is the space the surface needs in order to move at all. The second, and this is the one that decides everything, is that when the ship rolls back, the grain does not roll back with her. Gravity carried it down the slope; nothing carries it up again. So the ship does not swing back to upright. She keeps a lean, permanently, and the next heavy roll to that same side can move a little more. That is completely unlike slack water in a tank, which sloshes both ways and does no permanent harm to which side the ship sits on - and it is why the rules treat the two problems with different arithmetic. What the ship has lost is not simply uprightness. Her reserve of righting effort - the effort available to push back against a gust or a wave - is smaller, it starts from a leaning position instead of an upright one, and it runs out at a smaller angle. So the rules do not try to stop the grain moving, which cannot be guaranteed. They accept that it will move, and then insist the ship still be upright enough to work, strong enough in reserve to absorb a squall, and stiff enough at the outset for either of those to be true.
questions.memory_cue: Mechanism SETTLE - VOID - SLIDE - STAY. Consequence LIST, LOWER, SHORTER, SMALLER. Criteria 12 - 0.075 - 0.30, read as ANGLE, AREA, STIFFNESS. Those map onto the route steps (1 to 8): cargo and boundaries (1), mechanism (2), arithmetic (3), diagram (4), effect on the curve (5), the criteria (6), reading them off (7), controlling them (8).

steps.title: What is being carried, and why grain is regulated apart
points: Grain is a free-flowing granular cargo that will not stand steeper than its angle of repose
Governed by the International Grain Code, MSC.23(59), mandatory through SOLAS chapter VI
Grain is expressly OUTSIDE the IMSBC Code - do not answer with groups and TML
A shifting cargo is not a liquefying cargo: grain slides once and stays

steps.title: Why grain shifts, and why the shift does not come back
points: It settles, conventionally of the order of two per cent by volume, leaving a void under the deckhead
The void is what gives the surface somewhere to go
Rolling slides the high-side grain down to a new angle of repose
IRREVERSIBLE - nothing carries it back up, so the heel is permanent and can compound
G moves transversely, generating the heeling moment, and slightly vertically as well

steps.title: From heeling moment to heeling arm
points: Approved grain loading information gives an assumed volumetric heeling moment per compartment
Filled and trimmed compartments carry a far smaller assumed moment than partly filled ones
Heeling arm at zero = total assumed volumetric heeling moment / (stowage factor x displacement)
Heeling arm at forty degrees = 0.8 times the value at zero
Between them the heeling arm is assumed to vary as a STRAIGHT LINE

steps.title: Drawing the diagram
points: Angle of heel horizontally, lever in metres vertically
Plot the GZ curve for the loaded condition with GM already free-surface corrected
Mark forty degrees and the angle of flooding
Plot the heeling arm as a straight line from its zero value to 0.8 of it at forty degrees
Mark the first intersection - the angle of heel due to grain shift
Shade between the curves from that angle to the least of maximum-difference, forty, and flooding
Draw the tangent at the origin to 57.3 degrees to read GM

steps.title: What the shift does to the curve of statical stability
points: Effective righting lever reduced at every angle - the ship works to the RESIDUAL curve
Equilibrium moves from upright to the crossing angle and stays there
Maximum righting lever reduced and displaced outwards
Range of stability reduced
Dynamical stability - the area - reduced; this is what actually capsizes ships
The loss is not recovered, because the list is permanent
Initial GM also reduced by the small vertical rise of G

steps.title: The three minimum intact stability criteria
points: Angle of heel due to grain shift not more than 12 degrees, or deck edge immersion for ships built on or after 1 January 1994, whichever is the lesser
Residual area between the heeling arm and righting arm curves not less than 0.075 metre-radians
Measured to the angle of maximum difference, or 40 degrees, or the flooding angle - whichever is LEAST
Initial GM, corrected for free surface of liquids in tanks, not less than 0.30 m
Cumulative - all three - and satisfied throughout the voyage, not just on departure

steps.title: Reading the three criteria off the one diagram
points: Criterion 1 is a point on the horizontal axis - the first crossing
Criterion 2 is the shaded area between the two curves
Criterion 3 is the slope at the origin, read at 57.3 degrees
They are not independent - a larger heeling arm fails 1 and 2 together, and the cure for both is the same

steps.title: Reducing the heeling moment, and the document that proves it
points: Fill and trim - the cheapest stability the ship will get
Minimise slack compartments; keep any that are unavoidable low
Secure the surface - overstowing, strapping or lashing, saucer and bundling
Longitudinal divisions and shifting boards halve the transverse travel
Plan consumption so the criteria hold all voyage as double bottom weight is burned off
Document of Authorization plus approved grain loading information; the master demonstrates compliance BEFORE loading

quick_revision.recall_15s: Grain settles, leaving a void; the surface slides to a new angle of repose and stays there, so the heel is permanent - not a free surface. The ship then works to the residual curve: heeled equilibrium, lower maximum GZ, shorter range, smaller area. Criteria: heel not more than 12 degrees (or deck edge immersion, whichever is less, for ships built on or after 1 January 1994); residual area not less than 0.075 metre-radians; fluid GM not less than 0.30 m. Heeling arm is a straight line, 40-degree value 0.8 of the zero value.
quick_revision.critical_numbers: 12 degrees maximum heel due to grain shift, or deck edge immersion for ships constructed on or after 1 January 1994, whichever is the lesser. 0.075 metre-radians minimum residual area. 0.30 m minimum fluid initial GM. Heeling arm at 40 degrees is 0.8 of the value at 0 degrees, joined by a straight line. Settlement conventionally about 2 per cent by volume. Tangent read at 57.3 degrees to obtain GM.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: The International Grain Code, resolution MSC.23(59), made mandatory through SOLAS chapter VI. Naming it is worth a mark on its own, and it is what keeps the answer out of the IMSBC Code, which does not apply to grain.
quick_revision.major_trap: Treating the grain shift as a free surface effect and correcting it as a virtual rise of G. A liquid free surface is symmetrical and reversible; a grain shift is one-way and leaves a permanent list. That is precisely why the Code uses a heeling arm curve rather than a GM correction, and a candidate who models it as free surface has misunderstood the whole regime.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the grain stability question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 what grain is and why it is regulated apart; 2 why it shifts and why the shift is irreversible; 3 from heeling moment to heeling arm; 4 drawing the diagram; 5 the effect on the statical stability curve; 6 the three criteria; 7 reading them off the diagram; 8 reducing the heeling moment and the Document of Authorization.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the three minimum grain stability criteria with their units.
retrieval_cards.answer: Angle of heel due to grain shift not greater than 12 degrees, or the angle of deck edge immersion for ships constructed on or after 1 January 1994, whichever is the lesser. Residual area between the heeling arm and righting arm curves not less than 0.075 metre-radians. Initial metacentric height, corrected for free surface of liquids in tanks, not less than 0.30 metres. All three, in all conditions, throughout the voyage.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Between which angles is the residual area measured?
retrieval_cards.answer: From the angle of equilibrium - where the heeling arm and righting arm curves first cross - up to whichever is LEAST of the angle of maximum difference between the two ordinates, 40 degrees, and the angle of flooding. Saying forty degrees and stopping is the standard half answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can grain shift not be treated as a free surface effect?
retrieval_cards.answer: A liquid free surface is symmetrical and reversible - it sloshes both ways and is handled by a virtual rise of G. A grain surface slides down to a new angle of repose and stays there, because nothing carries it back up. The result is a permanent list, not a symmetrical loss of stiffness, so the Code models it as a heeling arm rather than a GM correction.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is the grain heeling arm constructed on the diagram?
retrieval_cards.answer: The heeling arm at zero degrees is the total assumed volumetric heeling moment divided by the product of stowage factor and displacement. The heeling arm at forty degrees is 0.8 of that value. The two are joined by a straight line, drawn on the same axes as the GZ curve. It is a straight line, not a cosine curve.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does grain shift change the curve of statical stability?
retrieval_cards.answer: The ship works to the residual curve - righting arm minus heeling arm. Equilibrium moves from upright to the crossing angle and stays there; the maximum righting lever is reduced and moves outwards; the range of stability is shortened; and the area under the curve, the dynamical stability, is reduced. The loss is not recovered because the list is permanent.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which instrument governs bulk grain, and which one does not?
retrieval_cards.answer: The International Grain Code, adopted by resolution MSC.23(59) and made mandatory through SOLAS chapter VI. The IMSBC Code does NOT apply to grain, so an answer built on cargo groups, transportable moisture limits and individual schedules is answering about a different regime. The general intact stability criteria in the 2008 IS Code are also not the grain criteria.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You sail meeting all three criteria and burn double bottom fuel for a week. What is the risk?
retrieval_cards.answer: The criteria must be met throughout the voyage, not merely on departure. Consuming fuel and water from double bottoms removes bottom weight and raises G, reducing GM and the residual area, so a ship compliant at the berth can fall outside the criteria mid-passage. Consumption has to be planned into the loading condition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do you reduce the assumed heeling moment before sailing?
retrieval_cards.answer: Fill and trim compartments so far as possible - a filled trimmed hold carries a far smaller assumed moment than a partly filled one. Minimise slack compartments and keep any unavoidable one low. Secure a partly filled surface by overstowing, strapping or lashing, or saucer and bundling. Use shifting boards or a centreline division to halve the transverse travel.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A two-part technical question testing whether the candidate understands a physical mechanism and can connect it to a regulatory test. The first part is naval architecture: what a shifting granular cargo does to a righting arm curve. The second is the Code: the three numbers and the conditions attached to them. The examiner has bound them together by asking for a diagram, which is the instrument on which the mechanism and the criteria meet, and that is the real discriminator - a candidate who draws the diagram properly can answer both halves from it.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Sixteen marks on the stem with no printed split. The stem gives roughly equal billing to the effect on the curve and to the criteria, and expressly requires a diagram. The answer therefore allots sections 1 to 3 and 5 to the mechanism and its arithmetic, section 4 to the diagram placed centrally so that it serves both halves, sections 6 and 7 to the criteria and their reading, and section 8 to the practical control, which is where a management-level paper expects the answer to land.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the shift is understood as irreversible and therefore as producing a permanent angle of heel rather than a free surface loss. That the heeling arm is drawn as a straight line with the 0.8 factor at forty degrees. That all three criteria are stated with their units and with the conditions attached - the deck edge alternative, the least of three angles, and the free surface correction. That the diagram is labelled. And that the answer says how the heeling moment is controlled in practice.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: There is no primary source available. MIW holds no copy of the International Grain Code and the corpus SOLAS holding does not extend to chapter VI. The plan is therefore explicitly two-track: derive the mechanism and the effect on the GZ curve from naval architecture, which needs no citation and is the larger half of the answer; and state the regulatory architecture and the three criteria as settled published knowledge, graded as authoritative secondary, named to MSC.23(59) and SOLAS chapter VI by identity, and flagged for verification before publication. No cargo property figure is to be asserted, consistent with MIW's standing position established on the IMSBC questions.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - lower than any other question on this paper. There is no donor, so there is no later prose to contaminate the answer. The Grain Code criteria have been stable for decades and the only date inside the answer is a ship construction date thirty years past at this sitting. The SOLAS Consolidated Edition 2024 boundary is ten months future but nothing here depends on an edition.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The regime is wholly international and reaches the ship through SOLAS and the flag State's implementation of it. The one boundary that must not be crossed is between instruments rather than between States: grain is outside the IMSBC Code and the grain criteria are not the general intact stability criteria of the 2008 IS Code. Both boundaries are stated expressly in the answer.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: 'Grain carrier' is not a defined ship type; it is taken to mean any ship carrying grain in bulk, which is what the Code addresses. 'The existing minimum criteria' is taken to mean the Code's three intact stability criteria rather than the general intact stability criteria, because the stem says 'for grain carrying ships'. 'How the shifting of grain affects the curve' could be read narrowly as the geometry alone; it is answered as mechanism plus geometry plus consequence, since the consequence is what the criteria then guard against. The word 'existing' is read as a plain adjective and not as a hint at a pending amendment.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections. Prose for the mechanism and the boundaries; a numbered construction list for the diagram so the candidate can reproduce it step by step; a numbered list for the three criteria so they are countable; and bulleted lists for the effects on the curve, the reading of the criteria and the practical controls. A closing proposition stating what the criteria are actually for.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The three numerical grain stability criteria - 12 degrees or deck edge immersion whichever is lesser for ships constructed on or after 1 January 1994; residual area not less than 0.075 metre-radians measured to the least of the maximum-difference angle, 40 degrees and the flooding angle; and fluid initial GM not less than 0.30 m.
reverify_before_publication.why: MIW HOLDS NO COPY OF THE INTERNATIONAL GRAIN CODE. These are the substance of what the question asks for and are universally published, so they are given in full rather than withheld - but they are authoritative secondary knowledge, not text read at source. They should be checked against MSC.23(59) when a copy is acquired. This is the single largest evidence limitation on the paper and it is stated in the answer's own uncertainty section as well as here.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the assumed heeling arm is a straight line from its value at zero degrees to 0.8 of that value at forty degrees, the zero value being the total assumed volumetric heeling moment divided by stowage factor times displacement.
reverify_before_publication.why: Same limitation as the criteria - settled published construction, not read at source. It matters because the diagram is drawn from it and a candidate reproducing the answer draws a straight line on the strength of it.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the International Grain Code is adopted by resolution MSC.23(59) and made mandatory through SOLAS chapter VI, and that grain is outside the IMSBC Code.
reverify_before_publication.why: RESOLVED IN REVIEW. SOLAS chapter VI was read at source from the corpus copy of the Convention: regulation 8 defines the International Grain Code as the Code adopted by resolution MSC.23(59), and regulation 9 requires a cargo ship carrying grain to comply with it and to hold a Document of Authorization, the Code's requirements being "treated as mandatory". The reading is of the 2024 consolidated edition, which post-dates this sitting; regulation VI/9 is not among the provisions amended since, so the position at September 2023 is the same, and that edition point is the only residue. That grain sits outside the IMSBC Code remains authoritative secondary knowledge.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That grain settles by of the order of two per cent by volume after loading.
reverify_before_publication.why: A conventional working value from grain loading practice, given in the answer as such rather than as a Code figure. It is illustrative and no criterion depends on it.

regulations: International Code for the Safe Carriage of Grain in Bulk (International Grain Code), adopted by resolution MSC.23(59) - the assumed volumetric heeling moments, the heeling arm construction and the three intact stability criteria
SOLAS chapter VI - the chapter through which the International Grain Code is made mandatory, and the source of the Document of Authorization requirement
IMSBC Code - named only to place the boundary; grain in bulk is outside it
International Code on Intact Stability, 2008 - named only to place the boundary; the grain criteria are not its general intact stability criteria

sources: P1 - International Convention on Load Lines, 1966 as modified by the 1988 Protocol, as amended, Annex I chapter II, headed 'Conditions of assignment of freeboard' - read at source from the official IMO consolidated publication held in the corpus.

P1 - Regulation 10, Information to be supplied to the master: approved stability information, and loading information related to ship strength, to be carried on board at all times together with evidence that the information has been approved by the Administration; the information to be in a form approved by the Administration or a recognized organization.

P1 - Regulation 17, Machinery space openings: openings in position 1 or 2 to be properly framed and efficiently enclosed by steel casings of ample strength; access doors complying with regulation 12(1) with sills at least 600 mm above the deck in position 1 and at least 380 mm in position 2; double doors with an inner sill of 230 mm in conjunction with the outer sill of 600 mm for ships assigned freeboards less than those based on table 28.2; fiddley openings fitted with strong permanently attached covers.

P1 - Regulation 18, Miscellaneous openings: sills to doorways in companionways at least 600 mm above the deck in position 1 and at least 380 mm in position 2; 600 mm to doorways in deckhouses on the freeboard deck where access is not provided from above, and 380 mm where it is.

P1 - Regulation 19, Ventilators: coamings of steel or other equivalent material efficiently connected to the deck; at least 900 mm above the deck in position 1 and at least 760 mm in position 2; coamings exceeding 900 mm to be specially supported.

P1 - Regulation 20, Air pipes: exposed parts of substantial construction; height from the deck to the point where water may have access below at least 760 mm on the freeboard deck and 450 mm on the superstructure deck; air pipes to be provided with automatic closing devices; pressure-vacuum valves may be accepted on tankers.

P1 - Regulation 21, Cargo ports and other similar openings: doors ensuring the same watertightness and structural integrity as the surrounding shell plating, opening outwards unless otherwise granted; the number to be the minimum compatible with design and proper working; lower edge not below a line at its lowest point at least 230 mm above the upper edge of the uppermost load line.

P1 - Regulation 22, Scuppers, inlets and discharges: non-return valve arrangements graded by the height of the inboard end above the summer load line, with 0.01L and 0.02L thresholds; valve controls readily accessible and provided with indicators showing open or closed; scuppers led through the shell from enclosed superstructures used for the carriage of cargo permitted only where the freeboard deck edge is not immersed when the ship heels 5 degrees either way; substantial-thickness pipe scantlings of 7 mm, 10 mm and 12.5 mm at external diameters of 80 mm or less, 180 mm, and 220 mm or more, with linear interpolation between.

P1 - Regulation 22-1, Garbage chutes, and regulation 22-2, spurling pipes: interlocked gate valves with controls clearly marked 'Keep closed when not in use'; the inboard end above the waterline formed by an 8.5 degree heel and not less than 1,000 mm above the summer waterline; spurling pipes provided with permanently attached closing appliances to minimize water ingress.

P1 - Regulation 23, Side scuttles, windows and skylights: approved design and substantial construction, non-metallic frames not acceptable; side scuttles defined as round or oval openings not exceeding 0.16 square metres and larger ones treated as windows; hinged inside deadlights required for stated spaces; sills not below a line whose lowest point is 2.5 per cent of the breadth, or 500 mm, whichever is the greater, above the summer load line; windows not fitted below the freeboard deck.

P1 - Regulation 24, Freeing ports: minimum area on each side for each well on the freeboard deck of A = 0.7 + 0.035l square metres where the bulwark length in the well is 20 m or less, and A = 0.07l where it exceeds 20 m; half that area for wells on superstructure decks; adjustment of 0.004 square metres per metre of well length for each 0.1 m by which average bulwark height differs from the 1.2 m and 0.9 m thresholds; gutter bars exceeding 300 mm around tanker weather decks in way of cargo manifolds treated as bulwarks, with closures arranged so that jamming cannot occur at sea.

P1 - Part 5 of the publication, the Form of record of conditions of assignment of load lines: the item-by-item record of doorways, machinery casings, ventilators, air pipes and other fittings, recording for each the deck it is fitted on, the number, the material, the coaming dimensions and height, the type, and the closing appliances including the number of clips.

P2 - The 1988 Protocol relating to the Convention, which harmonized its survey and certification requirements with those of SOLAS and MARPOL - the source of the survey cycle behind limb C. Read from the publication's foreword.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT AND SHIPBOARD EXPERIENCE: the whole of the deterioration analysis in limb C. The Convention prescribes what shall be fitted; it does not describe how a fitting fails, and the specific instances given are derived from engineering practice and labelled as such.
