blocks.h: 1. Where the term comes from - what a freeboard assumes

blocks.p: A ship is assigned a freeboard - the distance from the waterline to the freeboard deck - and that freeboard is a measure of her reserve buoyancy: the enclosed, intact volume above the waterline that will lift her when she is pressed down by a sea.

But that reserve is only real if the enclosed volume stays enclosed. A hull with a generous freeboard and an open engine room skylight has no reserve buoyancy at all in the only condition that matters. So the freeboard cannot be assigned on the hull form alone. It is assigned on the assumption that every opening in the hull and superstructure can be closed, and kept closed and tight, in the weather the ship will meet.
The conditions of assignment are that assumption written down as enforceable requirements. Hold that sentence and the whole question follows from it.

The conditions of assignment are the structural and closing-appliance requirements of chapter II of Annex I to the International Convention on Load Lines, 1966 as modified by its 1988 Protocol - the chapter is headed 'Conditions of assignment of freeboard' - which a ship must satisfy before a freeboard is assigned to her, and must continue to satisfy for that freeboard to remain valid.
Four points complete the definition and are worth stating separately, because each is markable:

ul: They are conditions, not recommendations. A freeboard is assigned subject to them, so a ship that no longer meets them no longer properly holds the freeboard she is marked for.
They are continuing, not a one-off entrance test. They are verified at the initial survey and re-verified at every survey thereafter, which is the whole subject of limb C.

They are ship-specific and recorded. The Convention provides a Form of Record of conditions of assignment of load lines which lists, fitting by fitting, the deck each is on, its number, its material, its coaming dimensions and height, its type and its closing appliances down to the number of clips. That record is what makes them auditable rather than a matter of opinion.

They are the price of the freeboard. A ship assigned a smaller freeboard is required to meet stricter conditions - regulation 17, for example, requires double doors to the machinery casing on ships assigned freeboards less than those based on the tabular value, with an inner sill of 230 mm in conjunction with the outer sill of 600 mm. Less freeboard is bought with more protection.

blocks.h: 3. A. What the conditions consist of

blocks.p: Chapter II runs from regulation 10 to regulation 26 and covers, in order: the information to be supplied to the master; superstructure end bulkheads; doors; the position of hatchways, doorways and ventilators; cargo and other hatchways and their covers; machinery space openings; miscellaneous openings in freeboard and superstructure decks; ventilators; air pipes; cargo ports and other similar openings; scuppers, inlets and discharges, with garbage chutes and spurling pipes; side scuttles, windows and skylights; freeing ports; protection of the crew; and special conditions of assignment for type A ships.

Note the first of these, because candidates always omit it. Regulation 10 is a condition of assignment too: the master must be supplied with approved stability information, and with loading information relating to ship strength, in a form approved by the Administration or a recognized organization, and it must be carried on board at all times together with evidence that it has been approved. Paperwork, on this instrument, is a condition of the freeboard in exactly the same way a hatch cover gasket is.

blocks.h: 4. B. Protecting the openings - position and sill height

blocks.p: The first mechanism by which the conditions produce watertight integrity is geography. The Convention divides the exposed decks into position 1 and position 2 according to how exposed to boarding seas an opening is, and then requires more protection where the risk is greater. The pattern is consistent throughout the chapter:

ul: Machinery space access doors - sills at least 600 mm above the deck in position 1, at least 380 mm in position 2.
Companionway doorways - the same 600 mm and 380 mm; and 600 mm to doorways in deckhouses on the freeboard deck where there is no alternative access from above, reduced to 380 mm where there is.

Ventilator coamings - at least 900 mm above the deck in position 1, at least 760 mm in position 2, of steel or equivalent, efficiently connected to the deck, and specially supported where the coaming exceeds 900 mm.
Air pipes - the height from the deck to the point where water may have access below at least 760 mm on the freeboard deck and 450 mm on the superstructure deck.

Side scuttles - sills not below a line whose lowest point is 2.5 per cent of the breadth, or 500 mm, whichever is the greater, above the summer load line; and windows are not permitted below the freeboard deck at all.

blocks.p: The principle is simple and is worth stating: lift the opening above the water that will run across the deck, and where you cannot lift it far enough, do not put an opening there.

blocks.h: 5. B. Closures, coamings and the valves that stop back-flooding

blocks.p: Height alone is not enough, so the second mechanism is the closure itself, and the third is control of the penetrations through the shell.

ul: Structural enclosure. Machinery space openings in position 1 or 2 must be properly framed and efficiently enclosed by steel casings of ample strength. The casing is part of the buoyant envelope, not a weather shelter.

Permanently attached closures. Covers to fiddley openings must be of steel or equivalent material and permanently attached in their proper positions. A cover that can be left ashore is not a closing appliance, and this is why the Convention keeps using the word 'permanently'.

Weathertight hatch covers, secured by gaskets and clamping devices or by equivalent means to the Administration's satisfaction, and located in the closed position by means capable of withstanding horizontally acting loads in any sea conditions - because a cover that lifts and shifts in a seaway has failed even if it has not come off.

Air pipe closing devices. Air pipes must be provided with automatic closing devices; pressure-vacuum valves may be accepted on tankers. This is the fitting that stops a tank being downflooded by a wave breaking over the deck.

Cargo ports and shell openings. Doors so designed as to ensure the same watertightness and structural integrity as the surrounding shell plating, opening outwards so that sea pressure seats them, kept to the minimum number compatible with the design and proper working of the ship, and with the lower edge not below a line at least 230 mm above the upper edge of the uppermost load line.

Scuppers, inlets and discharges. This is where integrity is most often lost from the inside. The Convention grades the non-return valve arrangement by how high the inboard end sits above the summer load line, using 0.01L and 0.02L thresholds, and requires the valve controls to be readily accessible and provided with indicators showing whether the valve is open or closed. Pipes needing substantial thickness are given minimum scantlings - 7 mm, 10 mm and 12.5 mm at external diameters of 80 mm or less, 180 mm, and 220 mm or more.

Scuppers from cargo spaces. Scuppers led through the shell from enclosed superstructures used for carrying cargo are permitted only where the freeboard deck edge is not immersed when the ship heels 5 degrees either way - a neat example of the Convention writing a stability condition into a piping rule.

Garbage chutes and spurling pipes, the two penetrations everyone forgets. Chutes require interlocked gate valves with controls clearly marked 'Keep closed when not in use', and the inboard end above the waterline formed by an 8.5 degree heel and not less than 1,000 mm above the summer waterline. Spurling pipes require permanently attached closing appliances to minimize water ingress.

blocks.h: 6. B. Draining the deck, and protecting the crew who must close things

ul: Freeing ports. Where bulwarks form wells on weather decks, ample provision must be made for rapidly freeing the decks of water and draining them, and the Convention sets the minimum area: A = 0.7 + 0.035l square metres per side per well where the bulwark length in the well is 20 m or less, and A = 0.07l where it exceeds 20 m, halved for wells on superstructure decks, with an adjustment of 0.004 square metres per metre of well length for each 0.1 m by which the average bulwark height differs from the stated thresholds. The reasoning is direct: water trapped on deck is a large free surface of weight in the worst possible place, and a ship can be lost to it without a single opening having leaked. Note too that gutter bars over 300 mm on tanker weather decks in way of cargo manifolds are treated as bulwarks, and their closures must be arranged so that jamming cannot occur while at sea.

Protection of the crew. Guard rails, lifelines, gangways and safe access are conditions of assignment in their own right, and the connection to integrity is not decorative. Every closing appliance on this list has to be shut by a human being, often in the weather that makes it necessary. If the crew cannot reach the ventilator head or the freeing port shutter safely, the closure is theoretical.

Information to the master. Regulation 10's approved stability and loading information is what lets the ship be loaded so that the freeboard she is marked for is the freeboard she actually floats to, and so that she is not stressed into a condition none of the above was designed for.

blocks.h: 7. C. Why they need periodic inspection

ul: They are the only part of the freeboard that can deteriorate. Length, breadth, depth, sheer and superstructure length do not change over a ship's life. Gaskets, cleats, coamings, valves and shutters change continuously. So the freeboard's validity depends entirely on the part of the calculation that decays.

They are worked every day. Hatch covers, weathertight doors and freeing port shutters are operating machinery handled by the crew in every port. Wear is not a fault; it is certain, and it is why the interval is periodic rather than once.
They corrode in the worst places. Coamings, compression bars, drain channels and cleat pads are wet, salt-laden and difficult to paint properly.
They are damaged by cargo work. Grabs, forklifts, spreaders and steel cargo strike coamings, air pipe heads, guard rails and ventilator heads routinely.

They are defeated for operational convenience. This is the important one, and it is where inspection earns its place: the crew that lashes a freeing port shut to keep spray off the deck, or paints a deadlight open, has removed a condition of assignment deliberately and for what felt at the time like a good reason.

They are lost. Portable covers, deadlights and ventilator closing appliances go missing. The Convention's repeated insistence on permanently attached closures is a direct response, and inspection is how the missing item is found.

Ships are modified. Conversions, new penetrations, removed bulwarks and altered gutter bars change the arrangement recorded in the Form of Record, and an unapproved modification is only ever caught by someone comparing the ship to that record.

There is a record designed to be checked against. Because the Form of Record lists each fitting with its dimensions and closing appliances, inspection is an item-by-item verification against a document rather than a general impression - which is exactly what makes the annual survey around the anniversary date, the renewal survey, and port State control able to find things at all.

blocks.h: 8. C. Specific instances where they are found less than fully effective

blocks.p: The examiner has asked for specific instances, so name them. These are the findings that recur:

ul: Hatch covers - gaskets permanently compressed, hardened, painted over or missing in the cross-joints; compression bars corroded, wasted or set over so they no longer bear on the packing; cleats slack, seized, bent or removed; and the non-return valves in the drain channels missing or seized open, which turns the drainage arrangement into a direct route into the hold. A hose test or ultrasonic test on a cover that looks perfectly sound routinely fails on these.

Weathertight doors - gasket painted, hardened or torn; dogs and clips seized, missing or wound back so the door merely rests closed; hinges worn so the door does not pull up square; the door leaf itself set in from an impact so it cannot compress the gasket evenly.
Ventilators - closing appliances not permanently attached and simply absent; mushroom heads seized; coamings wasted at the deck connection; a ventilator cut and re-sited without approval.

Air pipes - the automatic closing device defective: float seized, ball missing, seat corroded, or the gauze so corroded that the head is effectively blanked. Air pipe heads on deck are also the fitting most often struck by cargo gear and left distorted.

Freeing ports - shutters seized on corroded hinge pins, jammed by dunnage or cargo residue, or deliberately secured shut. Where gutter bars are involved, closures found jammed at sea, which is the specific outcome the Convention writes against.

Scuppers, inlets and discharges - non-return valves seized open or with the flap missing; positive-closing valve controls inaccessible behind later pipework; indicators missing or reading the opposite of the valve's actual position; ship-side pipework wasted below the required substantial thickness.
Side scuttles and windows - deadlights missing, painted open, or hinges corroded solid; deadlights fitted where the space now requires them after a conversion, and not fitted.
Garbage chutes - covers left open, interlocks disconnected or defeated, and the required marking painted over.

Protection of the crew - guard rails slack or with wires parted, stanchions bent by cargo work, gangway lighting and safe access degraded so that closing appliances cannot be reached safely in the conditions that require them.
Regulation 10 information - the approved stability and loading information superseded by a conversion, or the evidence of approval no longer on board.

blocks.p: The proposition to close on: the freeboard is a calculation, and the conditions of assignment are what keep the calculation true. A ship whose closing appliances have quietly degraded is not marked with the wrong load line - she is marked with a load line she is no longer entitled to, and that is why the inspection is periodic and why the record exists to inspect against.

The marks are printed - 5, 5 and 6 - and they are not equal. Limb C is the largest and it is also the one that asks for something a textbook cannot supply: specific instances. Budget accordingly and do not let limb A, which is a definition worth five, absorb a third of the answer.

Section 1 exists to earn limb A rather than to introduce it. If the answer opens by explaining that a freeboard is a measure of reserve buoyancy, and that reserve buoyancy is only real while the enclosed volume stays enclosed, then the definition in section 2 is a consequence rather than a recitation - and an examiner can see immediately that the candidate knows why the conditions exist. That single idea is the spine of all three limbs.

Limb B is answered as three mechanisms - lift the opening, close it properly, drain the deck - rather than as a list of regulations. That is deliberate: the regulations are numerous and a list of them is hard to remember and harder to mark, while three mechanisms with examples hung on them covers the same ground and is reproducible under pressure. Limb C is split into reasons and instances because the stem asks for both, and candidates who merge them typically give reasons and forget the instances, which is where half the limb's marks sit.

ul: Defining conditions of assignment as the load line marks, or as the freeboard itself. They are the requirements the ship must meet in order to be assigned that freeboard.
Treating them as a one-off entrance test. They are continuing conditions, which is the premise of limb C.
Omitting regulation 10. The approved stability and loading information carried on board is a condition of assignment, and it is the one candidates never mention.
Answering limb B with a list of regulation numbers and no mechanism. Say what each requirement does.
Giving reasons in limb C and no specific instances, when the stem asks for instances by name.
Confusing weathertight with watertight. The Convention uses both, and they are not interchangeable.
Forgetting the openings nobody thinks about - garbage chutes, spurling pipes, air pipe closing devices. Naming these signals real shipboard knowledge.
Discussing SOLAS damage stability instead. This is a Load Line question.

Weathertight is not watertight. Weathertight means water will not penetrate into the ship in any sea condition; watertight is the stronger requirement, capable of resisting head pressure. Cargo ports below the freeboard deck are required to match the shell for watertightness; a hatch cover on deck is weathertight.
Position 1 and position 2 are the organising idea of the whole chapter. Nearly every sill and coaming figure comes in a pair, and the higher number is position 1.

Less freeboard means stricter conditions. Regulation 17's double doors with the 230 mm inner sill apply to ships assigned less than the tabular freeboard. This is the point that shows you understand the trade.
Freeing ports keep water OUT of the ship by letting it OFF the deck. A crew securing them shut to reduce spray has inverted the purpose, and it is a favourite oral scenario.
Cargo port doors open outwards so that sea pressure seats them rather than forcing them open.
Closing appliances must be permanently attached. The word recurs throughout the chapter and it is the answer to 'the cover is ashore in the store'.
The Form of Record is a real document. Knowing it exists, and that it lists fittings down to the number of clips, is what makes limb C a survey answer rather than a general one.
What exactly is a freeboard, and what does it measure?
What is the difference between weathertight and watertight? Give me a fitting that must be each.
What are positions 1 and 2, and give me a sill height for each.
Why must a cargo port door open outwards?
What is fitted to an air pipe and why?
Your freeing port shutters are lashed shut because the deck was flooding on passage. What do you say?
What is recorded in the Record of Conditions of Assignment?
You are assigned a freeboard less than the tabular value. What extra is required at the machinery casing?
Name three penetrations of the buoyant envelope that a surveyor commonly finds defective.

blocks.p: The spine of the whole answer is one sentence: freeboard is reserve buoyancy, and reserve buoyancy is only real while the enclosed volume stays enclosed. Limb B compresses to three verbs - LIFT the opening, CLOSE it, DRAIN the deck - with crew protection as the fourth that makes the other three possible. Limb C compresses to WEAR, CORRODE, DAMAGE, DEFEAT, LOSE, MODIFY: six causes, each of which generates its own instances, so you never have to recall the instances as a separate list.

ul: ICLL 1966 as modified by the 1988 Protocol, Annex I chapter II, headed Conditions of assignment of freeboard - regulations 10 to 26.
Regulation 10 - information to be supplied to the master; approved stability and loading information carried on board with evidence of approval.
Regulations 11 to 16 - superstructure end bulkheads, doors, position of openings, and hatchways and their covers.
Regulation 17 - machinery space openings; steel casings; sills 600 mm and 380 mm; double doors with a 230 mm inner sill for less than tabular freeboard.
Regulation 18 - miscellaneous openings; companionway sills 600 mm and 380 mm.
Regulation 19 - ventilators; coamings 900 mm and 760 mm.
Regulation 20 - air pipes; 760 mm and 450 mm; automatic closing devices.
Regulation 21 - cargo ports; outward opening; 230 mm above the uppermost load line.
Regulation 22 - scuppers, inlets and discharges; non-return valves; 0.01L and 0.02L; the 5 degree heel rule; 7, 10 and 12.5 mm scantlings. 22-1 garbage chutes, 22-2 spurling pipes.
Regulation 23 - side scuttles, windows and skylights; 0.16 square metres; deadlights; 2.5 per cent of breadth or 500 mm.
Regulation 24 - freeing ports; A = 0.7 + 0.035l and A = 0.07l; gutter bars over 300 mm.
Regulations 25 and 26 - protection of the crew; special conditions for type A ships.
Part 5 of the publication - the Form of record of conditions of assignment of load lines.

questions.understand_first: Start with what the load line on the ship's side is actually promising. It is not a rule about how much cargo you may carry for its own sake; it is a statement that above the water there remains a certain volume of sealed, buoyant hull - the part that lifts her again when a sea presses her down. That volume is the whole safety margin. Now notice the assumption hiding inside it. That volume is only buoyant while it stays sealed. A hull sitting high in the water with a jammed-open engine room vent, or a hatch whose packing has gone hard, has no margin at all in the one condition where the margin was supposed to matter - it simply fills. So the mark on the side cannot be earned by the shape of the hull alone. It is granted on condition that every hole through that sealed volume - doors, hatches, vents, air pipes, discharge lines, scuttles, even the rubbish chute and the pipe the anchor cable runs through - can be shut and will stay tight in bad weather. Write that bargain down as a list of requirements and you have the conditions of assignment. Two consequences follow and they are the rest of the question. First, the requirements have a pattern: put the opening high enough that water running across the deck does not reach it, make the thing that closes it strong, tight and impossible to leave behind, and give the water on deck somewhere to run away to. Second, and this is why they must be looked at again and again: the hull's dimensions never change, but a gasket, a cleat, a hinge and a valve all do. The freeboard was calculated once; the things it depends on wear out continuously.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Freeboard = reserve buoyancy, and reserve buoyancy is only real while the enclosed volume stays enclosed. The conditions of assignment are chapter II of Annex I to the Load Line Convention - the closing-appliance and structural requirements a ship must meet and keep meeting to hold her freeboard, recorded fitting by fitting in the Form of Record. They work by LIFT the opening, CLOSE it properly, DRAIN the deck. They need periodic inspection because they are the only part of the freeboard that decays.
quick_revision.critical_numbers: Sills 600 mm position 1 / 380 mm position 2. Ventilator coamings 900 mm / 760 mm. Air pipes 760 mm freeboard deck / 450 mm superstructure deck. Machinery double doors: inner sill 230 mm with outer 600 mm. Cargo port lower edge 230 mm above the uppermost load line. Side scuttle sills 2.5% of breadth or 500 mm, whichever greater. Side scuttle / window boundary 0.16 m2. Discharges graded at 0.01L and 0.02L; cargo-space scuppers at 5 degrees heel. Pipe scantlings 7 / 10 / 12.5 mm. Freeing ports A = 0.7 + 0.035l to 20 m, A = 0.07l beyond. Gutter bars over 300 mm. Garbage chute 8.5 degrees heel and 1,000 mm.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Annex I chapter II of the International Convention on Load Lines, 1966 as modified by the 1988 Protocol - the chapter is literally headed 'Conditions of assignment of freeboard', which is the cleanest possible answer to limb A. Regulations 10 to 26.
quick_revision.major_trap: Confusing weathertight with watertight, and its practical cousin - assuming a fitting that looks sound is effective. The recurring real-world failure is the hatch cover drain channel non-return valve, missing or seized, which converts the cover's own drainage arrangement into a direct path into the hold on a cover that passes visual inspection.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the conditions of assignment question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 what a freeboard assumes; 2 limb A the definition; 3 limb A what the conditions consist of; 4 limb B position and sill height; 5 limb B closures, coamings and valves; 6 limb B draining the deck and protecting the crew; 7 limb C why periodic inspection; 8 limb C specific instances of ineffectiveness.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define conditions of assignment.
retrieval_cards.answer: The structural and closing-appliance requirements of Annex I chapter II of the Load Line Convention as modified by the 1988 Protocol - the chapter is headed Conditions of assignment of freeboard - which a ship must satisfy before a freeboard is assigned and must continue to satisfy for it to remain valid. They are conditions not recommendations, continuing not one-off, and recorded ship by ship in the Form of Record.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the position 1 and position 2 figures for door sills, ventilator coamings and air pipes.
retrieval_cards.answer: Door and companionway sills: at least 600 mm in position 1, at least 380 mm in position 2. Ventilator coamings: at least 900 mm in position 1, at least 760 mm in position 2, specially supported where over 900 mm. Air pipes: height to the point where water may enter below at least 760 mm on the freeboard deck and 450 mm on the superstructure deck.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Weathertight or watertight?
retrieval_cards.answer: Weathertight means water will not penetrate into the ship in any sea condition - the standard for deck closures such as hatch covers and exposed doors. Watertight is the stronger standard, capable of resisting head pressure - required for cargo ports and shell openings, which must ensure the same watertightness and structural integrity as the surrounding shell plating.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must cargo port doors open outwards, and how low may they be?
retrieval_cards.answer: Outward opening means sea pressure seats the door rather than forcing it open. The lower edge must not be below a line drawn parallel to the freeboard deck at side whose lowest point is at least 230 mm above the upper edge of the uppermost load line, and the number of such openings must be the minimum compatible with the design and proper working of the ship.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The crew have lashed the freeing port shutters shut because the well deck was flooding. What is wrong?
retrieval_cards.answer: It inverts the purpose. Freeing ports keep water out of the ship by letting it off the deck. Trapped water is a large weight with a free surface in the worst possible place, and a ship can be lost to it without a single opening having leaked. The Convention requires ample provision for rapidly freeing and draining the decks, and sets a minimum area for it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give five specific instances of conditions of assignment found less than fully effective.
retrieval_cards.answer: Hatch cover gaskets hardened or painted and drain channel non-return valves missing or seized; weathertight door dogs seized or missing and gaskets painted; ventilator closing appliances absent because not permanently attached; air pipe automatic closing devices with seized float or corroded gauze; freeing port shutters seized, jammed by dunnage or deliberately lashed shut.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why do conditions of assignment, uniquely, need periodic inspection?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because they are the only part of the freeboard that can deteriorate. Length, breadth, depth, sheer and superstructure length never change, so the calculation stays valid - but gaskets, cleats, coamings, hinges, valves and shutters wear, corrode, are damaged by cargo work, are defeated for convenience, go missing, and are altered by conversion. The freeboard's validity rests entirely on the part that decays.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Form of Record of conditions of assignment, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: A Convention form recording each fitting individually - the deck it is on, the number, the material, the coaming dimensions and height, the type, and the closing appliances down to the number of clips. It matters because it turns inspection into item-by-item verification against a document rather than a general impression, and it is how an unapproved modification is detected.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A three-limb question moving from definition to function to defect, and the marks rise as it goes. The examiner is testing whether the candidate understands that a load line is a conditional grant rather than a measurement - and then, in the largest limb, whether he has actually seen the fittings fail. Limb C is the discriminator: a candidate who has stood on a hatch top can name the drain channel non-return valve and the set-over compression bar, and one who has only read about it cannot.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Printed 5 + 5 + 6, summing to 16. The allocation is explicit and unequal, and it is the reason for the answer's shape. Limb A gets sections 1 to 3, with section 1 doing the conceptual work that makes the definition worth its five marks. Limb B gets sections 4 to 6, organised as three mechanisms rather than as a regulation list. Limb C, the largest, gets sections 7 and 8, split so that the reasons and the specific instances the stem separately demands are separately visible.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: A definition that names the instrument and the chapter and conveys that the conditions are continuing rather than an entrance test. In limb B, a mechanism for each requirement rather than a recitation of numbers - though the numbers, given in pairs by position, are what prove the knowledge. In limb C, both halves: reasons why inspection must be periodic, and named instances of ineffectiveness. Naming the less obvious fittings - garbage chutes, spurling pipes, air pipe closing devices, drain channel non-return valves - is what marks out a shipboard answer.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: This question has a genuine primary source and it is used. The corpus holds the official IMO consolidated publication of the Convention as modified by the 1988 Protocol. The file has no text layer, so the plan is to render and read Annex I chapter II directly - from its opening at regulation 10 through the machinery, ventilator, air pipe, cargo port, discharge, side scuttle and freeing port regulations - and to inspect the Part 5 Form of Record. Every dimension in the answer is to come from that reading and none from recollection. Limb C's deterioration analysis is expressly NOT to be sourced to the Convention, which prescribes fittings and not failure modes, and is to be labelled engineering judgement.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - lowest on the paper, for two reasons that are worth recording together. There is no donor, so no later MIW prose can contaminate the answer. And the source consulted consolidates the Convention as of 31 December 2021 - twenty-one months BEFORE the sitting - so it is structurally incapable of introducing a post-sitting amendment. The residual risk is the narrow window between 1 January 2022 and September 2023, which is recorded.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The Convention reaches the ship through her flag State, which at this sitting means the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 for an Indian ship, and the assignment and survey work is commonly performed by a Recognized Organization on the Administration's behalf. The one boundary to hold is between instruments rather than States: this is a Load Line question and not a SOLAS damage stability question, and the watertight subdivision requirements of SOLAS are a different regime that must not be imported.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: The stem says 'watertight integrity' while the Convention distinguishes weathertight from watertight and applies the weaker standard to most deck closures. The answer treats the phrase as the examiner's general term for the integrity of the buoyant envelope and states the distinction expressly rather than adopting the loose usage silently. 'Specific instances where they can be found to be less than fully effective' is read as inviting real survey findings rather than hypothetical failures, which is why limb C names fittings and modes rather than principles. The printed limbs are lettered A, B and C in upper case where the rest of the paper uses lower case or parentheses; that is preserved.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections following the printed limb order. Prose for the conceptual opening and the definition, because both are arguments. Bulleted lists everywhere else so that each requirement, each reason and each instance is separately countable - which matters more here than usual, because limb C's six marks are earned by the number of distinct instances named. A closing proposition tying the inspection back to the validity of the freeboard itself.

blocks.p: A survey is an examination of the ship herself - her structure, machinery, equipment and arrangements - against prescriptive technical requirements, to establish that her physical condition satisfies the relevant convention. A safety management audit is a systematic and independent examination to determine whether the safety management system and the activities carried out under it conform to planned arrangements, are implemented effectively, and are suitable to achieve the objectives.
Put shortly: a survey looks at the ship; an audit looks at the system and at the people who run it.

rows: Object
The ship - hull, machinery, equipment, arrangements
The management system and its implementation, ashore and afloat
Measured against
Prescriptive technical requirements of a convention
The Code's functional requirements and the Company's own documented system
Method
Physical examination, measurement, testing, witnessing
Sampling of objective evidence - records, documents, interviews, observation of practice
Finding is called
A deficiency
A non-conformity, a major non-conformity, or an observation

Is the ship in the required condition?
Is the system working, and is it being followed?

The statutory certificates of the ship's condition
The Document of Compliance and the Safety Management Certificate

blocks.h: 2. (a) Why the distinction matters on a real ship

ul: A ship can pass every survey and fail an audit, and the reverse. Equipment in perfect order that nobody has been trained to use, or maintenance carried out but never recorded, is a system failure with no physical defect. A wasted plate is a physical defect with no system failure - unless the planned maintenance system should have found it, in which case it is both.

A deficiency is corrected; a non-conformity requires a cause to be found. That is the practical difference for the Chief Engineer. Repairing the item closes a survey deficiency. Closing a non-conformity means establishing why the system permitted it and correcting that, which is why corrective action under the Code is the Company's responsibility and not the auditor's.

An audit samples; a survey examines. An auditor cannot see everything and does not pretend to - he takes objective evidence and reasons from it. This is why an audit finding is expressed as a conformity judgement about a system rather than as a list.
They are done by different people to different standards, and the same visit may involve both - which is exactly why a candidate must be able to say which is which.

blocks.h: 3. The position of the recognized organization

blocks.p: All four scenarios in limb (b) turn on one point, so state it once. Where the Administration has delegated ISM certification, the Administration remains responsible for verifying compliance with the Code and for issuing the Document of Compliance and the Safety Management Certificate. The recognized organization acts on its behalf, within a scope specified in the authorization.

So the RO makes the technical judgements that verification requires - is this a non-conformity, is it major, has corrective action been taken and is it effective. It does not have authority to alter the terms on which the flag State certified the ship. That distinction decides every one of the four answers below: where the question is one of verification the RO acts, and where the question is one of the certificate's terms the RO refers to the Administration.

blocks.h: 4. (b)(i) Where there is evidence of a major non conformity

blocks.p: A major non-conformity is an identifiable deviation posing a serious threat to the safety of personnel or the ship, or a serious risk to the environment, requiring immediate corrective action - and it includes the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the Code.

ul: The certificate must not be issued, and an existing certificate must not be endorsed for the annual or intermediate verification.
The finding must be downgraded to a non-conformity by immediate corrective action before a certificate can be issued or endorsed. Downgrading is a judgement on evidence, and it is the RO's to make.
Where the ship is the one holding a major non-conformity, the Administration and the port State are informed in accordance with the established procedures for observed major non-conformities.
Where corrective action is not taken, the RO reports to the Administration, which decides on withdrawal.

blocks.p: An ordinary non-conformity is an observed situation where objective evidence indicates the non-fulfilment of a specified requirement, but without the serious threat that makes it major. The consequences are materially different.

ul: The certificate may still be issued or endorsed.
The Company - not the RO - is responsible for determining and initiating the corrective action needed to correct the non-conformity or its cause, within an agreed time.
Corrective actions and any consequent changes to the system are recorded, and their completion is verified, normally at the next verification or earlier if the finding warrants it.

Failure to correct may itself become a major non-conformity, because it evidences a lack of effective and systematic implementation. That is the sentence which links this scenario to the previous one and it is worth stating.

blocks.h: 6. (b)(iii) Where an extension of the Safety Management Certificate is requested

blocks.p: Answer this one by first saying what is not there. Neither the ISM Code nor the guidelines contain a general power to extend a Safety Management Certificate. The Code provides for verification and for renewal before expiry, and it fixes what the validity of a renewed certificate is; it does not create a discretion to prolong a certificate that is running out.

ul: It follows that the RO has nothing of its own to grant. The request lies outside the delegated verification function.

The RO's action is to refer the request to the Administration, which alone may decide what to do with a certificate it issued, and to advise on the conditions under which any short extension might be contemplated - which is a technical judgement and therefore properly the RO's.

It also verifies the ship's actual position - when the renewal verification is due, what is outstanding, and whether the system is being maintained - so that the Administration decides on evidence rather than on assertion.
It does not endorse or annotate the certificate on its own authority.

blocks.h: 7. (b)(iv) Where revision of an entry on a certificate is requested

blocks.p: The entries on a Document of Compliance or a Safety Management Certificate record what the flag State certified - the Company and its address, the ship, and the ship types covered. The RO issues on the Administration's behalf and therefore may not amend that record on its own authority. Its first action is to establish which kind of change is being asked for:

ul: Administrative - a change of company name or address, or of ship name, where the underlying facts of certification are unchanged. The RO verifies that the change is genuine and supported, refers it to the Administration, and on its authority the certificate is re-issued with the corrected entry.

Substantive - a change of Company, or the addition of a ship type to the scope. This is not a correction at all: it changes what was certified, so it requires verification appropriate to the change - which for a change of Company means the new Company's system must be verified, and an interim certificate may be the proper instrument while that is done.

blocks.p: In both cases the RO records the change and reports it to the Administration. It does not simply amend the certificate in hand.

blocks.h: 8. (c) When the DOC and the SMC may be invalidated

blocks.p: The Document of Compliance may be withdrawn or cease to be valid where:

ul: the annual verification is not requested - it must be carried out within three months before or after each anniversary date;
there is evidence of major non-conformity with the Code;
it expires without renewal verification having been completed - the period of validity is five years;
the Company ceases to be the Company responsible for the operation of the ships, or the conditions on which it was issued otherwise fall away.

blocks.p: The Safety Management Certificate may be withdrawn or cease to be valid where:

ul: the Document of Compliance is withdrawn - all associated Safety Management Certificates and interim certificates are withdrawn with it. This is the trigger candidates most often miss and it is the most examinable point in the limb: the ship's certificate depends on the Company's.
the intermediate verification is not requested - at least one is required between the second and third anniversary dates;
there is evidence of major non-conformity with the Code;
it expires without renewal verification - again a five-year period of validity;
there is a change of Company or of flag, the certificate having been issued to that ship operated by that Company under that Administration.

blocks.p: Underlying all of these: failure to correct non-conformities may affect the validity of the Document of Compliance and of the related Safety Management Certificates, and failure to take adequate corrective action may itself be treated as a major non-conformity. Note finally the direction of authority, which is the closing proposition: the RO establishes the facts and reports; the Administration withdraws.

The marks are printed and they have shifted from the way this question is usually set. Limb (a) is worth four, not two, so a one-line contrast will not do - it needs a worked comparison, which is why the answer gives a table and then a section on why the distinction bites. Limb (b) is four separate two-mark parts, so each scenario must be a self-contained answer with its own action; a flowing narrative that covers all four in one breath will be marked as one. Limb (c) is worth four rather than six, so the grounds are given cleanly without extended commentary.

Section 3 is the structural decision that makes limb (b) work. All four scenarios turn on the same point - whether the question is one of verification, which the RO may decide, or one of the certificate's terms, which it may not. Stating that once, before the scenarios, means each of the four can then be answered in the two marks' worth of space it actually has, instead of re-arguing the principle four times.

Limb (c) is written as two separate lists because the DOC and the SMC have different triggers and the examiner is looking for both. The single highest-value sentence in the whole answer is that withdrawal of the DOC carries all associated SMCs and interim certificates with it.

ul: Answering limb (a) with one sentence. It is worth four marks at this sitting, which is a quarter of the question.
Saying an audit checks the ship and a survey checks the paperwork. It is the other way round in substance: the survey examines the ship, the audit examines the system.

Treating a major non-conformity as merely a serious non-conformity. It has a definition, and it includes the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a Code requirement - which is how a series of small failures becomes major.
Saying the RO withdraws the certificate. It does not. It verifies, reports and refers; the Administration withdraws.
Inventing a power to extend the Safety Management Certificate. There is no general extension power, and saying so is the correct answer to (b)(iii).
Treating a change of Company as a clerical correction. It changes what was certified and requires verification, not re-typing.
Forgetting that withdrawal of the DOC withdraws every associated SMC.
Giving the verification windows loosely. Three months either side of the anniversary for the DOC; between the second and third anniversaries for the SMC intermediate.

The operative guidelines at this sitting are the 2017 edition, resolution A.1118(30). The 2023 Guidelines, A.1188(33), were adopted 6 December 2023 - three months AFTER this paper - and revoked A.1118(30). Any study material written for a 2024 or later sitting cites the later resolution, correctly for itself and wrongly for this one.
Do not quote a guideline paragraph number. The paragraph numbering of the operative edition is not something you can safely reproduce, and the substance you need is in the Code itself.
Deficiency versus non-conformity. The word tells the examiner which process you are describing, and using the wrong one signals that the limb (a) distinction has not landed.

Downgrading a major non-conformity is a real mechanism. Immediate corrective action can reduce it to a non-conformity and allow the certificate to be issued. Knowing this separates a good answer from a list.
The Company owns corrective action. Not the RO, not the auditor. The auditor verifies that it was taken.
Five years for both certificates, with different intermediate arrangements - annual for the DOC, at least one intermediate between the second and third anniversaries for the SMC.
Interim certificates exist, and an interim SMC is the right instrument when a ship changes Company or flag. Reaching for it in (b)(iv) shows real familiarity.
Define a major non-conformity. What is the second half of the definition that everyone forgets?
Can a major non-conformity ever be downgraded? By whom, and on what?
Your DOC is withdrawn. What happens to your ship's SMC?
Who is responsible for corrective action on a non-conformity?
When must the DOC annual verification be carried out, and the SMC intermediate?
The Company is sold to a new manager mid-certificate. What happens?
Can your RO extend your Safety Management Certificate by two months?
You are surveyed and audited on the same day by the same organization. Are those the same thing?

blocks.p: Limb (a): SHIP versus SYSTEM, and the four consequences - object, method, finding, certificate. Limb (b): one principle, VERIFICATION the RO decides, TERMS the Administration decides, then MAJOR - MINOR - EXTEND - REVISE. Limb (c): two lists, and one sentence linking them - DOC falls, SMC falls with it. The numbers to hold are 5 years / 3 months either side / between the 2nd and 3rd anniversaries.

questions.understand_first: Two completely different kinds of checking happen on a ship and they are easy to confuse because the same organisation often does both, sometimes on the same day. One asks is the ship in the state she is supposed to be in - is the steel thick enough, does the pump run, is the lifeboat sound. Someone looks at the thing, measures it, tests it, and what he finds is a fault in an object. The other asks a quite different question: is there a working system here, and are people actually following it? That cannot be answered by looking at objects, because a ship can be immaculate and still be run by improvisation, and it can be shabby and still be run by a system that knows exactly what is wrong and when it will be fixed. So the second kind of checking works by sampling evidence - reading records, asking the third engineer what he would do, watching whether what the manual says actually happens - and what it finds is not a broken object but a gap between what the system promises and what is being done. That difference explains why the repair that closes the first kind of finding does not close the second: fixing the pump does not answer why the system let it fail unnoticed. The second half of the question is about a limit on authority. When a flag state hires an outside organisation to do this checking for it, that organisation gets to make the professional judgements - is this a gap, is it serious, has it really been fixed. What it does not get is the flag state's own power to decide the terms of the certificate it issues in the flag state's name. So on any request that would change those terms - extend it, alter what it says - the organisation gathers the facts and hands the decision upward. Sort each of the four situations into judgement or terms, and the answers fall out.
questions.memory_cue: Limb (a): SHIP versus SYSTEM (1), then WHY IT BITES (2). The RO's limit: VERIFICATION versus TERMS (3). Then MAJOR - MINOR - EXTEND - REVISE (4 to 7). steps.title: (a) Audit and survey distinguished
points: A survey examines the ship against prescriptive technical requirements
An audit is a systematic and independent examination of the safety management system and its implementation
The ship versus the system and the people who run it
Different object, method, finding and certificate - deficiency against non-conformity

steps.title: (a) Why the distinction matters on a real ship
points: A ship can pass every survey and fail an audit, and the reverse
A deficiency is corrected; a non-conformity requires its cause to be found and corrected
An audit samples objective evidence, a survey examines
Different people, different standards, often the same visit

steps.title: The position of the recognized organization
points: The Administration remains responsible for verification and for issuing the DOC and SMC
The RO acts on its behalf within a scope specified in the authorization
The RO makes the technical judgements verification requires
It has no authority to alter the terms on which the flag State certified the ship
VERIFICATION the RO decides; TERMS the Administration decides - this settles all four scenarios

steps.title: (b)(i) Where there is evidence of a major non conformity
points: Definition: serious threat to personnel or ship or serious risk to the environment, requiring immediate corrective action; includes lack of effective and systematic implementation
The certificate must not be issued and an existing certificate must not be endorsed
It must be downgraded to a non-conformity by immediate corrective action first
Administration and port State informed under the established procedures
If not corrected, report to the Administration, which decides on withdrawal

steps.title: (b)(ii) Where non-conformities are found
points: Definition: objective evidence indicating non-fulfilment of a specified requirement, without the serious threat
The certificate may still be issued or endorsed
The COMPANY determines and initiates the corrective action, within an agreed time
Corrective actions recorded and their completion verified
Failure to correct may itself become a major non-conformity

steps.title: (b)(iii) Where an extension of the Safety Management Certificate is requested
points: Neither the Code nor the guidelines contain a general power of extension
The RO therefore has nothing of its own to grant
It refers the request to the Administration, which alone may decide
It advises on the technical conditions and verifies the ship's actual position
It does not endorse or annotate the certificate on its own authority

steps.title: (b)(iv) Where revision of an entry on a certificate is requested
points: The entries record what the flag State certified - Company, address, ship, ship types
The RO may not amend that record on its own authority
Administrative change: verify it is genuine, refer, and the certificate is re-issued on the Administration's authority
Substantive change - change of Company or added ship type: verification appropriate to the change, and an interim certificate may be the proper instrument
In both cases record and report; do not amend the certificate in hand

steps.title: (c) When the DOC and the SMC may be invalidated
points: DOC: annual verification not requested, within three months before or after each anniversary date
DOC: evidence of major non-conformity; expiry without renewal; five-year validity; the Company ceasing to be the responsible Company
SMC: withdrawal of the DOC withdraws ALL associated SMCs and interim certificates - the trigger most often missed
SMC: intermediate verification not requested, at least one between the second and third anniversaries
SMC: evidence of major non-conformity; expiry without renewal; change of Company or of flag
Failure to correct non-conformities may affect validity, and may itself be a major non-conformity
The RO establishes the facts and reports; the Administration withdraws

quick_revision.recall_15s: Survey looks at the ship; audit looks at the system. Deficiency against non-conformity. The RO decides verification; the Administration decides the certificate's terms. Major NC - do not issue or endorse until downgraded by immediate corrective action; inform Administration and port State. NC - may still issue; the Company owns the corrective action. Extension - no such power exists; refer to the Administration. Revision - administrative means re-issue on the Administration's authority; substantive means fresh verification. DOC falls and every SMC falls with it.
quick_revision.critical_numbers: Five years - the period of validity of both the DOC and the SMC. Three months before or after each anniversary date - the DOC annual verification window. At least one intermediate verification of the SMC, between the second and third anniversary dates. MSC.353(92), in force 1 January 2015 - the Code text at this sitting. MSC/Circ.1059 - MEPC/Circ.401, 16 December 2002. A.1118(30), 2017 - the operative guidelines edition here.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: ISM Code section 13, certification and periodical verification. It is where the validities, the verification windows and the grounds of withdrawal all live, it is mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX, and - crucially for this sitting - it has not been amended since MSC.353(92), so it is the one place the answer can stand without depending on which edition of the guidelines was current.
quick_revision.major_trap: Citing A.1188(33), the 2023 Guidelines on implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations. It was adopted 6 December 2023, three months AFTER this sitting, and it revoked A.1118(30), which is the operative edition here. Every piece of study material written for a 2024 or later paper carries the later number, correctly for itself and wrongly for this one - and the substance is so similar between the editions that the error looks entirely plausible.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the audit, survey and ISM certificate question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 audit and survey distinguished; 2 why the distinction matters; 3 the RO's position - verification versus terms; 4 major non conformity; 5 non-conformities; 6 extension of the SMC; 7 revision of an entry; 8 when the DOC and SMC may be invalidated.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Audit or survey - what is the difference?
retrieval_cards.answer: A survey examines the ship - structure, machinery, equipment, arrangements - against prescriptive technical requirements, and reports deficiencies. An audit is a systematic and independent examination of the safety management system and its implementation, sampling objective evidence, and reports non-conformities, major non-conformities and observations. The survey asks whether the ship is in the required condition; the audit asks whether the system is working.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a major non-conformity.
retrieval_cards.answer: An identifiable deviation posing a serious threat to the safety of personnel or the ship, or a serious risk to the environment, requiring immediate corrective action - and it includes the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the Code. The second half is the part candidates forget, and it is how an accumulation of small failures becomes major.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Evidence of a major non-conformity is found. What does the RO do?
retrieval_cards.answer: It does not issue the certificate and does not endorse an existing one. The finding must first be downgraded to a non-conformity by immediate corrective action, which is the RO's judgement on evidence. The Administration and the port State are informed under the established procedures for observed major non-conformities. If corrective action is not taken, it reports to the Administration, which decides on withdrawal.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The owner asks the RO to extend the Safety Management Certificate. What is the answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: There is no general power to extend an SMC in the Code or the guidelines - the Code provides for verification and for renewal before expiry, not for prolonging a certificate. The RO therefore has nothing of its own to grant. It refers the request to the Administration, advises on the technical conditions, and verifies what is actually outstanding. It does not endorse or annotate the certificate on its own authority.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your Document of Compliance is withdrawn. What happens to the ships?
retrieval_cards.answer: All associated Safety Management Certificates and interim certificates are withdrawn with it. The ship's certificate depends on the Company's, and this is the trigger most often missed in the invalidation limb. The DOC itself may fall for a missed annual verification, evidence of major non-conformity, expiry without renewal, or the Company ceasing to be the responsible Company.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which edition of the ISM implementation guidelines applies at a September 2023 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: A.1118(30) of 2017. NOT A.1188(33) - that was adopted 6 December 2023, three months after the sitting, and it revoked A.1118(30). Material written for any later sitting carries the newer number, and because the substance is largely unchanged between the editions the error looks entirely plausible. Cite the Code itself where you can.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the ISM verification periods.
retrieval_cards.answer: Both the DOC and the SMC are valid for five years. The DOC is verified annually, within three months before or after each anniversary date. The SMC requires at least one intermediate verification between the second and third anniversary dates. Both require renewal verification before expiry.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who is responsible for corrective action on a non-conformity, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Company, not the recognized organization and not the auditor. The auditor identifies the non-conformity and later verifies that the action was taken and was effective. It matters because closing a non-conformity means finding and correcting the cause within the system - which only the Company can do - whereas closing a survey deficiency means repairing the item.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A three-limb question that moves from a conceptual distinction to four applied scenarios and then to a rule set. The examiner is testing whether the candidate understands that safety management is verified by a different process from the one that verifies the ship, and then - in the four scenarios - whether he understands the limit on delegated authority. The scenarios are chosen with care: two of them are matters of technical judgement, which the RO decides, and two are matters of the certificate's terms, which it does not. A candidate who sees that pattern answers all four correctly in very little space.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Printed 4 + (2+2+2+2) + 4, summing to 16, and the distribution differs from the way this question is usually set. Limb (a) at four marks needs a worked comparison, not a sentence, and gets two sections. Each scenario in limb (b) carries its own two marks and must therefore be a discrete, self-contained answer - which is why the shared principle is stated once, in its own section, before them. Limb (c) at four marks is given cleanly as two lists of grounds without the extended commentary a six-mark version could support.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: In limb (a), a distinction expressed in terms of object, method and finding - and the vocabulary used correctly, deficiency against non-conformity. In limb (b), a specific action for each scenario, with the recognition that the RO refers rather than decides where the certificate's terms are in question, and the recognition that no general power of extension exists. In limb (c), both certificates treated separately, with the dependency of the SMC on the DOC stated expressly.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: Anchor on the ISM Code itself rather than on the implementation guidelines, and do so deliberately. Section 13 supplies the validities, the verification windows and the grounds of withdrawal; the Code's own definitions supply non-conformity and major non-conformity; sections 9 and 12 supply reporting and the Company's ownership of corrective action. The corpus holds the full adopting and amending chain from A.741(18) to MSC.353(92) and records MSC.353(92) as the latest amendment, so the held text is the text operative at this sitting. Add MSC/Circ.1059 - MEPC/Circ.401 for major non-conformity procedures and the RO Code for the scope of delegation. Name A.1118(30) as the operative guidelines edition BY IDENTITY ONLY. Deliberately NOT planned: any paragraph number from A.1188(33), and any cross-walk between the two guideline editions.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH - The mandatory instrument is completely stable - the Code has been unamended since 1 January 2015 - but the recommendatory guidelines changed three months after this sitting, and the donor is built on the later edition. The risk is unusually severe because the two editions are substantively similar, so an imported citation reads as correct rather than as obviously anachronistic. The mitigation is structural rather than editorial: the answer is built on the Code, which did not move, and the guidelines are named without being relied upon.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MEDIUM, and it is the subject of limb (b) rather than a hazard to it. Three levels must stay distinct: the Code, mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX; the flag Administration, which certifies and withdraws; and the recognized organization, which acts within a scope specified in its authorization. The specific error to avoid is attributing withdrawal to the RO. For an Indian ship the Administration acts under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 at this sitting.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: The stem spells the same term two ways in adjacent sub-limbs - 'major non conformity' at (b)(i) and 'nonconformities' at (b)(ii) - which is preserved as printed and not remarked on. '(b)(iii) When an extension of the Safety Management Certificate is requested for' does not say by whom or on what grounds; it is answered generally, and the honest core of the answer is that no general extension power exists. 'Revision of an entry' is ambiguous between a clerical correction and a change in what was certified, and the answer resolves it by treating both, since the distinction is what carries the marks. 'Invalidated' in limb (c) is read as covering both active withdrawal and a certificate ceasing to be valid by operation of the Code.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections. A three-column comparison table for limb (a), because a table makes a four-mark distinction countable at a glance, followed by a short prose section on why it matters. A single principle section before the scenarios. Then four short scenario sections, each with its own bulleted action list sized to two marks. Limb (c) as two separate bulleted lists, DOC then SMC, closing on the direction of authority.
