blocks.h: 1. (a) The general obligation, and what makes Part XII unusual

blocks.p: The environmental provisions are in Part XII, and it opens with one of the shortest and most important sentences in the Convention. Article 192: States have the obligation to protect and preserve the marine environment.
Three things make that opening unusual and each is worth a mark:

ul: It is a free-standing obligation, not a limitation on a right. It is owed by every State, everywhere, and it is not confined to any zone. The zones in limb (b) allocate rights; article 192 imposes a duty that runs across all of them.

The sovereign right to exploit natural resources is expressly made subject to it. A State may exploit its resources pursuant to its environmental policies, but in accordance with its duty to protect and preserve - so development and protection are not balanced against one another; the second conditions the first.

Article 194 turns the duty into an obligation of conduct. States shall take all measures necessary to prevent, reduce and control pollution of the marine environment from any source, using the best practicable means at their disposal and in accordance with their capabilities - a standard that is demanding and differentiated at the same time - and shall ensure that activities under their jurisdiction or control do not cause damage by pollution to other States and their environment.

blocks.h: 2. (a) The sources of pollution, and the rule-making pattern

blocks.p: Part XII then works through pollution source by source: land-based sources including rivers, estuaries, pipelines and outfalls; seabed activities under national jurisdiction and activities in the Area; dumping; vessels; and the atmosphere. A separate article addresses the use of technologies and the intentional or accidental introduction of alien or new species - which is the treaty root of the ballast water regime.
The pattern running through them is the highlight a marine engineer should name, because it explains the whole architecture of his own professional world:

ul: UNCLOS sets the duty and delegates the detail. For pollution from vessels, States act through the competent international organization or general diplomatic conference to establish international rules and standards - which is UNCLOS pointing at IMO without naming it.
National law must be no less effective than those internationally agreed rules and standards. That is the hinge by which MARPOL and the rest reach the ship.
The rules are to be re-examined from time to time, so the framework is built to be updated rather than fixed.
States must not transfer damage or hazards from one area to another, or transform one type of pollution into another - the provision that forbids solving a problem by moving it.

blocks.p: This is why UNCLOS is properly called the constitution for the oceans: it does not contain a single discharge limit, and every discharge limit exists because of it.
The most original contribution of Part XII, and the one that reaches the ship most directly, is that it distributes enforcement between three States:

ul: The flag State shall ensure compliance by vessels flying its flag with the applicable international rules and standards, shall adopt laws and take other measures for their implementation, and shall provide for effective enforcement irrespective of where a violation occurs.

The port State may, where a vessel is voluntarily within its port or at an offshore terminal, undertake investigations and institute proceedings in respect of a discharge from that vessel outside its own internal waters, territorial sea or exclusive economic zone. This is the striking one: it is jurisdiction over a violation that did not happen in the port State's waters at all, and it is the treaty foundation of modern port State control.

The coastal State may institute proceedings in respect of violations occurring within its territorial sea or exclusive economic zone, with powers graded by the seriousness of the violation and the evidence available - from requiring information, through inspection, to detention.

Beyond all of them, after a maritime casualty a State may take and enforce measures beyond the territorial sea proportionate to the actual or threatened damage, to protect its coastline and related interests.
States are responsible for the fulfilment of their international obligations concerning protection and preservation of the marine environment and shall be liable in accordance with international law.

They must also ensure that recourse is available under their legal systems for prompt and adequate compensation in respect of pollution damage caused by persons under their jurisdiction - which is the treaty basis on which the civil liability conventions were later built.

The enforcement powers are not unqualified. Part XII contains its own safeguards limiting how they may be exercised, which is what prevents an environmental power from becoming an unlimited right to interfere with navigation.
The Part also requires monitoring, environmental assessment, scientific and technical cooperation and assistance to developing States - obligations of capacity as well as of restraint.

blocks.p: A belt of sea adjacent to the coast, extending beyond the land territory and internal waters, over which the coastal State has full sovereignty - extending also to the air space above it and to its bed and subsoil - exercised subject to the Convention and to other rules of international law.

Breadth: up to 12 nautical miles, measured from the baselines. The one qualification that must be stated, because it is what distinguishes this zone from land territory: sovereignty here is subject to the right of innocent passage of ships of all States.
A zone contiguous to the territorial sea in which the coastal State does not have sovereignty, but may exercise the control necessary to:

ul: prevent infringement of its customs, fiscal, immigration or sanitary laws and regulations within its territory or territorial sea; and
punish infringement of those laws committed within its territory or territorial sea.

blocks.p: Limit: may not extend beyond 24 nautical miles from the baselines. Two points carry the marks. The four subjects are exhaustive - it is not a general enforcement zone. And the control is referable to the land or territorial sea: it protects against infringements there, rather than creating new offences in the zone itself.
An area beyond and adjacent to the territorial sea, under a specific legal regime, extending not beyond 200 nautical miles from the baselines. The coastal State does not have sovereignty; it has:

ul: sovereign rights for exploring, exploiting, conserving and managing the natural resources, living and non-living, of the waters, the seabed and its subsoil, and for other economic activities such as the production of energy from the water, currents and winds;
jurisdiction over artificial islands, installations and structures, marine scientific research, and the protection and preservation of the marine environment.

blocks.p: Other States retain the freedoms of navigation and overflight and of laying submarine cables and pipelines. The distinction to state expressly: sovereign rights are resource rights, not sovereignty - a merchant ship navigates through an EEZ as of right.

The seabed and subsoil of the submarine areas extending beyond the territorial sea, throughout the natural prolongation of the land territory to the outer edge of the continental margin - or to 200 nautical miles from the baselines where the outer edge does not reach that far. The margin consists of the shelf, the slope and the rise, and does not include the deep ocean floor with its oceanic ridges. Where the margin does extend beyond 200 miles the entitlement is not open-ended: the outer limit must not exceed 350 nautical miles from the baselines, or 100 nautical miles from the 2,500 metre isobath, whichever line the coastal State establishes.
The coastal State has sovereign rights for exploring and exploiting its natural resources, and three features distinguish these rights from every other zone:

ul: they are exclusive - if the coastal State does not explore or exploit, no one else may without its express consent;
they do not depend on occupation, effective or notional, or on any express proclamation - they exist automatically;
they cover the seabed and subsoil only, not the water column above it, which is why the shelf and the EEZ are different things even where they occupy the same distance.

blocks.p: Defined by exclusion: all parts of the sea that are not included in the exclusive economic zone, the territorial sea or the internal waters of a State, or in the archipelagic waters of an archipelagic State.
They are open to all States, whether coastal or land-locked, and no State may validly claim sovereignty over any part of them. The freedoms comprise:

ol: freedom to lay submarine cables and pipelines;
freedom to construct artificial islands and other installations permitted under international law;

blocks.p: All are qualified in the same way, and the qualification is the mark: they shall be exercised with due regard for the interests of other States in their exercise of the same freedoms, and with due regard for rights relating to activities in the Area. A ship on the high seas is not beyond law - she is subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of her flag State, which is what makes the flag State's duties in limb (a) load-bearing.

The mark split has moved and it matters. Limb (a) is worth six here, not eight, and limb (b) is worth ten split into five separately weighted parts. The commonest way to lose marks on this question is to write a long essay on Part XII and then dispose of five zones in five lines. Reverse that instinct: the definitions are worth more than the essay, and each carries its own two marks.

Every zone in sections 5 to 9 is answered with the same three elements - the outer limit, what it is measured from, and the character of the coastal State's rights there. That consistency is deliberate. It makes each answer complete in about two marks' worth of writing, it makes them fast to produce under time pressure, and it forces the candidate to state the thing examiners actually test: that sovereignty, sovereign rights and control are three different strengths of entitlement.

Limb (a) is compressed to four themes - the obligation, the sources and rule-making pattern, enforcement, and liability. The enforcement theme is the one to protect if time runs short, because the three-way division is UNCLOS's own contribution and it is what connects the Convention to the candidate's working life.

ul: Over-writing limb (a) and under-writing limb (b). At this sitting the five definitions are worth ten of the sixteen marks.
Saying the coastal State has sovereignty over the EEZ. It has sovereign rights over resources and jurisdiction over three named matters - not sovereignty.
Giving the zone limits without saying what they are measured from. Every one of them runs from the baselines, and saying so is part of the definition.
Measuring the contiguous zone as 24 miles from the edge of the territorial sea. It is 24 miles from the baselines, so it is 12 miles wide where the territorial sea is 12.
Treating the continental shelf as a 200-mile rule. It is natural prolongation to the outer edge of the margin, with 200 miles as the entitlement where the margin falls short.
Confusing the shelf with the EEZ. The shelf is the seabed and subsoil; the EEZ includes the water column.
Defining the high seas positively. The Convention defines them by exclusion, and reproducing that is the cleanest two marks on the paper.
Forgetting the qualification on the high seas freedoms - due regard for the interests of other States.

Sovereignty, sovereign rights, jurisdiction and control are four different things. Territorial sea - sovereignty. EEZ and shelf - sovereign rights plus jurisdiction. Contiguous zone - control only, and only over four named subjects. Getting this ladder right is what the whole of limb (b) is testing.
The contiguous zone subjects are exhaustive - customs, fiscal, immigration, sanitary. It is not a general enforcement or security zone.
Continental shelf rights do not require proclamation. They exist automatically and are exclusive. This is a favourite oral question.
Port State enforcement under UNCLOS reaches discharges outside the port State's own waters. That is counter-intuitive and it is the treaty root of port State control.

UNCLOS contains no discharge limits. It obliges States to act through the competent international organization, and requires national law to be no less effective than the international rules. Naming that mechanism is worth more than any list.
Innocent passage qualifies sovereignty in the territorial sea. Omitting it makes the territorial sea sound like land.
The Convention is unamended. Do not attribute later instruments to it.
How wide is the territorial sea, and measured from what?
What may a coastal State do in the contiguous zone, and what may it not do?
Does a coastal State own the EEZ? What exactly does it have?
Your ship is transiting an EEZ. What rights does the coastal State have over you?
How can the continental shelf extend beyond 200 miles?
Define the high seas. Which court or State has jurisdiction over your ship there?
A discharge occurs on the high seas and you next call at Rotterdam. Can the Netherlands prosecute?
Where in UNCLOS does MARPOL get its authority from?

blocks.p: The zones are a ladder of decreasing entitlement measured from one datum: BASELINE - 12 - 24 - 200 - BEYOND, and the entitlement runs SOVEREIGNTY - CONTROL - SOVEREIGN RIGHTS - FREEDOM. For each zone say limit, datum, rights and stop. Limb (a) compresses to DUTY - SOURCES - ENFORCEMENT - LIABILITY, and inside enforcement, FLAG - PORT - COASTAL.

ul: UNCLOS 1982, in force 16 November 1994. Unamended.
Article 2 - sovereignty over the territorial sea, its air space, bed and subsoil. Article 3 - breadth up to 12 nautical miles from baselines.
Article 33 - contiguous zone; customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary control; not beyond 24 nautical miles from baselines.

Articles 55, 56 and 57 - the EEZ regime; sovereign rights over resources and jurisdiction over artificial islands, marine scientific research and protection of the marine environment; not beyond 200 nautical miles.
Articles 76 and 77 - the continental shelf; natural prolongation to the outer edge of the margin or 200 nautical miles; exclusive rights not dependent on proclamation.
Articles 86 and 87 - the high seas defined by exclusion, and the six freedoms exercised with due regard.

Part XII: 192 general obligation; 194 measures from any source, best practicable means; 196 technologies and alien or new species; 207 land-based; 210 dumping; 211 vessels, through the competent international organization; 212 atmosphere.
Articles 217, 218 and 220 - enforcement by flag, port and coastal States. Article 221 - measures after a maritime casualty. Article 235 - responsibility and liability.

Every article in this answer was read at source in this session from the corpus copy of the Convention, which is a born-digital publication with a full text layer. This is the most strongly evidenced question on the paper.

The detailed formulae in article 76 paragraphs 4 to 6, by which the outer edge of the margin is fixed beyond 200 nautical miles, were not read. No formula and no outer cap is quoted; the answer gives the entitlement and the natural-prolongation principle only.
Baseline construction was not read. The answer uses the Convention's own phrase, baselines determined in accordance with the Convention, and does not describe normal or straight baselines.
The Part XII section 7 safeguards on the exercise of enforcement powers are referred to generally; their individual articles were not read.

No claim is made about any particular State's declared zones, including India's.

questions.understand_first: The sea is not one legal space; it is a series of belts running outwards from the coast, and a country's grip loosens with every belt it crosses. Close in, the water is simply part of the country - the same authority applies there as ashore, with one important concession: foreign ships may pass through, provided they behave. A little further out there is a narrow band where the country is not in charge, but may still reach out to stop or punish smuggling, tax evasion, illegal entry and disease-related breaches connected with its own territory - and nothing else. Further out again is a much wider belt where the country's interest is economic rather than territorial: the fish, the oil, the wind and the seabed minerals are its to exploit and manage, but ships and aircraft still come and go freely, because the entitlement is over resources and not over the water. The seabed carries a separate story, because it belongs to the land it is geologically attached to, whether or not anyone claims it or works it. And beyond everything is water no country owns at all, where the only authority over a ship is the country whose flag she flies. Running across all of these belts is one duty that does not weaken with distance: every state must protect and preserve the marine environment. That is where the second half of the question sits, and the point to grasp is that this framework treaty contains no discharge limits, no equipment standards and no survey requirements. It obliges states to make those rules through a competent international body and then to enforce them - which is precisely why the detailed rules a marine engineer works to exist somewhere else entirely, and why they bind him at all.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Zones from the baseline: 12 territorial sea, 24 contiguous, 200 EEZ, then high seas. Entitlement weakens outwards - sovereignty (subject to innocent passage), control over customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary only, sovereign rights over resources plus jurisdiction over three matters, then freedom. Shelf = seabed and subsoil, natural prolongation or 200, exclusive and automatic. Limb (a): article 192 duty; rules made through the competent international organization; enforcement by flag, port and coastal States; responsibility and liability.
quick_revision.critical_numbers: 12 nautical miles - territorial sea. 24 nautical miles - contiguous zone. 200 nautical miles - EEZ, and the continental shelf entitlement where the margin falls short. All measured from the baselines. Six high seas freedoms. Four contiguous zone subjects - customs, fiscal, immigration, sanitary. 1982 concluded, 16 November 1994 in force.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: UNCLOS article 192 - States have the obligation to protect and preserve the marine environment. It is the shortest article that matters and the foundation of the whole of Part XII. Pair it with article 211, under which States act through the competent international organization to make the vessel-source rules - the two together explain why MARPOL exists and why it binds.
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying the coastal State has sovereignty over the exclusive economic zone. It has sovereign rights over resources and jurisdiction over three named matters, and other States keep the freedoms of navigation and overflight. Sovereignty, sovereign rights, jurisdiction and control are four different strengths of entitlement, and limb (b) is really a test of whether you can tell them apart.

retrieval_cards.answer: Limb (a): 1 the general obligation under article 192; 2 the sources of pollution and the rule-making pattern; 3 enforcement by flag, port and coastal States; 4 responsibility, liability and the safeguards. Limb (b): 5 territorial sea; 6 contiguous zone; 7 exclusive economic zone; 8 continental shelf; 9 high seas.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the four maritime limits and what they are measured from.
retrieval_cards.answer: Territorial sea up to 12 nautical miles; contiguous zone not beyond 24 nautical miles; exclusive economic zone not beyond 200 nautical miles; continental shelf to the outer edge of the continental margin or 200 nautical miles where the margin falls short. All are measured from the baselines determined in accordance with the Convention - not from the coast and not from the edge of the previous zone.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Sovereignty, control, sovereign rights - which zone has which?
retrieval_cards.answer: Territorial sea: full sovereignty, including air space, bed and subsoil, subject to innocent passage. Contiguous zone: no sovereignty, only the control necessary over customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary matters referable to the territory or territorial sea. EEZ and continental shelf: sovereign rights over resources plus jurisdiction over named matters. High seas: no sovereignty at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What may a coastal State do in the contiguous zone?
retrieval_cards.answer: Exercise the control necessary to prevent infringement of its customs, fiscal, immigration or sanitary laws and regulations within its territory or territorial sea, and to punish infringement of those laws committed there. The four subjects are exhaustive - it is not a general enforcement or security zone - and the control is referable to breaches connected with the land or territorial sea rather than to conduct in the zone itself.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What exactly does a coastal State have in the EEZ?
retrieval_cards.answer: Sovereign rights for exploring, exploiting, conserving and managing the natural resources - living and non-living - of the waters, the seabed and its subsoil, and for other economic activities such as producing energy from water, currents and winds. Plus jurisdiction over artificial islands, installations and structures, marine scientific research, and protection and preservation of the marine environment. Not sovereignty: navigation and overflight remain free.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the continental shelf differ from the EEZ?
retrieval_cards.answer: The shelf is the seabed and subsoil only, not the water column. It runs through the natural prolongation of the land territory to the outer edge of the continental margin, or 200 miles where the margin falls short. Its rights are exclusive - nobody may explore or exploit without express consent - and they do not depend on occupation or on any proclamation, so they exist automatically.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define the high seas and give the freedoms.
retrieval_cards.answer: All parts of the sea not included in the exclusive economic zone, the territorial sea or internal waters of a State, or in archipelagic waters - a definition by exclusion. Open to all States, coastal or land-locked, with no valid claim of sovereignty. Six freedoms: navigation, overflight, submarine cables and pipelines, artificial islands and installations, fishing, and scientific research - all exercised with due regard for the interests of other States.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does MARPOL get its authority from in UNCLOS?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 192 imposes the general obligation to protect and preserve the marine environment, and article 211 requires States, acting through the competent international organization or general diplomatic conference, to establish international rules and standards for vessel-source pollution, with national law to be no less effective than those rules. UNCLOS itself contains no discharge limit; it creates the duty and delegates the detail.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A discharge occurs outside any State's waters and the ship later calls at a foreign port. Can that port State act?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. Where a vessel is voluntarily within its port or at an offshore terminal, the port State may investigate and, where the evidence warrants, institute proceedings in respect of a discharge from that vessel outside its own internal waters, territorial sea or exclusive economic zone, in violation of applicable international rules and standards. This is the treaty foundation of port State control.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs testing quite different things. Limb (a) tests whether the candidate understands that UNCLOS is a framework rather than a rulebook - that it creates duties and allocates enforcement without setting a single discharge limit. Limb (b) tests precision: five zones, each with a limit, a datum and a character of entitlement, and the real discriminator is whether the candidate can distinguish sovereignty from sovereign rights from control. Five separately weighted definitions is an invitation to be exact rather than discursive.

blocks.h: 1. Where the port State's power comes from, and what it is not

blocks.p: Port State control is the inspection of foreign ships in national ports to verify that the condition of the ship and her equipment, and the competence of her crew, comply with the requirements of the international conventions. Two propositions frame the whole answer and should be stated first:

ul: It is a safety net beneath the flag State, not a substitute for it. It does not transfer flag State duty and it does not certify the ship. The flag State remains responsible for her.

The power is conferred by the conventions themselves, each of which carries its own control article - SOLAS regulation I/19, MARPOL articles 5 and 6, Load Lines article 21, STCW article X, TONNAGE article 12, AFS article 11, BWM article 9 - with UNCLOS above them all, under which a State may act against a vessel voluntarily within its port. The consolidated IMO Procedures for Port State Control then bring the practice together, and regional memoranda of understanding organise it. India is a member of the Indian Ocean MOU, and inspections are carried out under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 by the Directorate General of Shipping.

blocks.h: 2. The problem all three limbs exist to solve

blocks.p: A treaty binds only its Parties, and it applies only to the ships it says it applies to. Left there, the system would contain two enormous holes:

ul: a State could decline to ratify and its ships would trade the same routes free of the standards everyone else pays for; and
a ship could sit below a convention's size threshold and carry no certificate at all.

blocks.p: In both cases the ship would be advantaged by not being covered. That is the free-rider problem, and the three limbs of this question are the three answers to it: limb (i) removes the value of a non-Party's paperwork, limb (ii) removes the exemption of small ships from scrutiny, and limb (iii) is the principle that makes both of them work.

blocks.h: 3. (i) Certificates issued by non-party States to their ships

blocks.p: A non-Party flag State may perfectly well issue its own ships documents that look like convention certificates - and often does, because its ships must be accepted commercially. The port State's position on them rests on one point of treaty law:

ul: A convention certificate has treaty standing only because the issuing State is bound by the treaty. The certificate's legal force comes from the Convention, not from the paper. A State that is not a Party has no authority under the Convention to issue anything under it.
It follows that a certificate issued by a non-Party is not a convention certificate, whatever it is headed, and the port State does not accept it as having the status of one.

In particular it is not accepted as prima facie evidence of the ship's condition. For a Party's ship a valid certificate is normally accepted at face value and inspection stops there unless there are clear grounds; for a non-Party's ship that presumption does not arise at all.

The port State is not obliged to reject the document either. It may be examined for what it is worth as information - it may record a survey that was actually carried out - but it carries no entitlement.

blocks.h: 4. (i) What the officer actually does with such a ship

ul: He proceeds directly to a more detailed inspection, without needing clear grounds, because the trigger that would normally be required - a doubt about a valid certificate - has no application where there is no valid certificate.
He satisfies himself that the condition of the ship and her equipment, and the manning, are substantially equivalent to what the Convention would require of a Party's ship of that description.
The burden sits differently. On a Party's ship the officer must find something wrong; on a non-Party's ship the ship must show that she is up to standard.

If she is not, the port State takes the same action it would take against any ship - up to and including detention where the deficiencies are clearly hazardous to safety, health or the environment - and reports accordingly.
The practical consequence for the operator is severe and worth stating: a non-Party ship attracts a fuller inspection, more often, and her paperwork buys her nothing. That is the intended effect.

blocks.h: 5. (ii) Inspection of ships below convention size

blocks.p: Every convention has a threshold of application. In broad terms - and these are the figures a candidate should be able to give - SOLAS certification applies to cargo ships of 500 gross tonnage and upwards on international voyages; the Load Lines Convention to ships of 24 metres in length and upwards; MARPOL Annex I to oil tankers of 150 gross tonnage and above and other ships of 400 gross tonnage and above; and the Tonnage Convention to ships of 24 metres and upwards. A ship below the relevant threshold does not carry the corresponding certificate, and she is not in breach for not carrying it.
The provisions made are therefore these:

ul: The port State cannot demand a certificate the Convention does not require. An officer who detains a ship for the absence of a document she was never obliged to hold has exceeded his authority, and this is the first thing to say.

But he is not disabled from inspecting her. He may satisfy himself that the ship does not present a hazard to safety, health or the environment, which is a condition-based judgement rather than a documentary one.

The reference standard becomes national and regional. The flag State's own national requirements for a ship of that size apply, together with any applicable regional memorandum procedures and the port State's own law - in India, the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and the rules under it.

And the principle in limb (iii) reaches her. A ship below convention size must not be treated more favourably than a ship above it: being small is a reason for a different documentary regime, never a reason for a lower standard of safety.
Where she is found hazardous, the port State acts. The power to prevent an unsafe ship from proceeding to sea does not depend on which certificate she does or does not hold.

blocks.p: This is the principle the other two limbs depend on, and it should be stated in the conventions' own terms: Parties shall apply the requirements of the Convention as may be necessary to ensure that no more favourable treatment is given to the ships of non-Parties.
It is not a single provision but a repeated provision, written into instrument after instrument:

ul: MARPOL article 5(4);
The 1988 SOLAS Protocol, article I(3);
STCW article X(5);

MLC 2006 Article V(7), which puts it most plainly - a Member must ensure that ships flying the flag of a State that has not ratified do not receive more favourable treatment than ships flying the flag of a State that has;
and the same obligation appears in the later environmental conventions and is reflected in the III Code's port State provisions and in the IMO Procedures for Port State Control.

blocks.p: Three points complete the limb:

ul: It reaches two classes of ship, not one. Non-Party ships and below-size ships. Candidates almost always give the first and omit the second, and the second is half the principle.
It is an obligation on the port State, not a right. The wording is that Parties shall apply the requirements as necessary. A port State that waved a non-Party ship through would itself be in breach.

Its purpose is to remove the commercial advantage of staying outside. If non-ratification bought cheaper operation, ratification would be a competitive disadvantage and the conventions would unravel. This provision is what makes the whole system self-supporting, and it is why a ship cannot escape a convention by choosing a flag.

blocks.p: Set out as a single mechanism, which is what a good answer does at this point:

ul: The principle in limb (iii) says the standard must be applied regardless of flag or size.
Limb (i) is how that is done where the ship has paperwork with no legal standing - discount the paper and inspect the substance.
Limb (ii) is how it is done where there is no paperwork to have - inspect the substance against national and regional requirements instead.
In both cases the answer is the same: the port State stops relying on documents and looks at the ship. That single sentence is the heart of the question.

blocks.h: 8. The practical limits, and the position at this sitting

ul: The port State applies the convention standard; it does not make the ship a Party's ship. It cannot issue a convention certificate to a non-Party's ship, and it cannot confer status.
The jurisdiction is territorial and occasion-based. It bites while the ship is voluntarily in the port or at an offshore terminal; it is not a roving power over the flag.

Inspection must not be an instrument of discrimination. The requirement is that a non-Party ship is treated no more favourably - not that she is treated worse, and not that she is harassed. The standard applied is the convention standard, no higher.
Undue delay attracts a remedy. Where a ship is unduly detained or delayed she is entitled to compensation for loss or damage suffered, which is the balancing provision on the whole regime.

At this sitting the consolidated procedures in force are the 2021 edition adopted by the 32nd Assembly - resolution A.1155(32). The 33rd Assembly's revision was adopted on 6 December 2023, three months after this examination, and must not be cited here.

blocks.p: The proposition to close on: a convention binds its Parties, but port State control applies its standard to everyone in the port. Limbs (i) and (ii) are the two ways the gap is closed, and limb (iii) is the reason it must be.

The examiner has printed three named parts inside one sentence and attached sixteen marks to the whole. That is an invitation to answer three questions and a trap for candidates who write a general essay on port State control - clear grounds, detention, the appeal - none of which is asked here. Sections 3 to 6 answer the three limbs in the printed order and are the marks; sections 1 and 2 are short because they are only framing.

Section 2 is worth the twenty seconds it costs. Stating the free-rider problem before the limbs means each limb then reads as a solution to a stated problem rather than as a recited rule, and it sets up section 7, where the three are drawn back together into one mechanism. Section 7 is where a good answer separates itself: any candidate can define no more favourable treatment, and few connect it to the two operational limbs that implement it.

Limb (iii) is given slightly more space than the other two even though the marks are undivided, because it is the principle the others depend on and because it is the limb where the two-class point - non-Party ships and below-size ships - earns a mark that most candidates leave behind.

ul: Writing a general port State control essay. Clear grounds, detainable deficiencies, the Detention Review Panel and the right of appeal are not asked for and earn nothing here.
Saying a non-Party certificate is simply rejected or is worthless. It has no treaty standing, which is a different and more precise thing - it may still be examined for what it says.
Forgetting that no more favourable treatment covers below-size ships as well as non-Party ships. This is the single most commonly missed mark in the question.
Saying a below-size ship cannot be inspected. She can - on condition rather than on documents.
Saying a below-size ship can be detained for not holding a certificate. She cannot; she was never required to hold it.
Treating no more favourable treatment as a right of the port State. It is an obligation on it.
Describing port State control as replacing flag State responsibility.
Citing the 2023 edition of the Procedures. See the traps.

The procedures in force at this sitting are A.1155(32), adopted by the 32nd Assembly in December 2021. A.1185(33) was adopted 6 December 2023, three months AFTER this paper, and revoked A.1155(32). Every piece of study material written for a 2024 or later sitting carries the later number.
No more favourable treatment reaches two classes of ship. Non-Party flags and below-size ships. Saying only the first is a half answer.
It is an obligation, not a permission. The conventions say Parties shall apply the requirements as necessary.
A non-Party's certificate is not a convention certificate - because the Convention is the only thing that could give it force, and the issuing State is not bound by it.
Clear grounds are not needed for a non-Party ship. The clear-grounds threshold protects a ship with a valid certificate; there is no valid certificate to protect.
No more favourable treatment does not mean less favourable. The convention standard is applied, not a higher one, and the ship must not be harassed.
Undue delay carries a right to compensation. Mentioning it shows the balance in the regime and it is a natural oral follow-up.
A ship arrives flying the flag of a State that is not party to SOLAS, with a safety equipment certificate. What do you do with it?
Do you need clear grounds before a detailed inspection of that ship?
Where is no more favourable treatment actually written? Give me two conventions.
Which ships does the principle apply to besides non-Party ships?
A 300 gross tonnage coaster has no Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate. Can you detain her for it?
So can you inspect her at all, and against what?
Which Assembly resolution contains the port State control procedures, and when was it adopted?
Your ship is detained and the deficiency turns out to be unfounded. What remedy do you have?

blocks.p: The whole question compresses to one line: a convention binds its Parties, but port State control applies its standard to everyone in the port. Then PAPER - NO PAPER - PRINCIPLE: limb (i) is the ship with paperwork that means nothing, limb (ii) is the ship with no paperwork to have, and limb (iii) is the rule that says neither may profit by it. In both operational limbs the answer is identical - stop reading documents, look at the ship.

ul: SOLAS regulation I/19 - control. MARPOL articles 5 and 6. Load Lines article 21. STCW article X. TONNAGE article 12. AFS article 11. BWM article 9 - each convention's own control article.
UNCLOS articles 217, 218 and 220 - flag, port and coastal State enforcement; article 218 is the port State's treaty jurisdiction over a ship voluntarily in port.
MARPOL article 5(4) - no more favourable treatment for ships of non-Parties.
1988 SOLAS Protocol article I(3) and STCW article X(5) - the same obligation.
MLC 2006 Article V(7) - the clearest statement of the principle.
III Code, A.1070(28), port State section - the principle in the audit standard.
Resolution A.1155(32) - the Procedures for Port State Control operative at this sitting. Named only; no clause cited.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - the Indian statute under which port State control is exercised at this sitting; India is a member of the Indian Ocean MOU.

questions.understand_first: A treaty only binds the countries that have signed up to it, and it only covers the ships it says it covers. Both of those are perfectly ordinary features of international law, and together they would wreck the whole system of ship safety if nothing were done about them. Think about why. If a country simply declines to join, its ships carry no obligations under the treaty - yet they load at the same berths and compete for the same cargoes as ships that have paid for compliance. And if a treaty only applies above a certain size, a ship just under that size carries no certificates at all. In both cases the ship that is outside the rules is cheaper to run than the ship inside them, and once that is true, joining becomes a commercial mistake and the treaties start to empty out. So the conventions carry a repeated clause that closes the hole from the other end. It does not try to bind the non-member country, which no treaty can do. Instead it puts a duty on the ports: when such a ship turns up, you must not give her an easier time than you would give a ship that is properly covered. That flips the incentive completely - staying outside no longer saves anything, and may cost more, because the ship gets looked at harder. The two practical situations follow directly. A ship from a non-member country may well be carrying official-looking certificates, but they cannot be convention certificates, because only the convention could give them that force and her flag is not bound by it. A small ship may be carrying nothing at all, quite properly. In neither case can the inspector do what he normally does, which is read the documents and stop there. In both he has to do the harder thing: look at the ship.
questions.memory_cue: One line: a convention binds its Parties, but port State control applies its standard to everyone in the port. Then PAPER - NO PAPER - PRINCIPLE, mapping to the route steps (3 and 4), (5) and (6), with framing at (1) and (2), the synthesis at (7) and the limits at (8). In both operational limbs the action is the same: stop reading documents, look at the ship.

steps.title: Where the port State's power comes from, and what it is not
points: Inspection of foreign ships in national ports against the conventions
A safety net beneath the flag State - it does not transfer flag State duty and does not certify the ship
Each convention carries its own control article - SOLAS I/19, MARPOL 5 and 6, Load Lines 21, STCW X, TONNAGE 12, AFS 11, BWM 9
UNCLOS above them - jurisdiction over a vessel voluntarily within the port
The consolidated IMO Procedures, and regional memoranda; India in the Indian Ocean MOU under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958

steps.title: The problem all three limbs exist to solve
points: A treaty binds only its Parties and applies only to the ships it covers
A State could decline to ratify and its ships would trade free of the standards
A ship could sit below a size threshold and carry no certificate
In both cases the ship is advantaged by not being covered - the free-rider problem
The three limbs are the three answers to it

steps.title: (i) Certificates issued by non-party States to their ships
points: A convention certificate has treaty standing only because the issuing State is bound by the treaty
A non-Party has no authority under the Convention to issue anything under it
So the document is not a convention certificate whatever it is headed
It is NOT accepted as prima facie evidence of the ship's condition
It is not rejected outright either - it may be examined for what it says, but it carries no entitlement

steps.title: (i) What the officer actually does with such a ship
points: Proceeds to a more detailed inspection without needing clear grounds
Satisfies himself the ship, equipment and manning are substantially equivalent to the convention standard
The burden shifts - the ship must show she is up to standard
Detention where deficiencies are clearly hazardous, as for any ship
The practical effect - fuller inspection, more often, and the paperwork buys nothing

steps.title: (ii) Inspection of ships below convention size
points: Thresholds - SOLAS certification from 500 GT, Load Lines from 24 m, MARPOL Annex I from 150 GT for oil tankers and 400 GT otherwise, TONNAGE from 24 m
The port State cannot demand a certificate the Convention does not require
But it may satisfy itself that the ship does not present a hazard - a condition judgement, not a documentary one
The reference standard becomes the flag State's national requirements, regional MoU procedures and the port State's own law
No more favourable treatment reaches her - small is a different documentary regime, never a lower safety standard
The power to stop an unsafe ship does not depend on which certificate she holds

steps.title: (iii) No more favourable treatment
points: Parties shall apply the requirements as may be necessary to ensure no more favourable treatment is given to ships of non-Parties
Not one provision but a repeated one - MARPOL 5(4), 1988 SOLAS Protocol I(3), STCW X(5), MLC Article V(7)
Reflected in the III Code's port State provisions and in the IMO Procedures
It reaches TWO classes - non-Party ships AND below-size ships
It is an obligation on the port State, not a right
Its purpose is to remove the commercial advantage of staying outside - a ship cannot escape a convention by choosing a flag

steps.title: How the three interlock
points: The principle says the standard applies regardless of flag or size
Limb (i) is how that is done where the paperwork has no legal standing - discount the paper, inspect the substance
Limb (ii) is how it is done where there is no paperwork to have - inspect against national and regional requirements
In both, the port State stops relying on documents and looks at the ship

steps.title: The practical limits, and the position at this sitting
points: The port State applies the standard; it cannot confer status or issue a convention certificate
Jurisdiction is territorial and occasion-based - while the ship is voluntarily in port
No more favourable does not mean less favourable - the convention standard, no higher, and no harassment
Undue delay or detention carries a right to compensation
The procedures in force are A.1155(32) of the 32nd Assembly; the 33rd Assembly revision is three months future

quick_revision.recall_15s: A convention binds its Parties, but port State control applies its standard to everyone in the port. (i) A non-Party's certificate is not a convention certificate - no treaty standing, no prima facie effect, so a detailed inspection without needing clear grounds and the ship must show she is up to standard. (ii) A below-size ship cannot be required to hold a certificate she was never obliged to have, but she can be inspected on condition against national and regional requirements. (iii) No more favourable treatment - MARPOL 5(4), 1988 SOLAS Protocol I(3), STCW X(5), MLC V(7) - reaches both classes and is an obligation, not a right.
quick_revision.critical_numbers: 500 GT - SOLAS cargo ship certification threshold. 24 m - Load Lines and Tonnage. 150 GT oil tankers and 400 GT other ships - MARPOL Annex I. A.1155(32), December 2021 - the Procedures in force at this sitting; A.1185(33), 6 December 2023, is three months future. Three limbs, two classes of ship reached by the principle.
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL article 5(4) - Parties shall apply the requirements of the Convention as may be necessary to ensure that no more favourable treatment is given to the ships of non-Parties. It is the cleanest single statement of the principle and the one to quote, with MLC Article V(7) as the plainest-worded companion.
quick_revision.major_trap: Citing A.1185(33) for the port State control procedures. It was adopted 6 December 2023, three months AFTER this sitting, and it revoked A.1155(32), which is the operative edition here. The corpus's own holding on this subject is the 2023 set and nothing earlier, so the wrong edition is the easiest thing on this paper to reach for. The companion trap is giving no more favourable treatment as applying only to non-Party ships and forgetting below-size ships.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the port State control provisions question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 where the power comes from and what PSC is not; 2 the free-rider problem the three limbs solve; 3 non-Party certificates and their standing; 4 what the officer does with such a ship; 5 inspection of below-size ships; 6 no more favourable treatment; 7 how the three interlock; 8 the practical limits and the edition in force.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the status of a certificate issued by a non-Party State to its own ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is not a convention certificate, whatever it is headed, because a convention certificate has treaty standing only where the issuing State is bound by the treaty - and a non-Party has no authority under the Convention to issue anything under it. It is therefore not accepted as prima facie evidence of the ship's condition, though it may be examined for what it says.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A ship of a non-Party flag arrives in port. What does the PSCO do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Proceeds to a more detailed inspection without needing clear grounds - the clear-grounds threshold exists to protect a ship with a valid certificate and there is none here. He satisfies himself that the ship, her equipment and her manning are substantially equivalent to what the Convention would require of a Party's ship. The burden shifts: the ship must show she is up to standard.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A 300 gross tonnage coaster holds no Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate. Can you detain her for it?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. She is below the convention threshold and was never required to hold it, so detaining her for its absence exceeds the officer's authority. But she may still be inspected on condition - to satisfy the port State that she does not present a hazard - against the flag State's national requirements, regional MoU procedures and the port State's own law.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the no more favourable treatment principle and where it is written.
retrieval_cards.answer: Parties shall apply the requirements of the Convention as may be necessary to ensure that no more favourable treatment is given to the ships of non-Parties. It is a repeated provision - MARPOL article 5(4), the 1988 SOLAS Protocol article I(3), STCW article X(5), and MLC 2006 Article V(7) - and it is reflected in the III Code's port State provisions and in the IMO Procedures for Port State Control.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which ships does no more favourable treatment apply to?
retrieval_cards.answer: Two classes, not one: ships flying the flag of a non-Party, AND ships below convention size. Candidates almost always give the first and omit the second, and the second is half the principle. In both cases the point is that the ship must not be treated more favourably than a ship that is fully covered - being outside the treaty is never an advantage.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which edition of the port State control procedures applies at a September 2023 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: A.1155(32), adopted by the 32nd Assembly in December 2021. NOT A.1185(33) - that was adopted 6 December 2023, three months after the sitting, and revoked A.1155(32); and not A.1206(34), of December 2025. Material written for any later sitting carries a later number, and it is the easiest wrong citation to make on this paper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is no more favourable treatment a right of the port State?
retrieval_cards.answer: No - it is an obligation on it. The conventions say Parties SHALL apply the requirements as may be necessary to ensure no more favourable treatment is given. A port State that waved a non-Party ship through would itself be in breach. Equally it does not permit LESS favourable treatment: the convention standard is applied, no higher, and the ship must not be harassed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does a port State's power to inspect a foreign ship come from?
retrieval_cards.answer: From the conventions themselves, each carrying its own control article - SOLAS regulation I/19, MARPOL articles 5 and 6, Load Lines article 21, STCW article X, Tonnage article 12, AFS article 11, BWM article 9 - with UNCLOS above them, under which a State may act against a vessel voluntarily within its port or at an offshore terminal. The IMO Procedures consolidate the practice and regional memoranda organise it.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three named parts of the port State control regime, deliberately chosen and deliberately not the usual ones. The examiner has avoided clear grounds, detention and appeal entirely and asked instead about the edges of the system - the ship whose flag is outside the treaty and the ship that is too small for it. What is really being tested is whether the candidate understands that a convention binds only its Parties and covers only what it says, and that port State control is the mechanism by which that limitation is prevented from destroying the system. A candidate who does not see the free-rider problem answers three unconnected questions.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Sixteen marks printed against the stem with the three parts run inline and no mark against any of them. The three are treated as of comparable weight, with limb (iii) given a little more room because it is the principle the other two implement and because it carries the two-class point that is the most commonly dropped mark. Framing is kept short - two brief sections - so that the three named limbs take the great majority of the answer.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That a non-Party's certificate is described as lacking treaty standing rather than as being simply rejected, and that the consequence for the inspection is stated. That a below-size ship is recognised as properly certificate-free but still inspectable on condition. That the principle is quoted in the conventions' own language and attributed to at least two instruments. And, above all, that no more favourable treatment is recognised as reaching below-size ships as well as non-Party ships.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: Anchor the jurisdictional foundation on UNCLOS articles 217, 218 and 220, read at source in this session for this paper's Q8. Take the control articles of the individual conventions and the no-more-favourable-treatment provisions - MARPOL 5(4), 1988 SOLAS Protocol I(3), STCW X(5) - from the MIW verification record for QP2606 Q2, and MLC Article V(7) from the QP2403 and QP2510 records. Reason limbs (i) and (ii) from the conventions' own logic, no corpus question supplying them. State the size thresholds as authoritative secondary and flag them. Deliberately NOT planned: any clause number from any edition of the IMO Procedures, and any use of the corpus PSC folder, whose entire contents post-date this sitting.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - The treaty layer is completely stable - the control articles and the no-more-favourable-treatment provisions are decades old and unchanged - but the consolidated procedural guidance was revised three months after this sitting and revised again two years later, so there are two later editions to avoid and the corpus holds one of them and not the operative one. The mitigation is structural: the answer rests on the treaty provisions, which did not move, and names the operative Procedures without quoting any part of them.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: HIGH by the standards of this paper, and it is the subject rather than a hazard. The whole question is about the boundary of treaty obligation: who is bound, who is covered, and what a State may do about a ship that is neither. Three errors must be avoided - describing port State control as replacing flag State responsibility; suggesting that a port State can confer convention status on a non-Party's ship; and suggesting that a port State may require of a below-size ship a document the convention does not require. For an Indian port the power is exercised under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 at this sitting, with India in the Indian Ocean MOU.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: 'Provisions are made under Port State Control' is loose - port State control is a practice rather than an instrument, and the provisions are in the conventions and in the consolidated Procedures. The answer reads it as asking what the regime does about each of the three matters and says where each rule lives. 'Below convention size' is not defined and differs by convention, which is why the answer gives several thresholds rather than one. The stem prints 'favorable' in American spelling and inline sub-limbs without marks; both are preserved. Note also that limb (i) and limb (iii) could be read as the same question - they are not, and keeping them apart is part of the answer.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections following the printed limb order, with two short framing sections first and a synthesis section before the close. Prose for the treaty-standing argument in limb (i), which is a piece of reasoning rather than a list, and bulleted lists everywhere else so that each provision and each consequence is separately countable. The three limbs are drawn together explicitly in section 7 rather than left as three parallel answers.
